body:
## Summary

Dense self-attention cut of the MiniMax-H3 video DiT, targeting SM120 (RTX 5090 / RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell):

- dense, non-causal, BF16, 56 heads, head_dim 128, batch 1, packed token count `S` (dynamic, 1 .. 131072)
- inputs/outputs are contiguous BF16 `[S, 7168]` rows (element `[t, h * 128 + d]`); the NHD `[S, 56, 128]` view is zero-copy
- the query is pre-scaled in BF16 (`bf16(1/sqrt(128)) = 0.08837890625`, product rounded before softmax) and attention runs with `sm_scale=1.0`
- representative `S` values from the model's request types (T2VA / FL2VA / REF2VA at 124 and 345 frames, normal and SR-base resolutions): 15493, 17147, 30224, 37804, 41870, 42554, 44208, 52535, 57287, 104060, 108126, 118793

### Fused route: `flashinfer.diffusion_ops.minimax_h3_dense_attention`

One runtime-variable kernel does the row<->head re-layout, the BF16 query scale and the attention for any `1 <= S <= 131072`:

- `csrc/cake_minimax_h3_dense_attention_sm120a.cu`: generated SM120 device code (FA2-style 64x64 tiles, 128 threads, TMA tile loads with 128B swizzle, `ldmatrix` + `mma.sync` m16n8k16, exp2 online softmax, single-stage K/V buffers, register-resident scaled Q tile, deferred softmax denominator reduction, persistent head-major work loop, TMA zero-fill for `S < 64`, key mask on the last tile) plus the TVM-FFI host entry (tensor-map encoding, launch plan). It also compiles for SM90a/SM100a/SM103a so the route can be validated there; SM120 is the performance target.
- `flashinfer/jit/cake_minimax_h3_dense_attention.py` (JIT spec), `flashinfer/diffusion_ops/cake_minimax_h3_dense_attention.py` (custom op `flashinfer::minimax_h3_dense_attention`, `minimax_h3_dense_attention(q, k, v, out=None, *, ctas_per_sm=2)`)
- `tests/diffusion_ops/test_minimax_h3_dense_attention.py`: FP32-oracle checks at S = 1, 63, 64, 65, 128, 257, 1023, 4097 (`atol=rtol=1e-2` and the request's fixed `atol=0.01, rtol=0.02`), pre-allocated output / `ctas_per_sm=1`, argument validation.

### Benchmark: `benchmarks/bench_minimax_h3_dense_attention.py`

Times the fused route (`cake`), `single_prefill_with_kv_cache` (`auto`, which routes to `fmha_v2` on SM120, and `fa2`) and PyTorch SDPA (`efficient` / `cudnn` / `flash`) at the same boundary (the BF16 Q-scale launch is included, host transfers are not), with CUPTI cold-L2 timing, and checks every backend against a chunked FP32 oracle.

title: feat: add CuTe-DSL backend for layernorm_quant
body:
## 📌 Description

`layernorm_quant` is the only norm quant routine still running on the first-generation CUDA kernel only; `rmsnorm_quant` and `fused_add_rmsnorm_quant` already default to CuTe-DSL kernels. This PR ports `layernorm_quant` to CuTe-DSL and wires it as the default backend, with the CUDA kernel kept as the `FLASHINFER_USE_CUDA_NORM` fallback.

The new `LayerNormQuantKernel` derives from `RMSNormQuantKernel` (multi-row tiles, cluster reduction, cp.async staging, vectorized fp8 stores for both e4m3 and e5m2), with three deltas:

- LayerNorm needs two reductions (mean, then variance). The cluster path reuses a single mbarrier by waiting on phase 0 and then phase 1, with a cluster barrier in between; `cluster_reduce_multirow` and `row_reduce_sum_multirow` gain an optional `phase` parameter (additive, existing callers unchanged).
- gamma/beta are float32 while the input tile is fp16/bf16, so they are loaded through a dedicated tiled copy whose value mode is split into 128-bit pieces, keeping the fragment flat order aligned with the input fragment. Per-element scalar loads would serialize on L2 latency and dominate the kernel time (0.63 TB/s at batch 1024, H=8192, versus 1.48 TB/s with a constant-gamma control). Partial (non power of two) tiles keep predicated scalar loads.
- Tile tail columns are masked out of both reductions; cp.async does not zero-fill predicated-off columns, and `diff = -mean` at padded positions would otherwise leak `mean^2` into the variance.

The kernel also switches to 256 threads from H_per_cta >= 8192, one step earlier than RMSNormQuantKernel: with one row per CTA, the two reductions plus the gamma/beta loads leave too little parallelism to hide latency, and the wider block lifts batch 1024, H=8192 from 0.88 TB/s to 1.24 TB/s.

API and test changes:

- `layernorm_quant` gains `enable_pdl` (honored by the CuTe-DSL backend; the CUDA kernel does not support PDL) and dispatches like the other norm quant routines. Input validation on the CuTe-DSL path mirrors the CUDA error messages.
- One semantic difference: the CUDA kernel rounds the normalized value to the input dtype before scaling, the CuTe-DSL kernel stays in fp32 until the fp8 cast. The fp32 behavior matches the trace reference; tests and the benchmark compare each backend against its own reference.
- `test_layernorm_quant` and `test_layernorm_quant_invalid_inputs` are parametrized over both backends (672 cases total, including non-power-of-two H = 111 and 500 that exercise the tail masking).
- The benchmark routine times both backends in one process.

Measured on RTX 5090 (bf16 input, e4m3 output, CUPTI timing):

| batch | hidden | cuda | cute-dsl | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 256 | 4096 | 0.40 TB/s | 0.55 TB/s | 1.38x |
| 1024 | 4096 | 0.58 TB/s | 1.16 TB/s | 1.99x |
| 4096 | 4096 | 0.67 TB/s | 1.44 TB/s | 2.14x |
| 256 | 8192 | 0.56 TB/s | 0.76 TB/s | 1.35x |
| 1024 | 8192 | 0.96 TB/s | 1.24 TB/s | 1.30x |
| 4096 | 8192 | 1.18 TB/s | 1.50 TB/s | 1.27x |
| 256 | 16384 | 0.67 TB/s | 0.81 TB/s | 1.20x |
| 1024 | 16384 | 1.09 TB/s | 1.23 TB/s | 1.14x |
| 4096 | 16384 | 1.33 TB/s | 1.50 TB/s | 1.13x |
| 1024 | 65536 | error | 1.47 TB/s | n/a |

At H=65536 the CUDA kernel fails with "invalid argument" at launch (pre-existing block size limit); the CuTe-DSL kernel handles it through cluster_n=2.

Also verified on RTX 5090: the software fp8 conversion path (force compiled with use_hw_fp8=False) and the symbolic-stride compile variant used when M*H exceeds INT32_MAX are bit-exact against the torch reference, and the rmsnorm/fused_add_rmsnorm quant suites pass unchanged with the reduction signature extension.

title: feat: add is_deterministic mode to top_k_renorm_probs
body:
## Problem

`top_k_renorm_probs` returns bitwise-different results on repeated calls with bitwise-identical input. On GB300 (192x131072 fp32, k=50): 19/19 repeated invocations differed, max_abs_diff ~3e-8.

This matters for replicated execution: tensor-parallel LLM serving runs sampling/spec-decode verify redundantly on every TP rank with identical inputs, and per-invocation nondeterminism makes ranks compute rank-divergent `target_probs`. With shared rejection-sampling coins, committed tokens then flip exactly at inverse-CDF boundaries (measured ~1e-7..1e-5 per sampling decision, roughly linear in top_k), which diverges rank-local radix caches and eventually surfaces as collective-shape mismatch hangs — the exact chain independently root-caused in sgl-project/sglang#22458.

## Root cause

The radix **pivot selection is already deterministic** (integer histogram accumulation) — we verified the kept support is stable 20/20 across calls. The only nondeterministic step is the multi-CTA **renormalization sum**: per-CTA partial sums are combined with float `atomicAdd(&state->sum_topk, block_sum)`, so CTA arrival order changes the rounding of the normalizer, wobbling every output value in its last bits.

## Fix

Mirror `top_p_renorm_probs`' existing deterministic option: an `is_deterministic` flag (default `False`, existing behavior and performance unchanged) that switches the multi-CTA accumulation to order-independent fixed-point integer atomics:

- `RadixRowState` gains a `sum_topk_fixed` (u64) field; contributions are quantized at 2^44 scale and combined with integer `atomicAdd` (associative, order-independent).
- Overflow bound is a kept mass of 2^20 — far above probability-input magnitudes (docs note the assumption); quantization error (≤2^-44 per CTA) is below fp32 ulp.
- Single-CTA path already sums in a fixed block-reduction order and is unaffected; the flag only changes the multi-CTA path.
- Plumbed through `csrc/renorm.cu`, the sampling binding, and the Python API with the same signature/doc shape as `top_p_renorm_probs`.

## Validation (GB300, JIT build, 192x131072 fp32)

```
[det=True ] bitwise-different: 0/19            (was 19/19)
[det=False] bitwise-different: 19/19           (default unchanged)
[correct  ] same_support_vs_default=True  max_val_diff=1.5e-08  row_sum_err=2.4e-07
[k=2000   ] bitwise-different: 0/9             (per-row top_k tensor)
[perf     ] default=0.148ms  deterministic=0.151ms  overhead=+2.6%
```

Added `test_top_k_renorm_probs_deterministic` (bitwise stability across 10 calls, support equality vs default, value closeness, row-sum normalization) across batch/vocab/k/dtype parametrizations.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Added an optional deterministic execution mode for top-k probability renormalization.
  * Supports both scalar and per-row top-k values.
  * Works with float32, float16, and bfloat16 inputs while preserving existing default behavior.
  * Deterministic execution produces consistent results across repeated calls.

* **Tests**
  * Added coverage for deterministic and non-deterministic modes across supported data types and top-k configurations.

title: feat(gdn): prefix-cache state materialization kernel
body:
## 📌 Description
 
Adds `gdn_prefix_materialize`: reconstruct a request's GDN SSM state at a chosen token from its u-cache checkpoint + ring, and write it to a separate state-pool slot. Sources and rings are read-only; `count == 0` is an exact copy; rows with negative slot/count are skipped.
 
**Use case: prefix caching.** A cached prefix is only reusable if its state sits at a fixed boundary (e.g. every 128 tokens), but the u-cache decode kernels checkpoint wherever their flush lands.
 
Example: a request's last flush checkpointed the state after token 120, and decoding has since accepted tokens 121..129 into the ring. Token 128 is a boundary, so the scheduler calls this kernel once with `count = 128 - 120 = 8`: it replays ring entries 121..128 (not the 9th, token 129) onto the token-120 checkpoint and writes the exact token-128 state to the prefix cache's slot. Decode continues undisturbed.
 
The call must happen before the next flush moves the checkpoint past 128; per-request `src`/`dst`/`count` means one launch serves a whole batch in which different requests cross different boundaries (and most cross none: rows are `-1`).
 
```python
gdn_prefix_materialize(state, src_slots, dst_slots,
                       k_cache, u_cache, g_cache, cache_base, count,
                       active_request_indices, num_active)
```
 
### IO
 
`R` = ring depth (32 or 16, auto-detected from the tensors).
 
| Name | Shape | Dtype | Dir | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `state` | `[pool, HV, V, K]` | STATE | in/out | src read, dst written |
| `src_slots`, `dst_slots` | `[B]` | int32 | in | pool slots per request |
| `k_cache` | `[pool, H, R, K]` | RING | in | ring: L2-normalized keys |
| `u_cache` | `[pool, HV, R, V]` | RING | in | ring: corrections |
| `g_cache` | `[pool, HV, R]` | f32 | in | ring: cumulative log-decay |
| `cache_base` | `[B]` | int32 | in | ring window origin |
| `count` | `[B]` | int32 | in | entries to replay (<= 16) |
| `active_request_indices` | `[B]` | int32 | in | live rows first, then `-1` |
| `num_active` | `[1]` | int32 | in | device scalar: live rows |
 
### Precision
 
STATE/RING = bf16 (default) or fp16 via `GDN_UCACHE_STATE_DTYPE` / `GDN_UCACHE_IO_DTYPE`, matching the decode kernels; f32 accumulate, one rounding on store. SM90+, `K == V == 128`.
 
### Perf
 
B200, H=16 / HV=64, CUPTI:
 
- Idle launch ~2.5 us; 4-active ~11 us — both independent of batch size in 8..512.
- B=256, all folding: 189 us — at the memory floor (the equal-bytes `count == 0` case measures 174 us vs 172 us for a plain contiguous copy of the same 1.07 GB).

title: perf(prims-ts): optimize QToken-KvBlock-Sparse-Attention
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

Optimize existing PrimTS QToken-KvBlock-Sparse-Attention on Blackwell. Public plan/run APIs, supported shapes, KV-cache layouts, and standalone metadata outputs are unchanged.

### Optimization techniques

- Donate idle-warpgroups’ registers to full-row softmax within the CTA register budget.
- Stage full D256 FP8 heads and rebalance K/V buffer depths to reduce pipeline overhead.
- Use compile-time page-index access to avoid register-array spills.
- Use head-aware flat locators and rank-2 TensorMaps for eligible compact caches, without repacking K/V.
- Reuse warp-uniform FP8 coordinates, keep issue loops rolled, and advance TMA pointers incrementally.
- Skip redundant single-issuer statistics synchronization while preserving parallel multi-issuer startup and drain.
- Choose shared-memory byte/bit maps or bounded radix-sort union from capacity and occupancy.
- Prefetch metadata candidates and release PDL early to overlap attention setup.
- Vectorize membership loads and emit query-major masks for eligible FP8 G2–G8 routes to reduce masking work.
- Reduce S5–S16 partials across four lanes with warp shuffles, preserving accumulation precision.

### Performance

GB300, TP2-local Hq/Hkv=12/1, D256, real recorded block-4 selections and seeded Q/K/V. CUDA graphs, random cold L2, 20 warmups/300 samples, two reversed-order passes per revision. Times include metadata and reduction; decode rows below use KV8K.

| Case | Main 0a761d12 µs | 81e51360 µs | Speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BF16 decode, BS16/SQ5/G5 | 35.86 | 28.83 | 1.24× |
| BF16 decode, BS32/SQ5/G5 | 40.94 | 35.37 | 1.16× |
| BF16 prefill 8K, BS1/G8 | 386.35 | 374.76 | 1.03× |
| BF16 prefill 16K, BS1/G8 | 838.50 | 811.49 | 1.03× |
| BF16 prefill 32K, BS1/G8 | 1807.52 | 1741.72 | 1.04× |
| FP8 prefill 8K, BS1/G8 | 385.02 | 277.37 | 1.39× |
| FP8 prefill 16K, BS1/G8 | 825.62 | 593.70 | 1.39× |
| FP8 prefill 32K, BS1/G8 | 1775.12 | 1269.86 | 1.40× |

At measured revision `81e51360`, compared with main `0a761d12`, geometric-mean speedup is 1.128× across 56 cases; the largest latency increase is 1.17%. The separate pre-rebase comparison (`87d5a936`→`81e51360`) changes geometric-mean latency by +0.04%, with a worst increase of 0.92%. Q5 uses the maintained shared-request/cache proxy; the larger matrix uses disjoint request caches.

body:
## 📌 Description

Two fixes to the SM100/SM103 CuTe-DSL dense W4A16 (`mm_bf16_fp4`) path. Both affect only the no-autotune path; autotuned callers are untouched by change 2 and lose ~2.7% from change 1 (see below).

### 1. Restore `--opt-level 2` (regression from #4686)

#4686 dropped this path's explicit `--opt-level 2` and let the CuTe DSL default (3) apply. On B300 that is a 1.5-1.8x regression on the shapes the perf CI runs:

| case | m | before (O3) | after (O2) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 4K-hidden-prefill | 256 | 0.0952 ms | 0.0523 ms |
| 4K-hidden-decode | 1 | 0.0183 ms | 0.0120 ms |

Measured per tactic, **O3 is ~2-3% faster on 26 of the 30 tactics and 1.44-1.81x slower on exactly 4** — cluster `(1,1)` + `raster_along_m=True` + a narrow N tile, the same 4 at m=1 and m=256. The no-autotune path always selects `((128, 8, 256), (1, 1), True)`, the worst cell in that space, which is why #4686's autotuned benchmarks reported a real ~1.03x win while CI regressed. Reverting the level costs autotuned callers that ~2.7% and buys back 1.8x for everyone who does not autotune.

Not register pressure: `ncu` shows 128 registers/thread and zero local-memory traffic under both levels with an identical launch config; issued warps/scheduler drops 0.67 -> 0.39 at unchanged occupancy. The kernel goes latency-bound, so there is no register budget to retune. Worth reporting the cliff itself to the CuTe DSL team separately.

The 15 -> 30 raster-direction tactic expansion from #4686 is kept — it is inert on the no-autotune path and only widens the autotuner's search.

### 2. Shape-aware no-autotune default tactic

`forward()`'s `tactic == -1` path took `valid_tactics[0]`, which is always the smallest row tile (`route_tile=8`) regardless of `m`, because `get_valid_tactics()` filters on legality only. Each CTA streams all of K for its tile, so weights are re-read once per row tile — `ceil(m/8)` of them. That is harmless at m <= 8 (one tile) and degrades linearly above it: measured 2.1-5.1x off the best tactic at m=128, 6.1-9.1x at m=512, 8.7-10.2x at m=2048. Every caller that does not autotune pays this, including the perf CI suite.

`_select_sm100_bf16_fp4_default_tactic()` now ranks by `waves x per-CTA bytes` (`tile_n` FP4 weights at 1/2 byte, `tile_m` BF16 activations at 2; K is common to all tactics and cancels). The two terms oppose each other, so the optimum is an interior tile that widens with `m`. Ties go to `raster_along_m=False`, which also keeps the default clear of the level-3 cliff above.

Rejected on measurement, so they are not retried: ranking on wave count alone picks a 3-wave tactic over a faster 4-wave one at m=2048, n=k=4096 (it ignores per-CTA cost), and breaking ties toward the 2-CTA cluster helps m=512 but is worse overall (geomean 1.12 vs 1.07).

---

## ⏱️ Performance

End-to-end through `mm_bf16_fp4`, no `--autotune`, B200 (148 SMs), CUPTI, `--num_iters 30 --dry_run_iters 5`. Speedup of change 2 over the previous default, at `--opt-level 2`:

| m | (n,k)=(4096,4096) | (6656,19968) | (19968,6656) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 / 8 | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x |
| 32 | 1.00x | 1.84x | 2.14x |
| 128 | 2.65x | 4.87x | 4.64x |
| 512 | 5.50x | 7.28x | 7.71x |
| 2048 | 7.94x | 7.26x | 9.27x |

Geomean 2.64x, max 9.27x, no shape slower than before. Against per-tactic ground truth (30 tactics x 18 shapes) the heuristic lands 1.069 geomean from the per-shape optimum, worst 1.336x, versus 2.823 / 10.223 for the rule it replaces. It is a heuristic to stop the untuned path being catastrophic, not a replacement for autotuning.

---

## 🧪 Tests

*   **18/18 shapes:** the tactic actually launched matches the selector's independently computed prediction (verified by intercepting `_launch_cute_dsl_sm100`); all outputs finite.
*   **9/9 shapes:** pass `flashinfer_benchmark.py --refcheck` (fp32 reference).
*   **Linting:** `ruff check` and `ruff format` clean.

> **Note:** Measured on B300 SXM6 (cc 10.3) for change 1 and B200 (cc 10.0) for change 2; both report 148 SMs and share the code path. **Not measured on GB300.**

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

  * Improved no-autotune performance for supported SM100 BF16/FP4 matrix shapes by caching default tactic selections.
  * Streamlined tactic ranking for faster selection.

* **Reliability**
  * Added coverage validating deterministic tactic selection across matrix sizes and GPU configurations.
  * Verified dense kernels compile with the intended optimization level.

title: feat(cake_sampling): fused radix top-k / top-p sampling pipeline for SM100/SM103 (single source; SM90/SM107/SM110 compile targets)
body:
## Summary

Adds `flashinfer.cake_sampling`: a fused top-k → top-p → sampling pipeline for Blackwell (SM100 B200/GB200, SM103 B300/GB300), measured and tuned on B200 and B300, that implements the semantics of `top_k_top_p_sampling_from_probs(filter_apply_order="top_k_first")` in two kernels per call:

1. **Cluster radix top-k** (`radix_topk`): one thread-block cluster per row runs a three-pass radix select (11/11/10 bits of the float32 key) with 2048-bucket shared-memory histograms reduced across the cluster through distributed shared memory (`ld.shared::cluster.v4`), then writes a `[batch, 1024]` slab of exact top-k (value, index) pairs. Ties at the k boundary resolve toward the lower vocabulary index (ballot ranks + one block scan, no atomics), so the top-k set is exactly the first k entries of `lexsort(-prob, index)`.
2. **Sparse top-p + sample** (`sparse_topp_sample`): one CTA per row sorts the slab prefix by index and then stably by key (CUB block radix sort), maps the kept values to exact 64-bit fixed point, keeps the shortest prefix whose exclusive mass is below `top_p × mass(top-k)`, renormalizes, and draws by inverse CDF from `curand_init(seed, row, offset)`. Launched with programmatic dependent launch so its prologue overlaps stage 1.

The Philox seed/offset come from the same `get_seed_and_offset` path as the existing sampling kernels and the generator is advanced by `32 × batch` like the top-p routes, so a shared `torch.Generator` advances identically.

### One generated source, compiled per capability

The frozen kernels are one translation unit, `csrc/cake_sampling/generated/cake_sampling_kernels.cu`, plus `manifest.json` (every variant's launch resources; the loader verifies the source hash before JIT). The earlier `sm100a/` and `sm103a/` trees differed only in the shared-memory address idiom the generator emitted, and the PTX uses sm_90 features only (`ld.shared::cluster`, `mapa`, `barrier.cluster`, `griddepcontrol`, `redux.sync`, `shfl`), so there is no per-architecture source. `flashinfer/jit/cake_sampling.py` compiles the unit once per device compute capability with that capability's `-gencode` flags; the module cache, `cake_sampling_route` and the tests are keyed by capability.

**Validated:** SM100 (B200) and SM103 (B300) — every test and benchmark below ran there, and the dispatch-model constants were fitted on B200.

**Compile targets only (per review request, not validated):** the flag table also lists Hopper 9.0 (`sm_90a`) and Rubin 10.7 / 11.0 (`sm_107a` / `sm_110a`). The unit compiles standalone with CUDA 13.3 `nvcc` for `sm_90a` and `sm_110a`; `sm_107a` could not be compile-checked because that toolkit has no `compute_107` target. No test or benchmark has run on H100 or Rubin hardware; Rubin qualification (dispatch retune, correctness set, fallback behaviour) is a separate follow-up, and the dispatch model on those devices is the B200 fit until then.

12 register-resident stage-1 `(cluster, ept)` variants, 3 streaming stage-1 variants (clusters of 1/2/4 CTAs walking the row in 16-entry register chunks, for large `batch × vocab`) and 6 stage-2/3 `(threads, items)` variants are selected per call by a measured dispatch model: the resident candidate with the fewest waves given per-cluster-size occupancy (then larger register chunk, then larger cluster) is ranked against the streaming variants with a per-wave cost model fitted on 49 measured B200 cells (mean regret 7 % of the best variant's time). Per-request `top_k`/`top_p` tensors are read per row by the kernels (only the slab size comes from `top_k_max`). Requests the kernels cannot serve are dispatched to the existing `top_k_first` route: top-k disabled or `k ≥ vocab`, `k > 1024`, non-float32/non-contiguous rows, or a device whose compute capability is not in the flag table. There is no batch-size limit: rows with large `batch × vocab` run the streaming stage-1 variants. `cake_sampling_route` reports the decision.

## Performance

`python benchmarks/bench_cake_sampling.py --cupti --batches 1,4,16,64` on B200 (`flashinfer.testing.bench_gpu_time`, CUPTI kernel time, k = 50, p = 0.9, median µs; register-resident stage 1 unless noted):

| V | B | route | `top_k_first` | `joint` | `cake_sampling` | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32768 | 1 | pipeline | 42.6 | 40.9 | 18.4 | 2.31x |
| 32768 | 4 | pipeline | 45.1 | 57.5 | 18.9 | 2.38x |
| 32768 | 16 | pipeline | 49.6 | 72.2 | 19.1 | 2.59x |
| 32768 | 64 | pipeline | 52.8 | 83.1 | 21.8 | 2.42x |
| 128256 | 1 | pipeline | 103.0 | 152.8 | 25.9 | 3.99x |
| 128256 | 4 | pipeline | 102.7 | 219.6 | 26.6 | 3.86x |
| 151936 | 1 | pipeline | 102.8 | 181.1 | 29.2 | 3.52x |
| 151936 | 4 | pipeline | 103.4 | 256.2 | 30.1 | 3.43x |
| 262144 | 1 | pipeline | 104.0 | 318.6 | 32.9 | 3.16x |
| 262144 | 4 | pipeline | 104.4 | 467.4 | 34.1 | 3.06x |

With `--cuda-graph` (graph replay, batches 1/4/16): `top_k_first` 31.3–65.1 µs, `cake_sampling` 18.2–54.6 µs (1.2–2.3x). These are the numbers after the determinism / NaN-Inf hardening below; it costs 0–2.5 µs of span per call at batch ≤ 4 (V = 128256, B = 1: 23.5 → 25.9 µs) and nothing at batch ≥ 16.

### Large batches: streaming stage 1

For `batch × vocab` beyond what the register-resident variants cover in one wave, stage 1 is a streaming kernel: a cluster of 1-4 CTAs walks the row in 16-entry register chunks, a sampled first pass builds the first histogram from 16 contiguous entries of every 64 (four adjacent lanes issue 16-byte loads, so each 256 B of the row costs one 64 B block instead of touching every 32 B sector) and picks a lower bucket (capped so mostly-zero rows cannot overflow the list), one filter pass appends the candidates to per-warp shared-memory list segments, and the exact three-pass radix select plus ascending-index tie ranking run on the list; an unlucky sample or an overflowed segment takes a cluster-uniform exact fallback over the full row. Output is bitwise identical to the register-resident variants. Running two CTAs per SM (launch bound 2 with half the list capacity) was measured and rejected: 67.3 vs 62.2 µs stage-1 time at V = 262144, B = 128 on B200.

Every draw in the validity check landed inside the exact `top_k_first` support. The dispatch model was fitted on B200; B300 stage-1 times track B200 within a few percent for every cell above, so the same table is used there.

## Determinism and NaN/Inf semantics

There is exactly one behaviour (no non-deterministic mode). Repeated calls with the same inputs, seed and offset return bitwise identical `samples`, `renorm_out`, indices and counts across stream launch, CUDA-graph replay and every kernel variant that can serve the shape, because:

- the top-k set is exactly the first `k` entries of `lexsort(-prob, index)`; boundary ties are ranked by ascending vocabulary index inside each CTA with `__ballot_sync` counts and one block prefix scan and across CTAs with a DSM tie prefix — no shared or global atomics decide membership;
- stage 2/3 orders the slab by index and then stably by key, so positions are `lexsort(-key, index)` regardless of stage-1 layout; the slab written to the workspace and `renorm_out` are in that sorted order (first `count` entries per row);
- the kept values are mapped to 64-bit fixed point relative to the row maximum (1024 values fit in 63 bits, so every prefix sum is exact and associative for every `(threads, items)` variant); the top-p cutoff is the unique position with `excl < p × total ≤ incl` and the sample the unique position with `excl ≤ u × kept < incl`; `renorm = float32(float64(v) / kept_mass)`.

| input | result |
|---|---|
| NaN or negative probability | treated as `0`: excluded from the mass, never sampled |
| row containing `+inf` | exactly the `+inf` entries are kept (lowest indices first if more than `k`), the draw is uniform among them, `renorm = 1/m`; `top_p` is ignored |
| top-k mass is `0` (all-zero row, or only NaN) | `samples = ` smallest kept index, `renorm_out` all zeros |
| ties at the k boundary | lowest vocabulary indices win |
| ties at the p boundary | exact prefix in sorted order: kept iff `excl < p × total` |
| per-request `top_p ≤ 0` / NaN / `≥ 1` | clamped to `(0, 1]`: `≤ 0` keeps the argmax only, NaN / `≥ 1` keeps everything with mass |
| per-request `top_k ≤ 0` / `> min(vocab, 1024)` | clamped to `[1, min(vocab, 1024)]` |

`renorm_out` is finite and in `[0, 1]` for every input. Differences from `top_k_top_p_sampling_from_probs(filter_apply_order="top_k_first")` on the same inputs are intentional and limited to the cases where that route produces NaN renormalized probabilities or returns index 0 regardless of the input (`+inf` rows; all-NaN and all-zero rows also return index 0 here, so those coincide) and to tie order at the k boundary (it keeps every tied entry when they fit, otherwise arrival order; here the lowest indices win). Measured on B200 with the same inputs (`k ∈ {10, 50}`, `p ∈ {0.5, 0.9, 1.0}`, fast path and kernel route). For finite inputs without exact ties the support is identical, which `test_adv_top_k_first_parity` asserts against `top_k_renorm_probs` / `top_p_renorm_probs` on fixed seeds, together with every pipeline draw lying inside that support.

## Tests

`tests/utils/test_cake_sampling_upstream.py` replays the top-k / top-p cases of `tests/utils/test_sampling.py` on this sampler with the upstream parametrizations (batch 1/99/989, vocab 111/32000/128256, k 10/100/500, p 0.1/0.5/0.9; mask containment, 5M-draw frequency tests with cosine similarity > 0.99 against `top_k_renorm_probs` / `top_p_renorm_probs`, seed/offset reproducibility, variable k, per-request tensors, NaN rows, `from_logits` alignment): 207 passed / 18 skipped (the `k ≥ vocab` cases, which upstream skips too and which go to the fallback route). `tests/utils/test_cake_sampling.py` (35 tests, run on B200 and B300) compares every row bitwise against a self-contained numpy / float64 reference: equal probabilities straddling the k and the p boundary, fully uniform rows, fewer than k non-zero entries, all-zero, NaN, `+inf` and mixed rows, denormals, one probability near 1, `p` tiny / 0 / 1 / NaN, `k = 1`, `k = vocab − 1`, `k = 1024` with ties, odd vocabularies on every covering `(cluster, ept)` variant, Philox offsets not divisible by 4, identical rows, per-request `top_k` / `top_p` tensors with mixed values, bitwise replay across launches / CUDA-graph replay / every dispatch variant, deterministic sorted slab via `top_k_probs_to_slab`, generator-state parity with `flashinfer.sampling`, `top_k_first` support parity on fixed seeds, empirical total-variation distance to the exact distribution (20k draws), and every fallback route. The streaming variants additionally passed compute-sanitizer synccheck, memcheck and racecheck (0 errors) on the generator side. `benchmarks/bench_cake_sampling.py` compares the three routes.

Generated sources are excluded from formatting hooks like the other checked-in source-export directories.

title: feat(moe): add opt-in Prims-TS backend to the unified MoE API
body:
## 📌 Description

Add an explicit unified-MoE backend for Prims-TS so callers can run NVFP4 and BF16 MoE through `MoEConfig` / `MoELayer` instead of the flat `prims_ts_*` APIs.

The existing flat path already does TRT-LLM routing → Prims-TS GEMM → TRT-LLM finalize. This PR only adds the unified adapter (`PrimsTsConfig` / `PrimsTsRunner`, key `"prims_ts"`). It is **opt-in**: not in `_DEFAULT_BACKEND`, so `backend="auto"` never selects it.

### Scope (MVP)

- SM100 / SM103 only
- Quant pairs: NVFP4×NVFP4 and BF16×BF16
- Activations: NVFP4 supports SwiGLU / GeGLU / SiTU / ReLU2; BF16 supports SwiGLU / ReLU2
- `intermediate_size` must be a multiple of 128

Out of scope: FP8, MXFP4, MXINT4, fused shared experts, LoRA, and making Prims-TS compete with TRT-LLM in default autotune.

The remaining flat inner runners, for follow-up PRs (each reuses the matching TRT-LLM weight view the same way NVFP4 / BF16 do here):

| Inner runner | Unified pair | TRT-LLM view |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PrimsTsMxfp4Mxfp8MoERunner` | MXFP4×MXFP8 | `trtllm_fp4_routed` |
| `PrimsTsMxfp4Bf16MoERunner` | MXFP4×BF16 (W4A16) | `trtllm_fp4_routed` |
| `PrimsTsFp8PerTensorMoERunner` | FP8PerTensor×FP8PerTensor | `trtllm_fp8_per_tensor` |
| `PrimsTsFp8BlockScaleMoERunner` | DeepSeekFp8 / MXFP8 | `trtllm_fp8_block` |

### How it is wired

A Prims-TS forward is still three stages. Only the middle GEMM is new at the unified layer:

1. TRT-LLM routing (`trtllm_moe_run_routing*`)
2. Prims-TS FC1 / FC2 GEMM (CuTe-DSL batched GEMM, JIT)
3. TRT-LLM finalize (`trtllm_moe_run_finalize`)

Weight and activation layouts are reused from the matching TRT-LLM prepare helpers, so one physical view can be registered under both keys:

- NVFP4: `TrtllmFp4Config` / `"trtllm_fp4_routed"` (MajorK, shuffled)
- BF16: `TrtllmBf16Config` / `"trtllm_bf16_routed"` (BlockMajorK)

`import flashinfer` does not load CUTLASS task scheduling. `PrimsTsConfig` / `PrimsTsRunner` are eager exports; the inner `PrimsTs*MoERunner` is constructed lazily.

The staged C++ launcher (`trtllm_moe_run_routing*`) has no `routing_input_mode` argument and infers packed vs unpacked vs logits from tensor rank. The inner Prims-TS runner therefore normalizes the ids / weights buffers from the pack's `routing_input_mode` (`_staged_routing_io`) and selects finalize weights by the same mode, so the adapter allocates the same 2-D routing buffers as `TrtllmBf16RoutedRunner` and autotune's synthesized placeholders are never read as caller weights.

## 🔍 Related Issues

Follows the flat Prims-TS MoE APIs from #4361.

## 🚀 Pull Request Checklist

### ✅ Pre-commit Checks

- [x] I have installed `pre-commit` by running `pip install pre-commit` (or used your preferred method).
- [x] I have installed the hooks with `pre-commit install`.
- [x] I have run the hooks manually with `pre-commit run --all-files` and fixed any reported issues.

## 🧪 Tests

- [x] Tests have been added or updated as needed.
- [x] All tests are passing (`unittest`, etc.).

New: `tests/moe/test_unified_moe_prims_ts.py`
- CPU: config/registry, opt-in (not in `_DEFAULT_BACKEND`), arch / `I % 128` / activation gates, staged-routing placeholders
- SM100 GPU: NVFP4 and BF16 vs the unified references, direct `pack_inputs` + `forward`, CUDA-graph replay vs eager
 
Extended: `tests/test_prims_ts_import_isolation.py` (importing `PrimsTsConfig` / `PrimsTsRunner` still must not load CUTLASS TS)
- Local SM100: `pytest tests/moe/test_unified_moe_prims_ts.py` → **17 passed**

## Reviewer Notes

- One Config/Runner pair. Inner `flashinfer/prims_ts/moe/runner.py` (`PrimsTsNvfp4MoERunner` / `PrimsTsBf16MoERunner`) is **not** a unified runner; `MoELayer` only talks to `PrimsTsRunner`.
- Do not pass TRT-LLM-only kwargs such as `hidden_states_scale_layout` into Prims-TS `TuningConfig`.
- BF16 prepared weights are BlockMajorK; the unified runner must pass that layout. The flat BF16 API defaults to MajorK and is a different contract.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **New Features**
  - Added an opt-in Prims-TS backend for unified Mixture-of-Experts workloads on supported SM100/SM103 GPUs.
  - Supports BF16×BF16 and NVFP4×NVFP4 execution, multiple routing modes, and compatible activation functions.
  - Added public configuration and runner APIs, with weight preparation compatible with TRT-LLM layouts.

- **Documentation**
  - Added API documentation, usage examples, and updated MoE capability tables.

- **Tests**
  - Added coverage for validation, routing behavior, GPU execution, and CUDA Graph replay.

title: feat(prims-ts): add native two-source sparse MLA
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

Add native BF16/E4M3 D512 sparse MLA on SM100/SM103 using `plan()` / `run()` with externally prepared indices for one or two KV pools, sinks and LSE. Shared 1CTA/2CTA kernels handle prefill/decode with page-size-one TMA gather4 and KV reuse; the existing MLA frontend and reducers own planning, launch and finalization.

Key performance changes:

- **Work partitioning:** choose query/KV tiles, split-KV, V partitions and persistent scheduling from workload geometry and SM count. Small grids gain parallelism; larger grids avoid excess partial-output merging, repeated QK work and tile padding. Policy cutoffs are measured GB300 crossovers.
- **Sparse loading:** pipeline page offsets through the existing shared-memory ring and cache gather4 coordinates in registers across feature slices. Tune issuer warps and register budgets together. Bulk TMA replaces gathers only for verified runs of 32 consecutive physical rows, such as SWA; random compressed-KV selections still use gather4.
- **KV reuse:** retain K through PV when one CTA owns V and the shared-memory budget permits it. BF16 uses BK64 where two retained BK128 tiles would not fit, allowing the next QK tile to overlap the previous PV tile.
- **Short-split scheduling:** when a split has no steady-state loop, one warp group handles two independent softmax streams, reducing thread count and unnecessary statistics exchanges. Live request lengths still control masking.
- **Finalization:** reuse native row-shared reducers and their sink/LSE finishing. Fixed split slots with neutral inactive statistics remove repeated split-bound reconstruction; single-CTA reducers use constant rank zero and a non-cluster launch.
- **Numerics:** selected BF16 schedules use FlashMLA's six-log2 bounded-anchor optimization. FP8 keeps exact maxima and P scale 448; the deferred-max threshold is disabled for FP8.

title: feat(comm): add PCIe IPC all-gather and reduce-scatter
body:
## 📌 Description This PR adds out-of-place PCIe IPC all-gather and SUM reduce-scatter for single-node tensor-parallel communication on PCIe systems. It provides GPU-resident communication paths with topology-aware schedules and shape-specific launch tuning. Both operators reuse persistent CUDA IPC workspaces and synchronize through GPU system-scope flags. Their steady-state paths avoid host-side collective coordination. - All-gather: flat push for TP4, recursive doubling for TP2/TP4/TP8, and a copy-engine path for supported TP8 topologies. - Reduce-scatter: flat TP2/TP4 kernels and TP8 kernels that reduce within each four-GPU island before exchanging partial sums across islands. - BF16, FP16, and FP32 support; contiguous rank-2 tensors; CUDA Graph capture/replay; optional caller-provided outputs and launch configurations. - Correctness-checked tuning with exact-shape caching keyed by collective, dtype, world size, GPU placement, and workspace limits. The code follows the existing PCIe IPC all-reduce integration pattern: framework-independent CUDA headers, TVM-FFI bindings, JIT loading, workspace APIs, launch policies, and focused unit tests. It also includes AOT registration under `--add-comm`, per-rank `fi_trace` templates and examples, and API/design documentation. The new APIs are exposed through `flashinfer.comm`. Their Python implementation and shared helpers live in `flashinfer.comm.pcie_ipc_collectives`. All-reduce reuses the shared GPU UUID/NVML discovery and workspace lifecycle helpers while retaining its existing public imports and module paths. Operator-specific topology admission remains separate. The existing all-reduce CUDA kernels and launch policy are unchanged. ### API example Assuming an NCCL process group is initialized and each process has selected its CUDA device: ```python import torch import torch.distributed as dist import flashinfer.comm as comm group = dist.group.WORLD world_size = dist.get_world_size(group) local_rows, hidden = 8, 6144 x = torch.randn(local_rows, hidden, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16) reduction_input = torch.randn(world_size * local_rows, hidden, device="cuda", dtype=x.dtype) with comm.PcieIpcAllGatherWorkspace(group, x.numel(), dtype=x.dtype) as ag: gathered = ag.all_gather(x) # [world_size * local_rows, hidden] with comm.PcieIpcReduceScatterWorkspace(group, x.numel(), dtype=x.dtype) as rs: if rs.supports(reduction_input): shard = rs.reduce_scatter(reduction_input) # [local_rows, hidden] else: shard = torch.empty_like(x) dist.reduce_scatter_tensor(shard, reduction_input) ``` The same API accepts `torch.float16` and `torch.float32`. Call `workspace.tune([hidden])` collectively before capture to measure launch configurations; otherwise the workspace uses cached configurations when available and conservative defaults when not. ### Performance Measured on **NVIDIA RTX 6000D**, with **BF16**, **TP2/TP4/TP8**, hidden sizes **4096/6144**, and every power-of-two row count from **1 to 32768**: **192 shape points**, all passing correctness checks. These are tuned PCIe IPC versus NCCL CUDA Graph microbenchmarks, not end-to-end model measurements. Software: PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, NCCL 2.29.7, and NVIDIA driver 580.95.05. TP2/TP4 use GPUs 0–1/0–3; TP8 uses the verified ordered 4+4 placement. H4096 covers the text hidden size of both [DeepSeek-V4-Flash](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash/resolve/60d8d70770c6776ff598c94bb586a859a38244f1/config.json) and [GLM-5.3-Flash](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash/resolve/eb9eb208eb0d988989d07a6a12d0fdeb5f52574a/config.json); the same shape is measured once. Rows mean rank-local **AG input** rows or **RS output** rows. BF16 shard sizes span **8 KiB–384 MiB** across the two hidden sizes; full AG outputs and RS inputs are TP times larger. PCIe IPC has a lower measured median at **192/192** points. Equal-point geometric mean speedups are: | Rows | Points | Geometric mean speedup | |---|---:|---:| | **1–32** | 72 | **2.81×** | | 64–512 | 48 | 1.51× | | 1024–32768 | 72 | 1.39× | | All rows | 192 | 1.85× | The full measured speedup range is **1.06–5.81×**. This is a median-based result, not a claim that every sample is faster. TP8 has several variable small-row points: in particular, AG/H6144/rows64 is near parity (1.06× in the formal run, 1.04× in an independent same-config repeat). All 16 preselected TP8 repeat points passed correctness and retained lower medians than NCCL; those validation repeats do not replace any point below.

Self-contained BF16 benchmark reproduction Save the following as `bench_pcie_ipc_example.py` and run it with this PR's version of FlashInfer installed. It covers all-gather and reduce-scatter, TP2/TP4/TP8, hidden sizes 4096/6144, and every power-of-two row count from 1 through 32768. Rows mean rank-local input rows for all-gather and rank-local output rows for reduce-scatter. Each hidden size uses a fixed workspace capacity of `32768 * hidden` elements per rank-local shard. The PR tuner retains all legal candidates: rows 1–512 use 10 warmups and 50 repeats per candidate; rows 1024–32768 use 1 warmup and 3 repeats. Tuning runs independently from formal measurement; the latter loads its cache in a fresh process. The tuner times eager launches, so this is not a per-shape oracle search under CUDA Graph timing. Both backends use preallocated outputs, 20 operations per CUDA Graph, 5 configured warmup graph replays, and 20 measured samples, without L2 flushing. The shared timing helper additionally performs 3 eager warmups and 5 estimation graph replays. Latency is the lower median of the sample-wise maximum across ranks, in microseconds. BF16 inputs are integers in [-8, 8], keeping every TP8 sum exactly representable. Results are compared with NCCL before and after graph timing; this does not imply general bitwise agreement between RS implementations. ```python import argparse import os import torch import torch.distributed as dist import flashinfer.comm as comm from flashinfer.testing.utils import bench_gpu_time parser = argparse.ArgumentParser() parser.add_argument("op", choices=("ag", "rs")) parser.add_argument("--hidden", type=int, choices=(4096, 6144), required=True) parser.add_argument("--rows", required=True, help="Comma-separated powers of two") parser.add_argument("--cache", required=True, help="Shared tuning cache path") parser.add_argument("--tune", action="store_true", help="Tune only, then exit") args = parser.parse_args() rows = tuple(int(value) for value in args.rows.split(",")) if not rows or rows != tuple(sorted(set(rows))) or any( row < 1 or row > 32768 or row & (row - 1) for row in rows ): parser.error("--rows must contain increasing unique powers of two up to 32768") if min(rows) <= 512 < max(rows): parser.error("Run small and large rows in separate tuning/measurement stages") rank, local_rank = int(os.environ["RANK"]), int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"]) torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank) dist.init_process_group("nccl") world_size = dist.get_world_size() device, dtype = torch.device("cuda", local_rank), torch.bfloat16 timing = dict(use_cuda_graph=True, num_iters_within_graph=20, dry_run_iters=5, repeat_iters=20, cold_l2_cache=False) def group_median_us(samples): counts = torch.tensor([len(samples), -len(samples)], dtype=torch.int64, device=device) dist.all_reduce(counts, op=dist.ReduceOp.MAX) assert int(counts[0]) == -int(counts[1]) == 20 times = torch.as_tensor(samples, dtype=torch.float64, device=device) dist.all_reduce(times, op=dist.ReduceOp.MAX) times *= 1000 # milliseconds -> microseconds, before torch's lower median return float(times.median()) def check_outputs(out, reference): correct = torch.tensor(int(torch.equal(out, reference)), dtype=torch.int32, device=device) dist.all_reduce(correct, op=dist.ReduceOp.MIN) assert bool(correct.item()), "PCIe IPC result disagrees with NCCL" workspace = None try: cls = {"ag": comm.PcieIpcAllGatherWorkspace, "rs": comm.PcieIpcReduceScatterWorkspace}[args.op] workspace = cls(dist.group.WORLD, 32768 * args.hidden, dtype=dtype, tune_batches=rows, tune_cache=args.cache) if args.tune: warmup, repeat = (10, 50) if max(rows) <= 512 else (1, 3) workspace.tune([args.hidden], cache=args.cache, warmup=warmup, repeat=repeat) raise SystemExit(0) # finally still releases the workspace on every rank launch = workspace.all_gather if args.op == "ag" else workspace.reduce_scatter for row in rows: input_rows = row if args.op == "ag" else world_size * row output_rows = world_size * row if args.op == "ag" else row seed = (17 if args.op == "ag" else 29) + rank * 1009 + row * 31 + args.hidden generator = torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(seed) inp = torch.randint(-8, 9, (input_rows, args.hidden), device=device, dtype=torch.int32, generator=generator).to(dtype) config = workspace.tuned_launch_config(inp) if config is None: raise RuntimeError(f"unsupported {args.op} TP{world_size} shape/placement") torch.cuda.synchronize(device) workspace.rebind_stream() out = torch.empty((output_rows, args.hidden), dtype=dtype, device=device) reference = torch.empty_like(out) custom = lambda: launch(inp, out=out) nccl = (lambda: dist.all_gather_into_tensor(reference, inp)) if args.op == "ag" else ( lambda: dist.reduce_scatter_tensor(reference, inp, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)) custom() nccl() torch.cuda.synchronize(device) check_outputs(out, reference) workspace.rebind_stream() dist.barrier() custom_samples = bench_gpu_time(custom, **timing) dist.barrier() nccl_samples = bench_gpu_time(nccl, **timing) torch.cuda.synchronize(device) check_outputs(out, reference) custom_us = group_median_us(custom_samples) nccl_us = group_median_us(nccl_samples) if rank == 0: print(f"{args.op} TP{world_size} H{args.hidden} rows={row}: " f"NCCL={nccl_us:.2f} us, PCIe IPC={custom_us:.2f} us, " f"speedup={nccl_us/custom_us:.2f}x; {config}", flush=True) finally: if workspace is not None: workspace.destroy() dist.destroy_process_group() ``` Run on an otherwise idle single-node GPU system with the required peer access. Use a new shared cache directory, and preserve the same physical GPU placement between tuning and formal measurement: ```bash set -euo pipefail pcie_bench_run=$(mktemp -d -t fi-pcie-bench.XXXXXX) for rows_csv in 1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256,512 1024,2048,4096 8192 16384 32768; do for tp in 2 4 8; do case "$tp" in 2) pcie_bench_devices=0,1 ;; 4) pcie_bench_devices=0,1,2,3 ;; 8) pcie_bench_devices=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 ;; esac for hidden in 4096 6144; do for op in ag rs; do pcie_bench_cache="$pcie_bench_run/${op}_tp${tp}_h${hidden}.json" CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="$pcie_bench_devices" \ torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node="$tp" \ bench_pcie_ipc_example.py "$op" --hidden "$hidden" --rows "$rows_csv" \ --cache "$pcie_bench_cache" --tune CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="$pcie_bench_devices" \ torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node="$tp" \ bench_pcie_ipc_example.py "$op" --hidden "$hidden" --rows "$rows_csv" \ --cache "$pcie_bench_cache" done done done done ``` The first launch is tuning-only; the second performs the NCCL comparison. TP8 reduce-scatter requires the detected ordered 4+4 placement described below. FP16/FP32 correctness support does not imply their performance matches the BF16 results. This example is self-contained; no separate benchmark package or scripts added by the PR are required.
## 🔍 Related Issues Related to #4393 (PCIe IPC all-reduce). ## 🚀 Pull Request Checklist Thank you for contributing to FlashInfer! Before we review your pull request, please make sure the following items are complete. ### ✅ Pre-commit Checks - [x] I have installed `pre-commit` by running `pip install pre-commit` (or used your preferred method). - [x] I have installed the hooks with `pre-commit install`. - [x] I have run the hooks manually with `pre-commit run --all-files` and fixed any reported issues. > If you are unsure about how to set up `pre-commit`, see [the pre-commit documentation](https://pre-commit.com/). ## 🧪 Tests - [x] Tests have been added or updated as needed. - [ ] All tests are passing (`unittest`, etc.). Targeted validation of the current code on eight RTX 6000D GPUs: **19 passed, 0 skipped**, with ordered TP8 placement required. The tests focus on the collective operations: - AG/RS correctness at TP2/TP4/TP8 with BF16/FP16/FP32, default and explicit launch configurations, caller-provided outputs, and pack-aligned tails. Reduce-scatter also checks against an independent FP32 reduction reference. - BF16 queued calls and CUDA Graph replay while changing shapes, variants, and launch grids. - Active BF16 tuning for one small shape in each AG/RS test, followed by an operation using the tuned configuration and a fresh-workspace cache-reload smoke check. - Retained all-reduce regressions: TP2/TP4/TP8 correctness with BF16/FP16, CUDA Graph replay, stream binding, and CPU collective-admission checks. Workspace discovery, initialization, and normal cleanup run through the public APIs as part of these tests. The full BF16 performance matrix also passed correctness at all 192 shapes. To reproduce the targeted suite on a supported eight-GPU node: ```bash FLASHINFER_TEST_PCIE_IPC_ORDERED_4PLUS4=1 \ CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 \ pytest -q tests/comm/test_pcie_ipc_all_gather.py \ tests/comm/test_pcie_ipc_reduce_scatter.py \ tests/comm/test_pcie_ipc_all_reduce.py::test_pcie_ipc_all_reduce \ tests/comm/test_pcie_ipc_all_reduce.py::test_pcie_ipc_cuda_graph \ tests/comm/test_pcie_ipc_all_reduce.py::test_pcie_ipc_second_stream_rejected \ tests/comm/test_pcie_ipc_admission.py ``` The AG/RS tests are included in the single-node communication test entry point alongside the existing all-reduce tests. They require suitable multi-GPU resources; the command above additionally requires verified ordered 4+4 placement for TP8. Pre-commit, PR documentation checks, and the documentation build have passed. The full GitHub CI matrix is still running, so the all-tests-passing checkbox remains open. ## 🔬 Experimental Track - [ ] This PR is **experimental**: it adds or changes code under `flashinfer/experimental/` and/or an `@flashinfer_experimental_api`. Tracking issue: # - [ ] The tracking issue names an owner, the reason for the experimental path, and a graduation plan with a target release. - [ ] Core changes are limited to a thin entry point (signature, shared validation, feature-gate check, backend selection, handoff). - [ ] Tests live in `tests/experimental/` and were validated on the intended hardware; a runnable example is included. - [ ] Nothing is registered in `flashinfer/aot.py`, and no experimental backend is reachable from `backend="auto"` without `FLASHINFER_ALLOW_EXPERIMENTAL_AUTO_BACKENDS=1`. (Calling an `@flashinfer_experimental_api` or naming a backend explicitly is itself the opt-in and needs no environment variable.) - [ ] **Test scope declared below.** The experimental CI lane runs exactly these targets, so keep them as narrow as the change allows. ```experimental-tests # One target per line: a directory or a file. (A pytest ::selector is not # supported -- the sharding runner cannot consume one.) Must be under # tests/experimental/ and must exist. Delete these comment lines and add yours, e.g. # # tests/experimental/test_my_backend.py # tests/experimental/my_backend/ # # Declaring the whole tree (tests/experimental/) is allowed but means every # experimental PR pays for every other feature's tests, in every matrix cell. ``` ## Reviewer Notes - Every rank must issue the same collective sequence and launch configuration. One workspace belongs to one ordered CUDA stream and must remain alive until all calls and captured graph replays complete. - Tensors must be contiguous, rank-2, 16-byte aligned, and contain complete 16-byte packs. Input and output must not overlap. `max_numel` sizes one rank's shard: the all-gather input or the reduce-scatter output. - TP8 copy-engine all-gather and topology-aware reduce-scatter require live UUID/NVML evidence for the logical rank placement `0–3 / 4–7`. All-gather uses recursive doubling when that proof is unavailable; TP8 reduce-scatter reports unsupported placement for the caller to handle. - Reduce-scatter accumulates in FP32. The TP8 schedule also rounds a four-rank partial to the output dtype before the final accumulation, so bitwise agreement with NCCL is not part of the contract. - Suggested review order: the public workspace APIs in `flashinfer/comm/pcie_ipc_collectives/`, shared IPC lifetime and synchronization, all-gather schedules, TP8 reduce-scatter schedules, then tuning and tests. `docs/design_docs/pcie_ipc_ag_rs.rst` explains the package layout, seven variant schedules, topology boundary, and heuristic seed thresholds. - Shared topology discovery exchanges group members' physical GPU UUIDs before querying NVML, so it does not depend on every peer being CUDA-visible in every process. Evidence collection is shared; each collective retains its own admission decisions. - The integration includes JIT/AOT registration, trace templates, API/design documentation, and the single-node communication test entry point. It does not change global AutoTuner behavior or add benchmark infrastructure, FP8 paths, or serving-framework integration.

title: test(comm): cover the moe-a2a receive-view cache, and key it on coerced FFI ints
body:
## 📌 Description

Two small follow-ups to the `moe_a2a_dispatch` receive-view cache from #5336.

**1. Cover the cache with tests.** The cache is a host-side optimization and shipped
without a test, because the real `tests/comm/test_trtllm_moe_alltoall.py` path needs an
mpi4py harness and NVLink hardware. The four tests added here stub the FFI module, so
they need no GPU and no MPI, and they pin the properties that make the cache safe:

- `recv_view_cache=None` (the default) still rebuilds every view — behaviour is unchanged
  for direct callers of the free function.
- A populated cache serves identical keys without rebuilding and hands back the *same*
  view object. This is the property that actually delivers the speedup, and the one that
  fails silently: a cache that never hits still returns correct results, it just grows.
- A new workspace invalidates every cached view, so a view can never alias a freed
  allocation.
- The key hashes by **value**, not by the identity of the FFI-returned integers — see
  below for why that one needs a stub of its own.

**2. Coerce the FFI scalars in the cache key.** `recv_offsets` / `recv_sizes` come back
from the `moe_a2a_dispatch` FFI call as a `tvm::ffi::Array<int64_t>`
(`csrc/trtllm_moe_alltoall.cu`), and their elements go straight into the dict key.

To be clear about what this is and is not: **this is not a live bug.** I checked the
actual behaviour rather than assuming it — tvm-ffi materializes an `Array<int64_t>`
element as a real Python `int` on both 0.1.11 (our floor in `requirements.txt`) and
0.1.14, so the key already hashes by value today:

```
>>> a = tvm_ffi.convert([1, 2, 3])
>>> type(a[0])
<class 'int'>
```

The point of the coercion is that the cache's correctness should not rest on that FFI
implementation detail. Note that `Array.__getitem__` already boxes a **fresh** object per
read (`a[0] is a[0]` is False for values outside CPython's small-int intern range); it is
only value-based hashing that makes that harmless. An int-like that hashed by identity
would miss on *every* lookup, silently disabling the cache while the dict still grew
without bound — no wrong answers, no exception, just a slow leak. `int()` on an object
that is already an `int` returns it unchanged, so the hot path this PR protects is
unaffected.

This is also the idiom already used for FFI scalars elsewhere in the tree, so it is
consistency rather than a new convention:

- `_init_constants` in this same file (`int(value)`)
- `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` / `BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper`
  `workspace_size` (`return int(float_workspace_size), int(int_workspace_size)`)
- `flashinfer/jit/attention/modules.py` (`staged_int_workspace_bytes = int(...)`)

I also swept the rest of `flashinfer/` for the same shape — a value returned by a
TVM-FFI module call used as a dict key, set member, or `lru_cache` argument — using an
AST taint pass over every module call site plus the obvious cache greps. **There are no
other instances.** The near-misses all turned out to be fine: `_get_cache_buf` keys on
`(name, device)` and only *compares* the FFI-returned byte count; `MoERunner.runner_dict`
stores the FFI handle as the value, with the key built from constructor arguments;
`_METAINFO_INDEX` keys on an FFI string, but `tvm_ffi.core.String` subclasses `str` and
hashes by value.

**Out of scope, flagged rather than fixed:** even with the coercion, `runtime_max_tokens_per_rank`
varies batch-to-batch in serving and `offset`/`size` are derived from it, so the cache is
bounded but not small (worst case roughly *distinct token counts × payloads* entries; host
RAM only, since the views alias the existing workspace). The `_workspace` rebind is the only
eviction path and its identity does not change for the lifetime of a `MoeAlltoAll`. Whether
that wants an explicit bound is a separate design question for #5336, not this PR.

## 🔍 Related Issues

Follow-up to #5336.

## 🚀 Pull Request Checklist

Thank you for contributing to FlashInfer! Before we review your pull request, please make sure the following items are complete.

### ✅ Pre-commit Checks

- [ ] I have installed `pre-commit` by running `pip install pre-commit` (or used your preferred method).
- [ ] I have installed the hooks with `pre-commit install`.
- [ ] I have run the hooks manually with `pre-commit run --all-files` and fixed any reported issues.

> If you are unsure about how to set up `pre-commit`, see [the pre-commit documentation](https://pre-commit.com/).

I could not run the full `pre-commit` suite here, so I have left these unchecked rather than
claim otherwise. What I did run, on both changed files, is the repo's pinned formatter and
linter — `ruff-format` and `ruff-check` at `v0.12.8`, the revision in
`.pre-commit-config.yaml`: both report clean. The remaining hooks are untried.

## 🧪 Tests

- [x] Tests have been added or updated as needed.
- [ ] All tests are passing (`unittest`, etc.).

The four new tests are pure-Python and need neither a GPU nor MPI, but I could not execute
them in my environment (no `torch` available), so CI is the first run of them on this branch.
No behavioural change is expected for the cache itself.

One note on what the tests do and do not prove, since it matters for reviewing commit 2.
The first three stub the FFI module with plain Python ints, which hash by value, so they
pass identically with and without the `int()` — they cover the cache's semantics, not the
guard on its key. The fourth (`test_cache_key_survives_an_identity_hashing_ffi_int`) stubs
the dispatch return with an `int` subclass that hashes by identity, constructed freshly per
call. Under that stub the key misses on every lookup without the coercion and hits with it,
so removing the `int()` fails a test instead of silently disabling the cache. That test is
the only reason commit 2 is verifiable rather than merely asserted.

## 🔬 Experimental Track

     Leave this section untouched for normal PRs. -->

  - [ ] Core changes are limited to a thin entry point (signature, shared validation, feature-gate check, backend selection, handoff).
  - [ ] Tests live in `tests/experimental/` and were validated on the intended hardware; a runnable example is included.
  - [ ] Nothing is registered in `flashinfer/aot.py`, and no experimental backend is reachable from `backend="auto"` without `FLASHINFER_ALLOW_EXPERIMENTAL_AUTO_BACKENDS=1`. (Calling an `@flashinfer_experimental_api` or naming a backend explicitly is itself the opt-in and needs no environment variable.)
  - [ ] **Test scope declared below.** The experimental CI lane runs exactly these targets, so keep them as narrow as the change allows.

     watcher reads it verbatim to decide which targets to ask CI for. -->


## Reviewer Notes

The commit for the `int()` coercion is deliberately typed `refactor`, not `fix` — please
push back if you would rather not carry a defensive no-op on a hot path at all. The tests
stand on their own either way, and I am happy to drop that commit and land only the test
coverage.

Two things worth a reviewer's eye:

- **The "not a live bug" claim.** It rests on tvm-ffi unboxing `kTVMFFIInt` to a plain
  Python `int` (`tvm_ffi/cython/function.pxi`: `elif type_index == kTVMFFIInt: return
  result.v_int64`), checked across the supported `>=0.1.11,<0.2` range, and confirmed by a
  round trip through a registered C++ function rather than by reading alone. I also
  confirmed `register_custom_op` is currently `return lambda x: x` in `flashinfer/utils.py`,
  so no `torch.library` schema marshalling normalizes the return before it reaches the key.
  If either changes, the analysis needs redoing — but the coercion stays correct either way,
  since `moe_a2a_wrap_payload_tensor_in_workspace` is a pure function of the key components
  plus the workspace object, so coercing two members cannot widen or narrow the key.
- **Prior art, for what it is worth:** v0.7.0 shipped with this coercion. The release branch
  hand-ported #5336 ahead of its merge and added `int()` on the way in, so `main` and
  `release-v0.7.0` currently differ on exactly this line; this PR closes that gap. The
  dispatch path with the coerced key has run `tests/comm/test_trtllm_moe_alltoall.py`
  143/143 including 78 EP8 cases on 4×GB200 (NVL72).

title: feat(comm): add H5120 MNNVL CuTe DSL profiles (TP4/TP8) and an apply_rms_norm switch
body:
## 📌 Description

This PR extends the Blackwell MNNVL CuTe DSL all-reduce fusion backend (added in #4358) to a second static shape — `hidden_size=5120`, bf16, `top_k` 6 and 3 — for **TP4 and TP8**, and adds a compile-time switch that removes the fused RMSNorm from the epilogue.

No kernel algorithm changes: the existing LL/BT/HT protocols are reused as-is. The new shape is new tuning presets plus measured routing tables, which is what the tuning dataclasses are designed for — they carry launch knobs only, while `hidden_size` and `top_k` reach the kernels through `StaticProfile`.

### Profiles

New LL, BT and HT presets for `H5120` with routing tables mapping `M` ranges onto them. Two knobs are shape-derived rather than copied:

- **LL `cluster_size=5`.** A 5120-wide token is 640 bf16x8 fragments; `fragment_stride = cluster_size * threads / rank_lanes = 5 * 128 = 640`, so the Lamport RMSNorm covers one token in a single fully utilised trip. The H8192 `cluster_size` of 8 would leave 37% of the lanes idle here.
- **`prefetch_group` sized to `top_k`**, so the staged rmem tensor holds no unused slots.

**HT is structurally unreachable at `hidden=5120` for `tp >= 8`.** A token is 640 bf16x8 packs, so `packs_per_reduction_shard = 640/tp`: 160 at tp=4 (a multiple of one 32-thread reduction warp), but 80 at tp=8 and 40 at tp=16, neither of which divides evenly across any legal reduction-warp count. An exhaustive sweep of the 1080 legal knob combinations finds none. The TP8 routes therefore stay on BT all the way up, and only TP4 carries HT presets. Lifting this would need a predicated tail in the HT reduction loop — a kernel change, not a tuning change.

### Routing

Every boundary below is measured with the benchmark added in this PR, on NVIDIA GB200 — TP4 on one node, TP8 across two nodes over multi-node NVLink. Each bound is the largest swept `M` at which the lower-`M` protocol was still ahead.

| Path | TP | LL | BT | HT |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| finalize + AR + residual + RMSNorm, `top_k=6` | 4 | `M <= 42` | `43-56` (P0), `57-1024` (P1) | `M >= 1025` |
| finalize + AR + residual + RMSNorm, `top_k=3` | 4 | `M <= 38` | `39-40` (P0), `41-2048` (P1) | `M >= 2049` |
| AR + residual + RMSNorm | 4 | `M <= 36` | `37-192` (P0), `193-2048` (P1) | `M >= 2049` |
| finalize + AR + residual + RMSNorm, `top_k=6` | 8 | `M <= 24` | `25-64` (P0), `M >= 65` (P1) | — |
| finalize + AR + residual + RMSNorm, `top_k=3` | 8 | `M <= 24` | `25-32` (P0), `M >= 33` (P1) | — |
| AR + residual + RMSNorm | 8 | `M <= 20` | `21-512` (P0), `M >= 513` (P1) | — |

Two boundaries needed more key structure than the H8192 profiles use, and the measurements are why:

- **The finalize BT→HT crossover is keyed by `(tp, top_k)`.** HT hides the `top_k` gather in its producer warps, so its edge over BT arrives at `M=1024` for `top_k=6` but not until `M=2048` for `top_k=3`. A single tp-keyed bound would route `top_k=3` to HT ~1000 tokens too early (13% slower at `M=1536`).
- **The BT preset split is keyed per pattern**, as in the H8192 profiles. The finalize path leaves the narrow 2-element/256-thread tiling as soon as the gather dominates, while the plain all-reduce stays on it about four times longer (TP4: 56 vs 192). Sharing one number costs up to 8% on finalize.

### `apply_rms_norm`

A new compile-time workspace argument that drops the normalisation from the epilogue:

```python
MNNVLCuteDSLAllReduceFusionWorkspace(..., apply_rms_norm=False)
```

The chain then stops after finalize, shared-expert add, all-reduce and the optional residual add, and materialises that value into `residual_out`. This is for callers that need the un-normalised reduced tensor and would otherwise pay for a norm they discard.

The guards are `const_expr`, so the sum-of-squares, `rsqrt`, gamma multiply, norm store and LL's cluster-wide sum barrier are not emitted at all rather than branched around. Contract, mirroring the existing `add_residual`/`residual_in` rule:

- requires `write_residual_output=True` — otherwise the fusion would produce no output at all;
- `rms_gamma` and `norm_out` must be `None`;
- HT raises `NotImplementedError`: its norm lives in a dedicated warp group with its own named barriers and shared staging, so it is not a guardable block the way the LL and BT tails are.

Default is `True`, so existing callers are unchanged.

## 🔍 Related Issues

Follow-up to #4358, which added the backend and the H8192 TP8/TP16 profiles.

## Performance

NVIDIA GB200, bf16, `hidden=5120`. TP4 is one node; TP8 spans two nodes over multi-node NVLink. Exclusive nodes. Timed with `bench_gpu_time(use_cuda_graph=True, num_iters_within_graph=20)`, reporting the median over replays of the max across ranks — these are collective kernels, so per-iteration CUPTI or event timing measures rank launch skew, not kernel time (a 4 us LL all-reduce measures at ~235 us that way). "fused" is the protocol the shipped `DEFAULT_CONFIG` selects; "unfused" is a torch MoE finalize + NCCL all-reduce + FlashInfer `fused_add_rmsnorm`. All times in microseconds.

#### MoE finalize + shared-expert add + AR + residual + RMSNorm, `top_k=6`

Summary over the swept range:

| Semantics | TP | vs. unfused baseline |
|---|---:|---:|
| With finalize, `top_k=6` | 4 | `8.76-31.68x` faster |
| With finalize, `top_k=6` | 8 | `8.59-27.52x` faster |
| With finalize, `top_k=3` | 4 | `6.20-18.05x` faster |
| With finalize, `top_k=3` | 8 | `5.78-17.23x` faster |
| Without finalize | 4 | `1.21-5.10x` faster |
| Without finalize | 8 | `1.54-7.23x` faster |

LL leads decode, BT covers the middle, and at TP4 persistent HT takes over into prefill. At TP8 LL's per-rank mailbox traffic grows with `tp`, which is why its crossovers sit at much smaller `M` than TP4 (24 vs 42 for finalize) and why it degrades sharply at large `M` (955 us vs BT's 305 us at `M=8192`).

### Cost of the fused RMSNorm

Measured by compiling the same chain with and without the norm (GB200, TP4, `top_k=6`), which is what `apply_rms_norm` now exposes:

| | `M <= 128` | `M >= 2048` |
|---|---|---|
| LL | `0.82 us` — 12.8% of the chain | `4.63 us` — 1.6% |
| BT | `0.47 us` — 7.0% of the chain | `6.04 us` — 3.3% |

Below `M ~ 128` the norm is a near-constant fixed cost — the block reduction and `rsqrt`, latency rather than bandwidth — so it is proportionally largest exactly in the decode regime where LL is selected. Note that reading a profile is misleading here: BT's `MaterializeRMSNorm` kernel is 37-41% of the chain's GPU time, but most of that is the remote prenorm-mailbox read and the `residual_out` write that a norm-free variant would still have to do.

## 🚀 Pull Request Checklist

Thank you for contributing to FlashInfer! Before we review your pull request, please make sure the following items are complete.

### ✅ Pre-commit Checks

- [x] I have installed `pre-commit` by running `pip install pre-commit` (or used my preferred method).
- [x] I have installed the hooks with `pre-commit install`.
- [x] I have run the hooks manually with `pre-commit run --all-files` and fixed any reported issues.

## 🧪 Tests

- [x] Tests have been added or updated as needed.
- [x] All tests are passing (`unittest`, etc.).

`tests/comm/test_mnnvl_cutedsl_no_rms_norm.py` is new. It runs at **four or eight** ranks against `hidden=5120`, unlike `test_mnnvl_cutedsl_numerical_contract.py`, which is pinned to `hidden=8192` and eight or sixteen ranks — so this shape gets coverage in a 4-GPU lane. It asserts that with the norm disabled `residual_out` is bitwise equal to finalize + shared-expert add + all-reduce, and that each rejected operand combination raises. The HT-rejection case skips where no HT profile exists, since the workspace then fails earlier for a different reason.

Validated on GB200 at TP4 (one node) and TP8 (two nodes, multi-node NVLink):

| Check | TP4 | TP8 |
|---|---|---|
| `test_mnnvl_cutedsl_no_rms_norm.py` | 5 passed | 4 passed, 1 skipped (no HT profile at tp8) |
| Protocol-pinned numerics, both patterns, LL/BT/HT | ALL PASS | ALL PASS |
| `DEFAULT_CONFIG` routing, `M` straddling every boundary | ALL PASS | ALL PASS |
| `tests/comm/test_mnnvl_cutedsl_config.py` | 18 passed | — |

The numerics checks apply the same per-protocol contracts as #4358: LL and HT prenorm bitwise equal, BT within 1 BF16 ULP, norms within 1-2 ULP, with HT compared against `multimem_one_shot_all_reduce_out` to match its multicast reduction order.

## Reviewer Notes

The routing tables and their measured crossovers are the substance here; the kernels are unchanged apart from the `apply_rms_norm` guards. Worth a close look:

- the `(tp, top_k)` key on the finalize BT→HT bound and the per-pattern BT split — both are departures from the H8192 tables, justified by the measurements above;
- the HT divisibility argument for `tp >= 8`, which is why TP8 has no HT route;
- the `apply_rms_norm` operand contract, and the placeholder gamma / `residual_out`-as-`norm_output` substitution used to satisfy the compiled kernel signature when the norm is guarded out.

One consequence worth naming: a process that uses both `apply_rms_norm` settings compiles two specialisations per protocol.

title: perf(jit): disable pre-RA instruction scheduling for the trtllm-gen MoE manifest
body:
## 📌 Description

JIT-compiling `fused_moe_trtllm_sm107` takes ~565 s on aarch64, and a single translation unit accounts for essentially all of it: `trtllm_batched_gemm_runner.cu` compiles in 565 s on its own. 
This narrows that to ~91 s by disabling GCC's pre-register-allocation instruction scheduling for this module on aarch64 , which is the default x86 already uses.
### Why that one file is so expensive

`flashinferMetaInfo.h` declares `tllmGenBatchedGemmList` as `static const`, and it cannot be `constexpr`: `BatchedGemmConfig` embeds `BatchedGemmOptions`, which is polymorphic (virtual destructor) and holds `std::vector`/`std::string` members, so the type is not a literal type. 
The manifest therefore cannot live in `.rodata`.
The host compiler emits it as load-time initialization code instead, for the 3378-entry Rubin package that is 3.4 MB of `.text.startup` against 232 bytes of `.rodata`, driven by `GLOBAL__sub_I` / `static_initialization_and_destruction_0()`.

The whole manifest lands in one enormous straight-line basic block, and GCC's instruction scheduling is superlinear in block size:

| stage | time |
|---|---:|
| `gcc (compiling)` | 569.17 s |
| `cicc` | 2.69 s |
| `cudafe++` | 1.38 s |
| `ptxas` | 0.17 s |
| `fatbinary` | 0.16 s |

(`nvcc --time`, 575 s total.) Within that host compile, GCC's `-ftime-report` attributes **465 s (85%) to the `scheduling` pass**; nothing else exceeds 25 s.

### Why the pre-RA pass specifically

GCC schedules once before and once after register allocation. x86 disables the pre-allocation pass by default, because lengthening live ranges ahead of allocation costs more than it gains on a register-poor target; aarch64 leaves it on. An initializer that only stores constants gives that pass nothing worth reordering.

Per-module measurements on VR, cold JIT cache, 352-core aarch64 host:

| configuration | module | `batched_gemm_runner` TU |
|---|---:|---:|
| baseline | 565 s | 565 s |
| `-fno-schedule-insns` | **197 s** | **91 s** |

### Scope and safety

- Applied only when the host compiler is GCC **and** the target is aarch64. On x86 the pass is already off, so this is a no-op there.
- Post-allocation scheduling still runs on every target.
- `-Xcompiler` reaches only the host compiler; `cicc` and `ptxas` still see `-O3` and the emitted cubins are unchanged.
- What is given up is instruction ordering in code that runs once per process during initialization.

title: perf(jit): lock CuTe-DSL builds per kernel, not per module
body:
The CuTe-DSL build lock spans the whole compile and is module-level, so two
processes building different specializations of one op family serialize.
Narrowing it to one kernel -- keeping the module lock for the state siblings
share, the stale-module wipe and the export -- lets them build in parallel
while the same specialization still builds once.

Measured on `tests/gdn/test_decode_delta_rule.py`, 8 shards, private cache
root, B200:

| configuration | wall | compiles | artifacts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| serial | 1941s | 279 | 268 |
| 8 shards, module lock | 1551s | 286 | 268 |
| 8 shards, per-kernel lock | 363s | 286 | 268 |

Every configuration leaves the same 268 artifacts and passes all 418 tests, so
the fast one is doing the same work rather than less. A single process sees no
change: one build at a time either way.

Where this shows up in CI: `scripts/unit_test_runner.py` defaults `--workers`
to the visible GPU count (`nvidia-smi -L` when `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` is unset)
and runs one pytest subprocess per worker, all sharing one `FLASHINFER_JIT_DIR`
and therefore one module lock per op family. Multi-GPU runners queue on it
today; single-GPU lanes are unaffected either way.

`compile_and_persist()` existed to dodge the module lock for parallel
precompile workers. `build()` now does that for every caller, so it is folded
in and its one caller (the `mm_fp4` precompiler) calls `build()`.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Prevented duplicate kernel compilation when identical builds are requested concurrently.
  * Improved build-cache reliability across processes by ensuring compiled artifacts are reused safely.
  * Enabled independent kernel specializations to compile concurrently, reducing unnecessary build serialization.
  * Improved handling of stale cached modules so newly compiled artifacts are exported consistently.

## 📌 Description

<!-- What does this PR do? Briefly describe the changes and why they’re needed. -->

Introduces one rule for `@flashinfer-bot run <paths>`: **a targeted run on a lane never tests more than the bare run tests  (`@flashinfer-bot run`) on that lane.**
