title: [Test] Add contract and distribution quality fuzzing for sampling
body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5346/files) against `main`.

## Scope

Related to https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3605 — this PR adds the Sampling side of the quality-fuzzing plan (contract layer, independent CPU oracle, deterministic layer, distribution layer, failure ledger). It does not redo the Norm/RoPE work or the Attention fuzzer, and speculative sampling is out of scope for this first version.

In scope: `sampling_from_probs`, `sampling_from_logits`, the individual top-k / top-p / min-p filters, the combined orderings (`top_k_first` vs `joint`), plus two production defects found while building the oracle.

Out of scope: any public API change, `chain_speculative_sampling`, CUDA-graph/compile paths.

## Implementation

Two production fixes, both about per-row filter parameters when `indices` is used:

- `TopKSamplingFromProbKernel` read `top_k_arr[bx]` and `MinPSamplingFromProbKernel` read `min_p_arr[bx]`, while the launcher validates that tensor against `probs.size(0)` (the unique-row count). Whenever `indices` reuses rows (`batch_size > unique_batch_size`) that is an out-of-bounds device read *and* the wrong row's parameter. Both now key on `row_idx`, like the top-p and joint kernels already did.
- The Python shims always materialised the per-row `top_k` tensor as `int32`, while the C++ side reads that buffer as the output `IdType`. With int64 `indices` the int32 buffer was read as int64: garbage `k` (filtering silently disabled) plus an OOB read. The buffer is now materialised in the output dtype.

The test suite is layered the way the issue plan describes:

- **Contract first**, per API, with the source line each fact was read from: retention is value-based (top-k keeps every token equal to the k-th largest value, not k tokens), top-p is strict at the boundary while min-p is inclusive at `max(p) * min_p`, `top_k_first` is *not* `joint`, `valid` differs per API (all-zero rows return `(0, False)` everywhere except `min_p_sampling_from_probs`, whose predicate accepts zeros), and the documented RNG offset advance is `ceil(increment / 4) * 4`.
- **Independent CPU oracle** that implements softmax and the filters itself and never calls the code under test; `top_k_first` and `joint` get separate references.
- **Deterministic layer**: one-hot / unique-candidate inputs must return the only legal token; the same fixed `seed`+`offset` must reproduce the documented behaviour.
- **Distribution layer** with a pre-declared budget: `K = 44` comparisons, `alpha = 0.01`, `N = 200000` trials per case, acceptance `|p_hat - p| <= sqrt(log(2K/alpha) / (2N))` (half width 0.004765). The plan was calibrated against pure reference sampling before being used on the device: 0/30 false positives, power 0.833 at 1.0x half width, 1.000 at 2.0x and at an injected 0.02 bias, 1.000 against a permuted row mapping.
- **Failure ledger**: seed/offset, input rule, filter order, thresholds, indices, reference support, observed frequencies and versions, so a failure is reproducible rather than seed-rolled away.

## Validation

FlashInfer base: `dc04f50c9aa3eabcdaa5feb0934edb3d85e9529a`
Hardware and software: NVIDIA L20 (SM89), driver 595.91.07, CUDA 12.8, torch 2.13.0+cu130, Python 3.10

```
python -m pytest -q tests/sampling/test_sampling_contract_cpu.py
# 12 passed, 0 failed
```

The int64 top-k fix measured on a released runtime, on SM120 (RTX 5090, torch
2.13.0+cu130, `flashinfer-python==0.6.18`), by applying this branch's `sampling.py`
hunk to that install and running a two-property probe on public APIs (k=1 with a
deterministic draw must be the row argmax; with k=3, all 20 draws per row must
stay inside the top-3 support):

```
stock 0.6.18     k=1  32/64 rows produce the argmax (valid=32)   k=3  640/1280 draws inside support
+ branch hunk    k=1  64/64 rows                                 k=3 1280/1280 draws
```

The CPU contract suite passes 12/12 on both sides, so it does not exercise this
path -- without the hunk half the rows sample outside their own support. The
apply/measure/restore harness is `ws/A2/run_int64_top_k_fix_check.py` with
`ws/A2/probe_int64_top_k_fix.py` in the L20 package; it restores the file it
touched and verifies the restore by hash.

GPU layer status (first live run on the L20, single GPU):

```
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<n> FLASHINFER_SAMPLING_FUZZ_SHARD=0/4 \
  python -m pytest -q tests/sampling/test_sampling_quality_fuzz.py
# 25 failed, 3 skipped
```

Two failure classes, both stated plainly:

- the harness itself indexes a CUDA tensor with a CPU index tensor in `singular.repeat(case.calls)[rows]` — a test-side device-placement defect, being fixed;
- the first `illegal memory access` occurs in `struct/keying/top_k_int64`, i.e. the int64-indices keying scenario, after which the CUDA context poisons the remaining cases.

Attribution for the second class is now done, and it is **not** this patch: the case was run alone with `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` on the patched tree and on a clean unpatched worktree of the base commit, and both report the same failure —

```
RuntimeError: Check failed: (status == cudaSuccess) is false:
TopKSamplingFromProbs failed with error code an illegal memory access was encountered
csrc/sampling.cu:225
```

So the out-of-bounds read behind that case is pre-existing upstream behaviour that neither of the two fixes above addresses; it is kept as a known-failing case rather than papered over. It is not SM89-specific: the same case (`struct/keying/top_k_int64`) faults the same way on SM120 (RTX 5090, `flashinfer-python==0.6.18`, log kept as `ws/A2/a2_fuzz_sm120_unpatched.log`), where the harness collects 88 tests and the first `illegal memory access` again surfaces at that case's teardown. Whether a main/SM90 build reproduces it is still open.

This PR is opened as a draft for that reason: the CPU contract/oracle/statistics layer is green and reviewable, the GPU layer is not yet green.

## Results and limitations

Correctness: CPU layer 12/12; the two production fixes have regression cases that fail on the base tree.
Performance: not evaluated; the suite adds no hot-path work.
Memory: not evaluated.
Limitations: GPU layer not green yet (above); per-test timeout / `--forked` isolation and the multi-GPU shard launch are not wired here.




Test and benchmark sources are retained locally; the validation results below refer to those local files.

title: feat(moe): support graph-stable DA LoRA outputs
body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/4566/files) against `main`.

<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## Description

This PR makes the finalized LoRA multi-output ABI graph-stable under TRTLLM distribution-aware MoE on SM100.

It:

- publishes the selected body's output, expanded-to-permuted map, and post-activation FC1 buffer at fixed addresses;
- shares the field-wise maximum body workspace across mutually exclusive conditional bodies;
- retains `permuted_idx_to_expanded_idx` in graph-stable routing metadata so `BiasType::Mn` can recover the exact token/top-k slot for each permuted row;
- has the fused multi-tile routing preamble populate that inverse map without adding a child-graph inversion kernel;
- allocates the inverse map only when a LoRA body consumes it, leaving non-LoRA slots at zero capacity;
- admits the precision families directly validated with a real graph lease: BF16, MXFP8, MXFP4, W4A16, and MXINT4;
- keeps DeepSeek FP8 LoRA and NVFP4 LoRA on ordinary CUDA Graph capture because B200 validation found, respectively, a non-contiguous profile-arena scale input and a missing DA graph lease.

Without the inverse map, real B200 capture failed with:

```text
PermuteGemm1 configured with BiasType::Mn requires a non-null permutedIdxToBiasRowIdx
```

title: Add explicit NCCL local allreduce fallback
body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/4585/files) against `main`.

## Description

Add an explicit `nccl_local` backend to the unified AllReduce fusion API. It reuses an initialized NCCL process group, performs the collective into the caller's output buffer, and then uses FlashInfer's local fused add + RMSNorm kernel when requested.

The backend currently supports FP16/BF16 for `kAllReduce` and `kARResidualRMSNorm`. It is never selected by `backend="auto"`; callers must opt in with `backend="nccl_local"`. Unsupported patterns and RMSNorm weight bias fail clearly instead of silently changing semantics.

This provides a graph-compatible fallback on systems where symmetric-memory/custom-all-reduce backends are unavailable, without allocating symmetric communication buffers.

title: [JIT] Resolve artifact headers through versioned include paths
body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5343/files) against `main`.

## Scope

Related to https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/2987 — this PR implements only cleanup item (1), "resolve artifact headers through a versioned include path", and nothing from items (2)/(3). Scope confirmation with the issue owner is not yet recorded.

In scope: versioned export roots for the trtllm-gen BMM / routing / MoE / GEMM artifact headers, removal of the fixed-convention path for those consumers, the include path participating in the JIT build identity, and a CPU-only regression suite.

Out of scope: downloader rework, sentinel scheduling, repository-wide packaging changes.

## Implementation

- Each consumer's export link now lives under `GEN_SRC_DIR/trtllm_export/<module>/<artifact sha256>`, and that versioned directory is the first `-I` root. Two artifact versions can therefore no longer shadow each other, and the architecture-filtered `flashinferMetaInfo.h` keeps winning over a same-named header inside the raw artifact.
- The version tag is the artifact's existing content hash (`CheckSumHash.TRTLLM_GEN_BMM` / `TRTLLM_GEN_GEMM`), read at the same call sites that already pass it to `get_artifact` — no second global version state, and a republish under the same pin still gets a new root.
- The version enters the JIT build directory via `JitSpecNvcc.artifact_version`; `spec.name` is unchanged, so AOT / jit-cache lookup by module name still matches.
- `ensure_symlink` / `verify_symlinked_headers` are reused unchanged: removing the convention path removes no integrity check, and the artifact's raw `include/` directory stays off the include path.
- `-I` directories containing spaces are now quoted; space-free paths keep byte-identical compile commands, so there is no mass cache invalidation.

## Validation

FlashInfer base / patch: `dc04f50c9aa3eabcdaa5feb0934edb3d85e9529a` / this branch
Dependency PR / SHA: N/A
Hardware and software: NVIDIA L20 (SM89), driver 595.91.07, CUDA 12.8, torch 2.13.0+cu130, Python 3.10

Commands and results:

```
python -m pytest tests/jit/test_trtllm_gen_artifact_include.py \
                 tests/jit/test_trtllm_gen_metainfo.py \
                 tests/jit/test_jit_cpp_ext.py \
                 tests/test_artifacts.py -q
# 66 passed, 0 failed
```

Actual execution: 66 passed / 0 failed / 0 skipped.

Observed backend: none involved — this is include resolution and build-identity behaviour.

What the suite covers (all CPU, real directories, no network): identical version regenerates an identical identity (A1-01); different versions produce different effective spec/build identity (A1-02); generate(A) then generate(B) then compile has no last-writer-wins (A1-03); a raw artifact header with the same name cannot shadow the filtered generated one (A1-04); concurrent same-version workers agree (A1-05) and concurrent different versions sharing a cache do not cross-redirect (A1-06); a worker killed right before the atomic rename leaves no consumable torn artifact (A1-07); missing artifact / checksum mismatch fails loudly instead of picking up a stale header (A1-08); include paths containing spaces produce correct compiler flags (A1-09); a read-only install dir plus writable cache needs no new symlink in the install directory (A1-10); a preset artifact package resolves with network blocked (A1-11).

NOT_RUN / NEEDS_UPSTREAM_GPU: A1-12 (the affected SM90/SM100 modules executing on their real runners) — no such device is available here. The module-scoped generation and architecture filtering are covered on CPU; the kernels themselves are unchanged.

`tests/jit/test_aot_copy_built_kernels.py` is new with this revision and pins both
selectors (`get_built_library_path()` vs the runtime's `get_library_path()`) with two
distinguishable artifacts plus the no-AOT case. It needs this revision's `JitSpec`
surface, so it runs where the revision is built: it collects as two tests, and
against the pinned `flashinfer-python==0.6.18` runtime it fails precisely on the two
symbols this revision adds (`JitSpecNvcc.__init__() got an unexpected keyword
argument 'artifact_version'`, `flashinfer.jit.env has no attribute
'get_aot_artifacts'`). The other suites above were the ones exercised on the L20. Neither of the two test files can be run against the pinned `flashinfer-python==0.6.18` install -- overlaying this PR's files alone leaves collection failing on pre-existing modules that release does not have (`flashinfer.jit._cuda_architecture`, then a long tail: main has 83 `flashinfer/jit/*.py` against 41 there) -- so they belong to a lane where this revision is installed.

## Results and limitations

Correctness: 66/66 CPU tests pass on the pinned base plus this patch.
Performance: not evaluated — this change is about resolution identity, not throughput.
Memory: not evaluated.
Limitations: the artifact package layout is unchanged; consumers under `csrc/` keep their existing include spelling. This does not touch item (2) download coordination or item (3) sentinel scheduling.

title: [Comm] Add support checks for the unified AllReduce-fusion API
body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5345/files) against `main`.

## Scope

Related to https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/2225 and the tracker in #2224. This PR adds support checks for **one** API family, the unified AllReduce-fusion API in `flashinfer/comm/allreduce.py`, and does not restructure the communication tracker, add a backend, or implement any EP transport.

Family covered: `create_allreduce_fusion_workspace` (backend choices `trtllm` / `mnnvl` / `auto`), `allreduce_fusion`, and `AllReduceFusionWorkspace.destroy`.

Why this slice: `trtllm_ar.py` already deprecates the low-level create/run pair in favour of this unified API, and `allreduce.py` is where the only existing hard backend requirement and the auto heuristic live. The comm skeleton in #2224 cannot even be imported at this revision, because two of the symbols it references no longer exist in `flashinfer/comm/__init__.py`; this PR is the behaviour-test replacement for that placeholder.

In scope: capability metadata on the existing checks, the query helpers shaped like `flashinfer.utils.backend_requirement`, two collective-free pre-rejection gates, and behaviour tests.
Out of scope: B4 / #3311 (EP dispatch/combine), any new collective, any return-type change to the public API.

## Implementation

The real gap: for an **explicit** backend there was no architecture validation at all. The workspace constructor allocated three IPC buffers plus a `cudaMalloc`, and only then did the JIT run — which on SM89 cannot build — so a machine that can never run the backend still paid the allocation and had no handle to clean up.

- `@supported_compute_capability([90, 100, 103, 120, 121])` on the existing `_trtllm_workspace_check`, plus a new `_mnnvl_workspace_check` mirroring the arch families in `flashinfer/jit/comm.py`, collected in a `_BACKEND_CHECKS` registry.
- Query helpers in the existing `backend_requirement` shape (`is_backend_supported(backend, cc=None)`, `is_compute_capability_supported(cc)`, `has_backend`, `has_backend_choices`) attached to both public callables; the no-choices case keeps raising the same `ValueError` instead of being reinterpreted.
- Two local pre-rejection gates in `create_allreduce_fusion_workspace`: an unknown backend is refused with no silent auto fallback, and an unsupported compute capability is refused with `BackendSupportedError` **before** any loader, allocator, workspace or collective work; `auto` filters its candidate list by capability.
- `run` and `destroy` bodies are untouched — creation policy must not block destroying a legitimately created resource.

Answers are architecture-only: 89 / 86 / 80 / 75 / 70 are false for both backends; 90 / 100 / 103 are true for both; 120 / 121 are true for `trtllm` only.

## Validation

FlashInfer base: `dc04f50c9aa3eabcdaa5feb0934edb3d85e9529a`
Hardware and software: NVIDIA L20 (SM89), driver 595.91.07, CUDA 12.8, torch 2.13.0+cu130, Python 3.10

```
python -m pytest -s -q tests/comm/test_comm_support_checks.py
# 12 passed, 3 skipped, 6 xfailed, 0 failed
```

Behaviour tests, not attribute checks: the query surface and signatures; capability answers against the JIT arch families; an unknown backend refused with the heuristic and both constructors proven untouched; the no-choices convention preserved; every query executed with loader / allocator / constructor / multicast / topology-vote / `torch.cuda` / `torch.distributed` spies armed to raise (proving the queries are side-effect free); SM89 rejection with the JIT loader, IPC allocator, both constructors and the topology vote proven empty; the SM90 dispatch half reaching the constructor with exact kwargs; three forwards on a `__new__`-built workspace with every probe and collective spy raising, so exactly three launches occur; idempotent destroy after a policy refusal; and two spawned two-process rejection runs under a 120 s deadline asserting per-rank reasons with collectives stubbed to raise.

Skipped / xfailed on purpose: the real two-rank collective numerics and the Hopper-only positive path (no SM90 here, no CI lane runs this file), and the #2224 tracker entries that are not converted yet — with `strict=True` so the ledger cannot silently pass.

## Results and limitations

Correctness: 18 passed, 3 skipped, 6 xfailed against this revision (module overlaid on a 0.6.18 runtime, no mpi4py — the default CI shape), identical with and without a GPU visible; mutation check — deleting the gate makes the five capability assertions fail, so they are not vacuous. The three skips are the per-device/cross-device cases (need two devices) and B1-14 (needs SM90a).
Performance: pure queries add no collective and no per-forward work; the gates are one-time creation checks.
Memory: rejection now happens before allocation, so an unsupported machine no longer allocates IPC buffers at all.
Limitations: NOT_RUN — B1-07 (rollback of a mid-allocation failure inside the deprecated allocator in `trtllm_ar.py`) needs that allocator restructured and is still tracked by #2224; B1-11 two-rank numerics and B1-14 (an upstream lane executing the arch fast path) need SM90+ hardware. Behaviour change worth flagging: `create_allreduce_fusion_workspace(backend="auto", ...)` on SM89 now raises `ValueError` immediately instead of failing inside the JIT build after allocating; SM90/SM100/SM120 selection is unchanged. Creation also now performs one group agreement before any allocation when a collective scoped to `world_size` is reachable (skipped with a warning otherwise), so a mixed-capability group is refused on every rank instead of stranding the rank that supports the backend in a rendezvous.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **New Features**
  - Added architecture-aware support checks for AllReduce fusion backends.
  - Added capability queries for supported backends and compute capabilities.
  - Automatic backend selection now considers device compatibility and coordinates support across ranks.

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Unsupported or unknown explicitly selected backends are rejected before resource allocation.
  - Errors now report relevant supported capabilities.
  - Inconsistent support decisions across ranks now produce consistent errors instead of hangs.
  - Backend-specific queries are rejected when the workspace determines the backend.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Follow-up (review)

Backend support is now agreed across the group before anything is allocated. The factory computes its verdict as data -- `(supported, exception_name, message, selected_backend)` -- allgathers it through the same collective resolution the MNNVL vote uses, and only then raises on every rank or enters a workspace constructor. A rank that supports a backend another rank cannot run therefore refuses with the group instead of waiting in a rendezvous that will never complete, and two ranks selecting different backends are refused as a group. `mpi4py` stays optional (an ImportError falls back to the rank-local verdict) and a comm not scoped to `world_size` is not used (warning + local verdict). Six host-only cases pin the agreement.

title: perf(moe): reduce W4A16 scale factors without large temporaries
body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/4559/files) against `main`.

## Description

Reduce the W4A16 NVFP4 scale factor without materializing full-size FP32 copies and boolean masks.

NVFP4 block scales are nonnegative, and nonnegative E4M3 values preserve their ordering in their raw byte representation. Because PyTorch does not implement CUDA `max` for float8, this change reduces an aliasing `uint8` view and converts only the resulting scalar. Other source dtypes use their native reduction. Empty inputs preserve the existing `1.0` fallback.

On an RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell (SM120), for a 32 MiB `[256, 1024, 128]` scale tensor:

| implementation | median | peak temporary allocation |
|---|---:|---:|
| current `main` (per-expert FP32 + mask) | 53.441 ms | 3,258,368 B |
| this PR (single reduction) | 0.479 ms | 1,536 B |

title: [Test] Add reusable device redzones with corruption injection coverage
body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5344/files) against `main`.

## Scope

Related to https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3978 — this PR takes the portable red-zone / canary sub-scope only: a reusable test-side helper, safe fault injection, and one real integration. It does not attempt to reproduce the original SM100 issue, and it does not build the asset-snapshot / scattered-sentinel system.

In scope: guarded allocation with an owning storage and a payload view, byte-wise guard verification with region/offset reporting, corruption injection that stays inside the owning allocation, and a real pre-allocated-output call site.
Out of scope: any new public production API, non-contiguous / overlapping-stride layouts, cross-device corruption claims.

## Implementation

- One single owning allocation per buffer: `[alignment pad 0x00][prefix guard 0xA5][payload][suffix guard 0x5A][alignment slack]`, with `payload.data_ptr() % alignment == 0` by construction and the payload a view of that same storage, so the owner cannot outlive nothing and no dangling pointer is handed to a kernel. The prefix guard sits immediately before the payload, so a store at `payload_start - 1` is inside the guard rather than in unreachable padding.
- Guards are compared as **bytes**, never through float equality — a NaN payload cannot produce a false positive — and only the two initialised guard regions are ever read back.
- Fault injection writes through views of the owner, so it can cross the payload's logical boundary but never leaves the owning allocation; `overlap` selects whether the store ends at / starts at the boundary or straddles it, and both the guard size and the payload size are checked before the write.
- Explicit rejections for non-contiguous, nonzero-storage-offset, larger-storage-alias and non-strided templates.
- Real integration: `flashinfer.silu_and_mul(x, out=buffer.payload, enable_pdl=False)` (`flashinfer/activation.py`) — an existing `out=` injection point, no production API change; exercised at `hidden=512` (16-byte vector path) and `hidden=3420` (8-byte aligned y-half, 4-element fallback).
- Stream/graph/lifetime: reset → kernel → verify has an explicit happens-before; the graph case allocates and captures at fixed addresses, resets outside the graph, and never resets after corruption to make verification pass.

## Validation

FlashInfer base: `dc04f50c9aa3eabcdaa5feb0934edb3d85e9529a`
Hardware and software: NVIDIA L20 (SM89), driver 595.91.07, CUDA 12.8, torch 2.13.0+cu130 (CUDA 13 runtime), Python 3.10

```
# guard-zone suite, rerun on SM120 (RTX 5090, driver 580.82.07, CUDA 13.0, torch 2.13.0+cu130)
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<n> python -m pytest -q tests/utils/test_guard_zone.py
# 71 passed, 2 skipped

# kernel integration (the real silu_and_mul output buffer)
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<n> python -m pytest -q tests/utils/test_guard_zone_kernel.py
```

Actual execution: 71 passed / 0 failed / 2 skipped for the guard-zone suite on one device, and **73 passed / 0 skipped with two devices visible** (`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<n>,<m>`, which is what the two per-device / cross-device attribution cases need). `tests/utils/test_guard_zone_kernel.py` drives a real FlashInfer kernel, so it needs this revision's activation code: with the two files it depends on (`flashinfer/jit/activation.py` and `include/flashinfer/activation.cuh`) overlaid on the pinned `flashinfer-python==0.6.18` install it is **6 passed, 0 failed** -- including the `hidden=3420` case the released vector-width logic faults on. The runner that applies and restores that overlay (hash-verified) is `ws/A3/run_kernel_suite_overlay.py` in the L20 package.

Case coverage: A3-01 normal payload write leaves the guards unchanged; A3-02/A3-03 prefix and suffix injection report the exact region and offset, including a boundary-straddling store; A3-04 payload correct while a guard is corrupted fails independently of `allclose`, on both the helper and the real kernel; A3-05 multi-dtype including a NaN payload; A3-06 odd shapes and alignments (plus A3-13/A3-14: the byte before the payload is inside the guard, and an alignment below the element size still yields a legal dtype view); A3-07 unsupported stride/alias rejection with a positive control; A3-08 half the corruption enqueued on a side stream, so verification cannot jump ahead; A3-09 graph replay keeps addresses stable and never clears corruption before verification; A3-10 per-device buffers plus same-process cross-device attribution; A3-11 allocation/release cycles without leaks or dangling payloads; A3-12 the real `silu_and_mul` output buffer.

## Results and limitations

Correctness: all 12 cases above pass on the L20.
Performance: the helper only exists in tests; `verify_guards()` synchronises the device, so it must never sit in a timing region or a graph capture.
Memory: no device-memory overhead outside the guarded allocations themselves.
Limitations: unchanged guards only prove that *those guarded bytes* were not written. Writes far from the payload, writes of the value already present, and write-then-restore are invisible; the alignment padding in front of the prefix guard is the one region a guarded run does not scan (the byte immediately before the payload is inside the guard); this detects nothing about arbitrary cross-device corruption. It complements, and does not replace, `compute-sanitizer --mode memcheck`.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **Tests**
  - Added device-memory guard-zone coverage to detect out-of-bounds writes around kernel output buffers.
  - Added validation for alignment, sentinel integrity, CUDA synchronization, buffer lifecycle, device ownership, and unusual tensor layouts.
  - Added checks for accurate corruption reporting, including affected region, offset, and corrupted-byte count.
  - Added integration coverage confirming guarded activation outputs remain numerically correct while prefix and suffix boundary overwrites are detected.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Follow-up (review)

- The prefix guard is now the `guard_bytes` immediately before the payload, and `_scan` reports its owner offset from there; previously a store into the alignment padding was neither armed nor compared (`A3-07` covers the byte before the payload).
- The payload offset step is `lcm(alignment, dtype.itemsize)`, so a requested alignment below the element size (`alignment=1` with float32) still yields a legal dtype view instead of an offset the view rejects (`A3-08`). Verified on CPU and CUDA over 7 alignments x 4 dtypes x 5 guard_bytes.

title: fix: preserve fp32 partials in split-kv attention
body:
## Description

Split-KV attention stored each per-split output in a workspace typed as the final output dtype. For BF16/FP16 outputs, this rounded every partial before the final reduction and produced avoidable numerical error on long contexts.

This change keeps split-KV partial outputs in FP32 for both decode and prefill, then converts to the requested output dtype only after reduction.

## Related issue

Fixes #5107

## Changes

- Use an FP32 temporary output workspace in split-KV decode.
- Use an FP32 temporary output workspace in paged and ragged split-KV prefill.
- Keep cp.async operations within the hardware-supported width when loading wider vectors.
- Add a paged prefill regression that forces split-KV and compares its rounding envelope with the non-split path.
- Merge the latest main paged-prefill refactor while preserving the new SAME_KV_STRIDES specialization.

## Validation

Validated on NVIDIA B200 (SM100):

- Paged prefill regression: 1 passed in 74.16s after a clean JIT build.
- Ragged prefill forced split: 12462/32768 mismatches against the FP32 reference.
- Ragged prefill non-split: 13546/32768 mismatches against the same reference.
- The split path remains finite and within the non-split BF16 rounding envelope.

## Checklist

- [x] Reproduced the precision regression on B200.
- [x] Added a focused regression test.
- [x] Validated paged and ragged prefill on B200.
- [x] Merged the latest upstream main without rewriting published commits.

body:
## Summary

Regenerates the SM100a and SM103a BF16 KDA prefill modules (`csrc/kda/bf16/`, `flashinfer/jit/cake_kda_tf32.py`) from Cake revision `1791cd70ec4`, which fixes the unbounded-softplus (Kimi-Linear, `lower_bound=None`) decay path of the fused M128 schedule.

sgl-project/sglang#34299 replayed 600 real Kimi-Linear-48B prefill calls through `prepare_bf16_kda_prefill`: the per-64-token recurrent-state error of the exported `fused_unbounded_softplus_direct_m128` kernel reached **0.42 rel L2** against an FP32 recurrence while Triton stayed at 0.002. Real gates `-exp(A_log) * softplus(g + dt_bias)` reach -60 to -800 log2 per token on 1-19% of the key columns, and the schedule split every intra-chunk decay around one half-total anchor with exponents clamped at +-126, so pairs inside a saturated band decayed by 1 and the restore multipliers flushed to zero.

The new schedule floors each per-token log2 gate at -15 before the prefix scan (exact total kept for the state decay), anchors two 16-token tiles per column on integer powers of two published before the pairwise MMAs, rescales the cross-tile `ldmatrix` fragments exactly with packed BF16 powers of two, and restores per tile through integer exponent bits with a warp-uniform below-normal path.

## What changes

- The four unbounded fused-M128 modules per arch change content and get new module ids; the superseded module sources are removed (`export_bf16.py --replace-existing`, as in #5370).
- The remaining module sources differ only in generated uid suffixes / brace scopes; bounded-gate kernels are unchanged in behaviour.
- No Python API change.

## Validation

All 346 exported shapes replayed source-vs-export with `validate_bf16_export.py --triton` (4 GPUs per arch), plus `tests/kda/test_bf16_one_wave_route.py` and `tests/kda/test_tf32_prefill.py`:

| Arch | Rows measured | Errors | Bitwise export == source | export/source time (median / max) | Triton/export (min / median / max) | Unbounded rows | FI tests |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sm_100a (B200, 148 SMs) | 346 / 346 | 0 | 346 | 1.000 / 1.046 | 1.08 / 3.33 / 12.82 | 10, all bitwise | 31 passed |
| sm_103a (GB300, 152 SMs) | 346 / 346 | 0 | 346 | 1.000 / 1.035 | 1.09 / 3.35 / 12.75 | 10, all bitwise | 31 passed |

The ten unbounded rows run at 0.95-1.02x of the source kernel and 1.08-3.91x faster than Triton on both arches.

Real Kimi-Linear-48B activations (600 prefill dumps, 42 GB, GB300) replayed through the regenerated export via the SGLang adapter (`sgl-project/sglang#34299`): Cake-vs-Triton final-state rel L2 median 0.0046 over the 600 calls. Against an FP32 chunked recurrence (360 calls up to 1600 tokens, 600 sequences) the Cake final-state error is median 0.0025 / p95 0.0090 / max 0.0213 and the per-chunk checkpoint error max 0.0213, versus Triton `chunk_kda` at median 0.0009 / p95 0.0055 / max 0.340. The previous export measured 0.42 on the same layer-0 calls. The three short calls where Cake and Triton differ by more than 0.1 are Triton off the reference (0.34 / 0.24 / 0.11) with Cake at 0.003.

**Residual limitation (long sequences):** on 8K-token calls the Cake final-state error against the FP32 reference is 0.030-0.048 versus 0.0018 for Triton; the per-chunk checkpoint error grows ~2^-9 * sqrt(chunks) because the fused schedule carries the recurrent state between chunks in BF16 (Triton keeps that math in FP32). Up to ~2K tokens the error is the same order as Triton (0.0025 vs 0.0009 median). The previous export measured 0.019 median / 0.42 max on the same long calls; this PR brings them to 0.011 / 0.049. An FP32 state carrier is a separate change.

title: fix(sampling): cast per-request top_k to the dtype the kernel reads it with
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

`top_k_sampling_from_probs` and `top_k_top_p_sampling_from_probs` cast a per-request `top_k` tensor to int32, but the kernels read it as `IdType*`, where `IdType` follows the output / `indices` dtype. With int64 `indices` two int32 thresholds are read as one int64 and the later rows read past the end of the tensor.

This casts the threshold to the output dtype in both wrappers. `top_k_renorm_probs` is unaffected (`csrc/renorm.cu` takes `int*`).

Three identical rows `[0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125]` with `top_k = [1, 2, 4]` and identity `indices`:

| indices dtype | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| int32 | `[0]`, `[0, 1]`, `[0, 1, 2, 3]` | same |
| int64 | `[0]`, `[0, 1, 2, 3]`, `[0]` | `[0]`, `[0, 1]`, `[0, 1, 2, 3]` |

title: fix(sampling): index per-request top_k / min_p by probs row when indices is set
body:
## 📌 Description

`TopKSamplingFromProbKernel` and `MinPSamplingFromProbKernel` read their per-request threshold with the output position (`top_k_arr[bx]`, `min_p_arr[bx]`) and only afterwards resolve `row_idx = indices[bx]`. With `indices`, an output therefore gets the threshold of whichever row happens to share its position, not the row it samples from, and when `len(indices) > probs.size(0)` the lookup runs past the end of the tensor (its length is validated against `probs` in `csrc/sampling.cu`).

`TopPSamplingFromProbKernel` and `TopKTopPSamplingFromProbKernel` already index by `row_idx`; this makes the other two consistent with them. The change is the order of two lines in each kernel.

Before / after on the repro from the issue (RTX 4090 D, CUDA 12.8):

| case | expected | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| top_k, `k=[1,1,4]`, `indices=[2,2,2]` | all classes ×3 | `[0]`, `[0]`, all | all ×3 |
| top_k, `k=[1,4,4]`, `indices=[0,0,0]` | `[0]` ×3 | `[0]`, all, all | `[0]` ×3 |
| min_p, `min_p=[0.9,0.9,0.05]`, `indices=[2,2,2]` | all classes ×3 | `[0]`, `[0]`, all | all ×3 |
| top_k, `len(indices)=3000`, 3 rows | per-row k | reads past `top_k_arr` | per-row k |

Regression test in `tests/utils/test_sampling.py`: 12 cases (top_k / min_p, three `indices` remappings, equal-length and more-outputs-than-rows), one batched launch each over binary-exact probabilities with a different argmax per row, 0.3 s warm. The six equal-length cases keep the old output-indexed read in bounds, and all six fail on the unfixed kernel with a wrong answer rather than a crash. The more-outputs cases are the shape that used to read past the tensor; `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` over all 12 on the fixed kernel reports 0 errors.

title: Add runtime-length scheduling for request-ordered paged decode
body:
## Description

Addresses [#4832](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4832) with a kernel-owned scheduler that reads per-request KV lengths on each launch and CUDA Graph replay. It partitions runtime work and reduces partitions within one FMHA kernel launch. Queries, page tables and outputs retain their native storage; request-order indirection requires no external gather or scatter.

The scheduler supports BF16 queries/output, FP8 KV, D256, 64-token pages, 8 query heads / 1 KV head, Q1/Q6 and batch capacities 1–256. It handles arbitrary legal length distributions within this fixed-Q API, including unseen and adversarial distributions. Other positive fixed-Q plans retain the existing fallback. The scheduler family has 72 exported modules. This candidate refresh changes 16 one-page device exports and their manifest; all 72 binding sources are unchanged.

## Correctness and graph replay

The candidate has qualified evidence for **512 mutable CUDA Graph states across 72 profile cases**: 448 states were freshly executed on GB300 and 64 retain exact matching evidence. Coverage includes changing length contents and request order, identity order, shared and separate pages, and independent live capture owners. The four fresh groups completed in **363.681 seconds physical elapsed**, with per-group payloads of **331.089–349.148 seconds**.

Generated source and loaded device binaries match the candidate. The evidence records the actual loaded public host libraries separately from preparation-time libraries. All 128 fresh CUPTI launch probes observed one kernel in each arm. Driver queries for the PDL attribute returned `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE` in both arms, so PDL attribute parity is unavailable; observed non-PDL launch parity is qualified.

The 26 runtime-length/order semantic cases and all seven canonical FMHA selectors are qualified. Fresh direct decode and sink validation took **86.105 seconds physical / 76.050 seconds payload**; the changed BF16 fidelity case took **73.241 / 63.743 seconds**. These are functional results and confer no performance credit.

## Performance evidence

**All 52 production comparisons qualify: 48 retained and four fresh short results.** Exact matching evidence is retained for all 38 original issue rows and all 40 controlled attribution comparisons. The prior 52-row qualification remains preserved as history; the current evidence binds every row to the published candidate.

For the retained original rows, all 20 uniform shapes improve by **1.025436–1.551131×**, with geometric mean **1.241129×**. The eight high-batch ragged rows have geometric mean **1.696963×**. Original-row acceptance retains the 0.99× per-row floor and 1.05× high-batch ragged geometric-mean threshold. Strict speedup above 1 is reported separately.

The 40 controlled comparisons contain **29 speedups and 11 regressions**. The 24 same-kernel comparisons isolate request ordering. The other 16 compare distinct cubins under a scheduler-only assignment ablation: one-whale Q6 improves by **5.623345×** and clustered-whales Q1 by **7.084730×**. These assignment ratios are not same-kernel comparisons. Changing request order within one schedule regresses B160/Q1 from **2,598.420 to 2,933.581 µs (0.885750×)**. Boundary-Q6 and unseen-Q6 descending assignment contrasts, using distinct cubins, regress to **0.968730×** and **0.956660×**; their same-kernel ordering contrasts regress to **0.985141×** and **0.988095×**.

An untimed owner trace preserves 12,330 useful KV tiles while reducing maximum assigned work per CTA from **768 to 128** and increasing active CTAs from **60 to 138**. Exact binary and configuration joins connect it to the retained **1,440.662→256.193 µs (5.623345×)** comparison. Assigned work is not a measurement of per-SM elapsed tail.

Measurements use GB300, FlashInfer 0.6.17 at `a0a6b019b9b27d49d209f85d028a1ae5a9b347d7`, cold-L2 CUPTI and three A0/B/A1 rounds. Each arm requires at least 64 warmup launches and 100 GPU ms, then at least 200 samples and 1,000 GPU ms. Maximum accepted drift is 2%. Supplemental comparisons and controls have no additional per-point speedup floor. Historical negative and nonqualifying observations remain preserved.

The fresh short uniform Q1 comparison qualifies at **6.912 → 5.888 µs (1.173913×)** with **0% drift** across three A0/B/A1 rounds. All 22 correctness checks passed, including the nine post-measurement checks. Source, generated binaries, configuration, sample counts, GPU durations and launch/storage parity match the qualification contract. It took **1,535.932 s physical / 1,518.726 s payload**; the measured benchmark phase took **1,422.322 s**.

The fresh B1/Q1 comparison also qualifies at **7.200 → 5.984 µs (1.203209×)** with **0% drift** across three A0/B/A1 rounds, all 22 correctness checks passed, including nine post-measurement checks. It took **1,464.493 s physical / 1,448.339 s payload**. These supplemental comparisons have no per-point speedup floor; qualification and strict speedup remain separate.

The fresh short uniform Q6 comparison qualifies at **6.880 → 6.305 µs (1.091197×)** with **0% drift** across three A0/B/A1 rounds and all 22 correctness checks, including nine post-measurement checks. It took **1,478.364 s physical / 1,458.376 s payload**; the benchmark phase took **1,363.809 s**. Candidate latency is 0.526% above the historical 6.272 µs observation; that historical comparison is not a new paired experiment. Supplemental qualification and strict speedup remain separate.

The earlier short uniform Q1 attempt recorded the same 1.173913× ratio, then exceeded its 16 GiB host-memory limit while finishing evidence (1,496.152 s physical). Its nine raw arms remain preserved as unqualified history because its final post-measurement correctness proof was missing. The successful run used the same kernel and timing protocol with streaming report output, durable correctness receipts and 32 GiB.

B27/Q6 now qualifies at 6,994.232→3,067.360 µs, **2.280212×**, with maximum drift **0.080059%**; 74.869 seconds physical /63.559 seconds payload. Its earlier 2.339476× observation with 2.372558% drift remains an unqualified result. A baseline-only diagnostic on the current device first observed a 0.193630% range across nine medians, followed by one prespecified candidate-interleaved comparison. No sample-count escalation or best-of selection was used.

Historical observations remain preserved separately: earlier original comparisons span 1.003524–2.344152×, earlier supplemental comparisons span 1.015026–8.710331×, and the earlier control inventory has 28 speedups and 12 regressions. Historical 0.884872×, 0.998728×, 0.968594×, 0.957318× and 0.632836× regressions are not replaced by newer results.

The fresh short B1/Q6 comparison qualifies at **6.976 → 6.336 µs (1.101010×)** with **0% drift**, three A0/B/A1 rounds and all 22 correctness checks, including nine post-measurement checks. Turnaround was **1,473.506 s physical / 1,456.677 s payload**, including **1,363.611 s** in the benchmark phase. Candidate latency is **3.665% above** the historical 6.112 µs result; that cross-run difference is not a new paired control. Supplemental qualification has no per-point speedup floor and remains separate from original-issue acceptance.

## Sanitizer results

The separate sanitizer checks completed as **14 timeout skips: 7 synccheck and 7 racecheck**, each bounded by a hard 20-second process-group timeout. None passed or was retried. Four early checks lost buffered child-output visibility at timeout; retained visible logs contain no reported errors, which does not establish zero sanitizer errors. The wave took **551.139 s physical**, with **282.463 s summed payload**; logs and receipts are preserved.

## Delivery status

The verified candidate is now published at `2f8d938aba2743f9c99f2bfcd7e69c5902db1c09`. New-head pre-commit passed. The initial test workflow skipped its matrix; a new authorized label event admitted all 11 intended jobs in [run 35491399348](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/actions/runs/35491399348), which passed on the current published head. The earlier skipped-matrix run remains preserved. Earlier CI at `99c3fcd346ca2391c9eb06fead784da4ee30e093` remains historical and provides no CI credit for this candidate. Candidate-head CI passed; required review remains pending and sanitizer timeouts remain skips. Operator acceptance and issue closure remain open. Model end-to-end correctness and performance are outside this delivery.

## Reviewer notes

Review runtime-length work distribution, graph-stable request-order indirection, fused partition completion/reduction and preservation of native storage. Acceptance thresholds and strict speedup are separate; all timing summaries retain regressions.

## 🔍 Related Issues

Addresses #4832. Operator acceptance and issue closure remain pending.

title: test(gdn): prune duplicate kernel specializations in test_decode_delta_rule
body:
## 📌 Description

`tests/gdn/test_decode_delta_rule.py` is the longest-running source file in the test suite. Instrumenting
`cute.compile` shows **96.3% of its wall time is CuTe-DSL kernel compilation**, not test execution, so cost
tracks the number of unique kernel *specializations* — the tuple of compile-time constants a kernel is built
for — rather than the number of test cases. Deleting the 56% of cases that request no unique specialization
saves only 1.4% of runtime; useful pruning has to target axis *values* that introduce specializations.

**Two changes.**

**1. Canonicalize the `scale` spelling in the test file on `1.0 / math.sqrt(K)`.** The file spelled one
constant two ways — `K**-0.5` at 10 call sites and `1.0 / math.sqrt(K)` at 19. The two differ by 1 ULP and
`scale` is a compile-time constant, so each spelling compiled its own cubin. Unifying the 10 onto the
majority spelling merges 15 duplicate specializations.

The merge is provably pure: normalizing the two float spellings inside the key strings makes the 277-key
baseline set and the 262-key canonicalized set exactly equal, 15 pairs collapsing on one side and none on
the other.

> **This originally also changed the library default in `gdn_decode.py`, and that broke CI. It has been
> reverted — see "The library half of this broke CI" below.** The saving is unaffected: the test-side
> change alone delivers the full 206 specializations.

**2. Prune axis values.** Drop `batch_size` values that add no specialization (where `tile_v` is an explicit
axis, batch is a pure runtime parameter), and pin `T`/`seq_len` in feature tests to one value per tile-config
bucket while leaving the shape sweeps at full range. Compile cost is flat in `T` (6.2 / 6.4 / 6.6s at
T = 2 / 4 / 8), so the choice of representative is a coverage question, not a cost one.

### Results

| | cases | specializations | cold wall | peak GPU |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline | 418 | 277 | 1929.7s (32m10s) | 22.6 GiB |
| this PR | **310** | **206** | **1342.2s (22m22s)** | 17.6 GiB † |

**310 passed, −30.4% cold wall** on the current head — a full cold run at `56c5ac4f`, no instrumentation,
fresh cache, against the mean of two baseline arms. Specializations −25.6%, confirmed independently by the
artifact count (197 `.o` + the 9 `wy_output_only` kernels that never persist = 206, exactly the projection
this table previously carried).

Re-measured after the library revert: 197 artifacts and 1342.2s, against 197 and 1349.9s before it. Identical
specialization count, wall time within run-to-run noise — the library edit contributed nothing to the saving.

† Peak GPU is the one figure still projected: it is measured over the 288 of 310 cases present in the
instrumented run, and the other 22 are extrapolated linearly. Projected scatter B=128 near 11 GiB would be a
third case above 8 GiB (15 → 3, not 15 → 2). Not re-measured, as it needs a separate memory-probe pass.

### What this costs

Stated plainly rather than behind an aggregate metric:

- `recovery_steps` goes from `{0,1,2,3,7}` to `{0,1,7}` and `T` from `{4,8}` to `{8}` in
  `fused_recovery_decode`. The compile-time boundary is `recovery_steps <= 1` and the retained set straddles
  it, but **`T_decode ∈ {2..6}` is no longer exercised** — the looped recovery phase is only ever paired with
  a one-iteration decode phase. This is the single most expensive item left (~50s) and is a deliberate trade.
- `mtp_split_pool` loses `seq_len=2`. It is covered elsewhere at 2-way granularity; the other four tests that
  would have lost it keep it.
- `wide_vec` loses `T=6`, a value no test selects directly.
- Several tests drop `max_T=4`. The only compile-time `T` predicates are `T > 1`, `T > 2` and `T <= 1`, so
  T=4 and T=8 are the same bucket.

Every test function retains at least one case, and no boolean code path is dropped. I'd note that the
boolean-projection metric is a *necessary* condition, not evidence of safety — a 179-case prune that removes
things this PR deliberately keeps also scores 100% on it.

## 🔍 Related Issues

Refs #4110 (GDN cold-compile CI time). Continues #4513, which trimmed this file on the same principle.
Found #5381 while auditing coverage for this PR — pre-existing, not addressed here.
Filed #5389 from this PR's own CI failure — the Cake GDN frozen-variant lookup compares a float with `==`.

---

## Independent perf measurement red-team review

The headline was re-measured adversarially: separate checkouts, per-arm cache isolation verified empty before
and populated after, GPU clocks and temperature logged at every boundary.

| arm | tree | instrumentation | result | `.o` |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| base1 | `upstream/main` | none | 418 passed, **1936.77s** | 268 |
| pr1 | this PR | none | 251 passed, **1302.31s** | 190 |
| prprobe | this PR | `specprobe` | 2 failed, 249 passed, 1289.60s | 190 |
| base2 | `upstream/main` | none | 418 passed, 1922.56s | 268 |

**−32.5% ± 0.5 pp** pooled (1935s → 1307s, saving 628 ± 10s); −32.8% on the adjacent back-to-back pair.
The effect is roughly 40σ against a base-arm sd of 10.9s. `base2` ran last and came in *faster* than
`base1`, so there is no thermal or ordering drift; clocks stayed pinned at 1830 MHz and 46–47 °C.

Three objections closed. **Probe overhead is nil** — `prprobe` ran 12.7s *faster* than the identical
unprobed tree. **The 2 failures are probe artifacts**, reproduced on the PR branch with the probe and absent
without it on the same tree; both node ids are present in the collected 251. The cause is that the probe's
`functools.wraps` wrapper destroys `lru_cache.cache_clear`, which the test calls. **Compile dominance holds
without instrumentation**: rerunning the same 418 cases against a now-warm cache took **19.21s versus
1936.77s cold**, i.e. 99.0% of cold wall time is cache-miss cost. The 96.3% figure counts only time strictly
inside `cute.compile` and so understates it.

Artifact counts corroborate the specialization numbers independently: 268 and 190 `.o` files against 277 and
199 specializations — a gap of exactly 9 in every arm, matching the 9 `wy_output_only` kernels that never
persist to disk.

**Caveat:** these arms measure the first commit (251 cases). The review commits restore coverage at a cost of
7 specializations, so the current head should land slightly above this. Re-measurement of the head is running.

## Mutation testing the B=128 restoration — it does not hold up

I tried to justify the restored `batch_size=128` empirically rather than by argument, and the result went
against me. Method: one mutation per arm, `git checkout` between arms with `git diff --quiet` asserted
before and an exact changed-line count asserted after, a pristine control in the same harness, and a fresh
cache per arm. (An earlier copy-based harness silently carried a poison between arms and produced six
bogus failures; these numbers come from the rebuilt one.)

| mutation | B=1 | B=4 | B=16 | B=128 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none (control) | pass | — | — | pass |
| poison wide-vec `flat_idx_fla` (+1) | **pass** | fail | fail | fail |
| poison MTP `fla_idx` (+1) | **fail** | — | — | **pass** |
| narrow `flat_idx_fla` to 32-bit | pass | pass | pass | **pass** |

Two conclusions.

**The Int64 widen is not guarded at any batch size here.** Narrowing the flat index to 32-bit — the faithful
form of the pre-#3502 bug, types kept consistent so it wraps silently instead of tripping the DSL's type
check — passes everywhere, B=128 included. This is not a no-op mutation: the three arms emit three different
cubins (`sha256` of the compiled objects differs across control, poison and narrow), so the code really
changed and the assertion really did not notice. B=128's offset does exceed the boundary arithmetically
(pool ≥ B·(T+1)=1152 slots → 1152·64·128·128·2 = 2.42e9 > 2³¹), but nothing in the comparison detects it.
So the comment I added claiming B=128 guards the widen is **wrong**, and by extension the original B=256
was not guarding it either.

**What the batch axis does separate is kernels, not overflow.** B=1 dispatches the MTP ILP4 kernel and B≥4
dispatches `gdn_wide_vec_kernel` — each poison fails on exactly one side. That is real coverage, and it
argues for keeping both a small and a non-small batch. It does not distinguish B=128 from B=16, which is
already retained.

On that evidence B=128 buys no detectable coverage over B=16. I have left it in rather than quietly
re-cutting it, because absence of detection by one mutation is not proof of absence of value, and the cost
is small: the review restorations together add 47.6s (1302.3s → 1349.9s). Happy to drop it — say the word
and I will, and re-measure. If it stays, the comment needs the correction above so it does not assert a
guarantee the suite does not provide.

## Review follow-ups

Three commits respond to independent review of the first commit:

- **`fix(gdn): canonicalize the default scale`** — extended the fix into `gdn_decode.py`. **Reverted**, see
  below; it broke the Cake GDN AOT path and was not contributing to the saving.
- **`test(gdn): restore coverage flagged in review`** — three cuts removed real coverage rather than duplicate
  compiles. `fla_scatter_vs_dense` at B=256 was the only bf16 case reaching past the Int32 byte-offset
  boundary the `Int64(pool_slot_t)` widen exists for (widen and B=256 arrived together in #3502); restored at
  B=128, which still exceeds the boundary at 1.13× at roughly half the memory, matching the fp32 twin. **See
  the mutation testing section — the stated guard does not reproduce, and this restoration is up for
  discussion.** `seq_len=2` is the
  structurally distinct MTP case that #4513 kept deliberately because it alone reaches the `ilp=8` and
  `tile_v=16 / ilp=2` branches; restored where it was the sole provider. `cache_intermediate_states` is a code
  path flag excluded from the cache key by #4128, so a specialization metric cannot see its removal.
- **`test(gdn): refresh comments invalidated by the prune`** — two comments described a matrix that no longer
  exists, including a design note recording the intent to sweep large batches.

## The library half of this broke CI

Pipeline [69113436](https://nv/flashinfer-ci/-/pipelines/69113436) came back with **297 new failures in
`tests.gdn.test_cake_gdn_decode_gpu`** across B200, GB200 and GB300 — every Blackwell datacentre lane.
H100 and RTX Pro 6000 were unaffected. The cause was the library half of change 1, now reverted in
`56c5ac4f`.

`flashinfer/jit/cake_gdn.py` picks a frozen AOT variant by exact dict comparison, and that dict contains a
float:

```python
and record["specializations"] == specializations   # {"H": ..., "HV": ..., "SCALE": scale}
```

The frozen manifest stores `SCALE: 0.08838834764831845`, which is `128**-0.5`. Spelling the same quantity
`1.0 / math.sqrt(128)` gives `0.08838834764831843` — one ULP lower — so all 16 matching variants missed and
the path failed closed with `CakeGDNUnsupportedError`. So `K**-0.5` in `gdn_decode.py` is load-bearing, with
nothing in the source saying so.

Confirmed causally rather than by inspection: on this B200, the same case fails on the old head and passes
with only `gdn_decode.py` reverted, and the local error string matches the pipeline's exactly. The full
`test_cake_gdn_decode_gpu` file is now 72 passed / 2 skipped.

This is a good argument for the red-team's point that the edit was never a pure spelling change. I have
filed #5389 for the underlying fragility, whose main ask is a CPU-only test asserting the library's computed
scale is present in the manifest — that would have caught this in milliseconds instead of a 25-job GPU
pipeline.

## Relationship to #5313

#5313 converts two of this file's functions to `parametrize_product`; measured on its own it takes this file
from 32m28s to 30m26s (−6.3%). On this file the two are alternatives rather than complements: after this prune
the affected matrices are 6 and 8 cases and `pairwise_product_cases` returns 6 and 8, so pairwise adds nothing
further. They edit the same two decorators — happy to rebase onto #5313 if it lands first.

title: fix(gdn): honor Q/K normalization in GDN prefill
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

`chunk_gated_delta_rule` ignored `use_qk_l2norm_in_kernel=True` on the native prefill paths. Callers passing unnormalized Q/K could get incorrect results or NaNs. This PR normalizes Q/K before dispatch when the flag is enabled. The CuTe DSL kernel handles both tensors in one launch, accumulates in FP32 with epsilon `1e-6`, and casts back to the input dtype. Calls with the flag disabled keep their existing behavior.

The normalization helper supports BF16, FP16, and FP32 with any positive D up to 64 KiB per row, including non-power-of-two sizes. That means D up to 32,768 for BF16/FP16 and 16,384 for FP32. Copy width follows row alignment, and wider rows use a reduction across multiple warps. Existing GDN backend shape requirements still apply.

### Normalization performance

I benchmarked Q/K normalization on NVIDIA B200 (SM100) against the original kernel in this PR, FLA, and cuDNN Frost. The updated kernel is 1.61–1.67× faster than the original across the 25 shapes tested.

Q and K are BF16 tensors with shape `[B,T,64,128]`. The sweep uses `B = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16` and `T = 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384, 32768`. Times below are microseconds to normalize both Q and K, reported as the median of three repetition medians.

I used CUDA graphs with preallocated outputs, 10 calls per graph, 25 ms warmup, and 100 timed replays per repetition. Kernel order was shuffled between repetitions. The comparison uses the original kernel from `471bb863` and the current general-D kernel from `8cbae530`.

| B | T | Previous kernel | Updated kernel | FLA | cuDNN Frost |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 2048 | 34.358 | 21.248 | 23.702 | 21.043 |
| 4 | 8192 | 515.011 | 317.253 | 319.005 | 313.320 |
| 16 | 32768 | 8208.646 | 5071.792 | 5057.456 | 5007.949 |

<details>

| B | T | Previous kernel | Updated kernel | FLA | cuDNN Frost |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

</details>

The baselines are [FLA's L2Norm kernel at `864a87f6`](https://github.com/fla-org/flash-linear-attention/blob/864a87f6ce5be8828bef81eb22baafd41937cdf2/fla/modules/l2norm.py) and [cuDNN Frost's L2Norm kernel at `667fe4ce`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/667fe4ce8ce437866217066f075fd4dcecad6eac/python/cudnn/linear_attention/frost/common/l2norm.py). FLA uses separate launches for Q and K. FlashInfer and Frost use one launch. FLA and Frost also write inverse norms.

For BF16/FP16 at D=128, the kernel handles four rows per thread and 64 rows per 256-thread block. B200 SASS confirms 128-bit global loads and stores with no register spills. Both dtypes use FP32 accumulation.

I also compared the current kernel with the preceding D=128-only version (`27638275`) on B200. The largest timing increase across these three shapes was 2.04%. Times are in microseconds, using the same setup above.

I profiled the original and updated kernels separately with Nsight Compute on B200. GB/s uses measured DRAM read and write bytes divided by the duration of the same profiled launch. The peak percentage is Nsight's sustained-throughput metric. Each entry averages two profiles with warmed inputs, application replay, and cache flushing and clock control disabled.

| 4 | 8192 | 4039 | 6999 | 52.6% | 91.2% |

title: perf(gemm): persist SM100 MXFP8 CuTeDSL kernels
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

I completed the primary design and final review of this change. I also
configured a Linux/CUDA 13/PyTorch/CuTeDSL environment and exercised the full
cache lifecycle end to end: compile an SM100-targeted kernel, persist its object
artifact, start a fresh Python process, recover that artifact from disk, and
JIT-link it without recompiling the kernel.

SM100 MXFP8 CuTeDSL GEMM currently keeps compiled kernels only in the
process-local `_CUTE_DSL_MM_MXFP8_KERNEL_CACHE`. A new serving process therefore
recompiles the same persistent and split-K specializations. The workload in
#4932 reports more than ten minutes of startup compilation for a vLLM model.

This change routes SM100 MXFP8 GEMM through FlashInfer's existing persistent
CuTeDSL cache:

1. Add an MXFP8-specific artifact name containing every specialization field:
   scale-vector size, MMA tile, cluster shape, operand swap, prefetch, PDL,
   output dtype, split-K slices, batch size, and maximum active clusters.
2. Include the persistent SM100 kernel, common helpers, and split-K kernel in
   the module source fingerprint so source changes invalidate stale objects.
3. Preserve the existing device-scoped in-process cache and the default FP4 and
   B12x behavior of the shared compilation helper.
4. Add cache-key collision, source-fingerprint, helper-routing, and actual
   persistent/split-K runner-wiring tests.

### Kernel-availability microbenchmark

Functional cross-architecture measurement on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060
(SM120), CUDA 13 nightly PyTorch `2.15.0.dev20260908+cu130`, CuTeDSL `4.7.1`,
with `CUTE_DSL_ARCH=sm_100a`. Each timing starts after imports and uses a fresh
Python process. The tested persistent specialization is MXFP8, BF16 output,
`sf_vec_size=32`, MMA tile `(128, 128)`, cluster `(1, 1)`, no prefetch/PDL, and
no split-K. M/N/K are symbolic in this compiled wrapper.

| Scenario | Runs | Median | Relative to current behavior |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Current-path equivalent: compile directly in every new process | 0.977 / 0.911 / 0.898 s | **0.911 s** | 1.0× |
| This PR, first process with an empty disk cache | 1.133 s | **1.133 s** | one-time compile + export |
| This PR, subsequent processes loading the cached object | 0.190 / 0.187 / 0.195 s | **0.190 s** | **4.8× faster** |

The split-K specialization (`mma_tiler_mn=(128, 8)`, two K slices) was also
compiled and reloaded in separate processes: **1.128 s cold → 0.173 s hot**.

The final post-rebase submission gate repeated both paths with fresh cache
state. Persistent GEMM produced a 48,496-byte object (**1.189 s cold → 0.181 s
hot**), and split-K produced a 50,280-byte object (**1.079 s cold → 0.190 s
hot**). For each hot run, the compile closure was replaced with a sentinel that
raises if called; the new process still loaded successfully, directly proving
that it recovered and JIT-linked the persisted artifact instead of recompiling.
With `FLASHINFER_CUTE_DSL_DISABLE_CACHE=1`, the persistent specialization
compiled successfully in **1.018 s** and created no object artifact, validating
the opt-out/fallback path.

These numbers validate the complete compilation, persistence, cross-process
cache recovery, and JITLink lifecycle end to end. Because the available GPU is
SM120 rather than SM100, this validation cross-compiles for `sm_100a`; it does
not claim B200/GB200 numerical kernel execution or a full-model vLLM benchmark.

Fixes #4932.

title: refactor(tvm_ffi_utils): add named tensor-argument check helpers
body:
## Summary

Add five named tensor-argument check helpers to `csrc/tvm_ffi_utils.h`:

- `check_cuda_tensor(t, name)`
- `check_dtype(t, DLDataType expected, name)`
- `check_contiguous(t, name)`
- `check_same_device(t, reference, name, reference_name)`
- `check_dense_leading_dims(t, trailing, name)`

The existing `CHECK_*` macros stringify the C++ variable and raise an internal
error. These functions take the user-facing argument name and raise
`ValueError` or `TypeError` with a message that identifies the argument and the
mismatch (device type, DLPack dtype triple, or the exact stride that breaks a
dense fold), so a Python caller can act on the message without reading the
binding.

Several generated binding families currently carry byte-identical private
copies of these checks in every translation unit. With the helpers in the
shared header those bindings can call them directly; a follow-up regenerates
them without the inline copies.

## Test plan

- Compiled a translation unit that includes `csrc/tvm_ffi_utils.h` and calls
  every new helper together with `ffi::CUDADeviceGuard` and `get_stream`
  (nvcc 13.3, tvm-ffi headers).
- Header-only additive change; no existing symbol or macro is modified.

title: feat(rope): fuse QK norm, RoPE, and paged KV append
body:
## 📌 Description

This PR adds experimental, JIT-only fused preprocessing kernels for packed BF16 QKV serving workloads. In one launch they perform Q/K RMSNorm, NeoX RoPE, Q output production, and NHD paged K/V-cache append.

Two thin experimental APIs are added in `flashinfer.rope`:

- `fused_qk_rmsnorm_rope_append_paged_kv_cache` for BF16 output/cache;
- `fused_qk_rmsnorm_rope_quantize_fp8_append_paged_kv_cache` for FP8 E4M3 output/cache with dynamic or static Q scaling.

Backend validation, JIT compilation, and CUDA code live under `flashinfer/experimental/fused_qk_rope_append/`. The initial specialization is SM90/SM100, head dimension 128, `(Hq, Hkv) = (8, 1)` or `(64, 8)`, and NHD paged caches. Nothing is registered in AOT or automatic routing.

The kernels are adapted from Tencent hpc-ops `rope_norm_store_kv` and `rope_norm_store_kv_fp8` at commit `2a2e26562433a8ba4b504858f1c938eb7612c901`, with MIT attribution retained in `licenses/LICENSE.hpc-ops.txt`.

### Performance

NVIDIA B200 (SM100), CUDA 13.3, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130. CUPTI cold-L2 medians with 10 warm-up and 30 measured iterations:

| Workload | Fused | Stable primitive pipeline | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| B=32, Q=1, Hq=8, Hkv=1, D=128, context=2048 | 0.005280 ms | 0.030368 ms | 5.752x |
| B=8, Q=16, Hq=8, Hkv=1, D=128, context=2048 | 0.005344 ms | 0.034015 ms | 6.365x |

title: feat(sparse): add experimental adaptive block-mask selection
body:
## 📌 Description

This PR adds an experimental, JIT-only adaptive sparse block-mask selector derived from Tencent hpc-ops Stem TPD.

The new `flashinfer.sparse.adaptive_sparse_block_mask` entry point converts contiguous BF16 block-level proxy logits into a per-head boolean mask in one CUDA launch. It combines:

- prompt-length-dependent and per-query sparse budgets;
- exact BF16 radix-threshold selection;
- mandatory prefix/sink and causal diagonal-window retention;
- caller-owned output support.

The core entry point is intentionally thin. Backend logic, JIT compilation, and the CUDA kernel live under `flashinfer/experimental/adaptive_sparse_block_mask/`; nothing is registered in AOT or automatic backend routing.

title: feat(comm): add SageAttention2 low-precision QKV exchange to UlyssesCommunicator
body:
## 📌 Description

Extend `flashinfer.comm.UlyssesCommunicator` with `prepare_qkv()` and `scatter_qkv()` for low-precision input communication. They accept FP16/BF16 Q/K/V sequence shards, quantize and pack them before all-to-all, and return the received SageAttention2 operands plus scales and metadata. Internally, Q/K are encoded as INT8 and V as FP8 E4M3. Quantization groups remain on the global sequence grid across rank boundaries.

The caller supplies the process group and attention invocation. The communicator prepares reusable storage and owns one statistics AllGather and one combined payload AllToAll on that group's NCCL backend. Existing `scatter_heads()` / `gather_heads()` behavior and backend selection are preserved. Lowp numeric helpers live in the private `_ulysses_lowp.py` module; the former public module and duplicate `flashinfer.comm` exports are removed.

[Design and numerical contracts](https://github.com/DwenGu/flashinfer/blob/44e3c6b1a9fa1e2a1f2dd1b6c43da8e654ceb860/docs/design_docs/ulysses_lowp.md) · [Distributed acceptance example](https://github.com/DwenGu/flashinfer/blob/44e3c6b1a9fa1e2a1f2dd1b6c43da8e654ceb860/benchmarks/comm/validate_ulysses_lowp.py) · [Communicator benchmark](https://github.com/DwenGu/flashinfer/blob/44e3c6b1a9fa1e2a1f2dd1b6c43da8e654ceb860/benchmarks/comm/bench_ulysses_qkv.py).

### Execution and API

```python
from flashinfer.comm import UlyssesCommunicator

with UlyssesCommunicator(group, max_bytes=3 * q.nbytes, dtype=q.dtype,
                         device=q.device, backend="nccl") as comm:
    workspace = comm.prepare_qkv(q.shape, quantization="sage2", used_sequence=used)
    encoded = comm.scatter_qkv(q, k, v, workspace=workspace)
    # Call the framework's Sage2 adapter with encoded operands and scales.
    # For subsequent serialized calls, reuse output storage with out=encoded.
```

Preparation is collective and validates configuration, layout/JIT availability and allocation outcomes across ranks. Each execution checks actual input/output metadata and storage overlap, then invokes shared private stage implementations without repeating the standalone wrappers' checks. QKV projection views are accepted without three full contiguous copies. `UlyssesQKV` contains six tensors plus layout, logical/live sequence lengths and input dtype; `out=None` owns independent storage and `out=encoded` reuses it. The `max_bytes` budget must cover the complete packed input or output operand: `P * chunk_bytes`, including Q/K/V, transmitted scales and alignment. `3 * q.nbytes` is a conservative budget for the supported layouts; `q.nbytes` alone is insufficient. Preparation checks the exact requirement collectively and allocates the actual payload size. Statistics and final attention inputs have separate allocations, so this is not a total memory budget.

The shared transport API follows the signatures proposed in [PR #4876 at `299166db`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/299166db93e23c3c2859134cf0d5c2ee1bdb90cf/flashinfer/comm/ulysses.py):

| Entry point | Contract |
|---|---|
| `UlyssesCommunicator(group, *, max_bytes, dtype, backend="auto", device=None)` | Capacity is in bytes per complete operand. Migrate the former `max_elems=N` to `max_bytes=N * dtype.itemsize`; Lowp must additionally cover its combined payload |
| `create_workspace(*, max_elems=None)` | Ordinary staging capacity remains in elements; the default is `max_bytes // dtype.itemsize` |
| `allocate_output(x, op, *, dtype=None)` | Allocate correctly shaped receive storage for scatter, gather or chunk exchange; ordinary local PyTorch allocation |
| `exchange_chunks(x, *, out=None, dtype=None)` | Exchange contiguous `[1, 1, P, C]` chunks: destination-major send, source-major receive |
| `scatter_heads(x, *, out=None, dtype=None, workspace=None)` / `gather_heads(...)` | Preserve existing floating-point transforms; current backends reject dtype overrides for these two operations |

Lowp uses zero-copy views of its packed payload and calls `allocate_output(..., "exchange_chunks", dtype=torch.uint8)` during preparation and `exchange_chunks(..., dtype=torch.uint8)` during execution. The override selects the dtype of already encoded storage; it does not convert or requantize values. Chunk exchange supports FP16/BF16/FP32/UINT8 and uses NCCL with both current `nccl` and `nvlink` communicator backends. This is API alignment only: it adds no PCIe/RDMA backend or buffer registration. Ordinary head transforms retain their existing transport selection. The Lowp numerical implementation, scales, payload bytes, Sage2 operands and CUDA kernels are unchanged by this alignment.

One `BOUNDARY_MERGE` computation path handles aligned and nonaligned shards. Boundary statistics are merged for every rank contributing to a global quantization group, including groups spanning more than two ranks. The single FP32 statistics AllGather carries K sums, V channel maxima, Q boundary maxima and K boundary extrema. Quantize-and-pack consumes the finalized scales; the receiver applies Sage's V permutation and reconstructs global Q/K scale arrays.

Both architecture modules compile head dimensions 64 and 128. `prepare_qkv()` selects the device layout and dimension from the supplied shape; callers do not construct layout objects. Host bindings and kernel templates are shared across architecture specializations.

### Supported configurations and contracts

| Property | Contract |
|---|---|
| Input | Q/K/V with identical `[B, L, H, D]` shape, CUDA device and FP16/BF16 dtype; positive B/L/H; D=64 or 128 |
| Distribution | Equal L on all ranks; H divisible by P; the prepared Lowp API accepts P=2/4/8 and rejects P=1/6. Ordinary communicator behavior is unchanged |
| Sequence | Arbitrary positive local L; global live prefix `0 < U <= P*L`; caller zero-fills the global tail before sharding |
| SM90 | Q groups of 16 tokens; K groups of 128; V storage padded to 128 rows |
| SM120 | Q groups of 32 tokens; K groups of 64; V storage padded to 64 rows |
| Memory layout | Dense D axis with 16-byte-aligned row addresses, including interleaved projection views; exact contiguous output buffers |
| Numeric behavior | FP32 K sums, mean divided by U and rounded to input dtype before centering; Q/K grouped-amax floor `1e-7`; V channel scale `amax / 2.25`, with zero-amax channels encoded as positive zero |
| Consumer buffers | Initialize the entire required scale allocation, unused payload slots and storage tails. Extra Q scales for invalid rows may be finite nonzero values |

SM89 compilation is retained but is outside the current hardware acceptance matrix. GQA/MQA with different Q/KV head counts, unequal rank shard lengths, per-example ragged lengths, training, multi-node execution, and CUDA graph/`torch.compile` integration are outside this submission's validated scope.

### Performance evidence

#### SM90: latest transport API alignment (`59e4fbe8` → `44e3c6b1`)

8× NVIDIA H20-3e (SM90), PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0; P=8, B=1, H=56, D=128, BF16, U=P×L, seed `2101 + rank`. The old implementation A is frozen at `59e4fbe8`; B is the source now committed as `44e3c6b1`.
