title: perf: DSA Indexer-Topk fused kernel: litetopk
body:
## 📌 Description

Hi @yzh119 @bkryu @aleozlx @yongwww @yyihuang, could you please take a look at this PR when you have a chance?

This PR proposes a fused DSA Indexed-TopK kernel (LiteTopk), which never materializes the [num_q, seq_len] matrix. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first of its kind. The corresponding paper is available at https://github.com/Heisenberg-Yin/LiteTopK/blob/main/flashtopk.pdf. **LiteTopK accelerates GLM-5.2 1M-token prefill by 1.2× without accuracy loss.**

DSA models such as **GLM-4.6 / GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-V3.2, and DeepSeek-V4** run a lightweight
*indexer* before main attention: an fp8 multi-query attention scores every KV
position against each query to produce a `[num_q, seq_len]` logit matrix, and the
**top-k** KV positions per query are selected so that main attention only attends
to those.

**At long context (256K–1M) this indexer top-k becomes a real bottleneck for both memory overhead and latency**, because the common path **materializes the full `[num_q, seq_len]` fp32 logit
matrix** in HBM and then runs a per-row top-k over it — an `O(num_q × seq_len)`
transient buffer and two passes over it.

LiteTopK avoids storing the score matrix in the following way:

1. **fp8 MQA scoring** of each KV tile against the queries (tcgen05 UMMA, compiled
   against the SM100 headers of the installed `deep_gemm` package);
2. maintain an **online bucketed gate** that keeps only candidates above a running,
   self-calibrating threshold, so the vast majority of positions are discarded on
   the fly — spare warps tighten the threshold while the scan runs;
3. a **compact, exact top-k** over the surviving candidates.

Working memory is a **constant-size candidate buffer** (`cand_cap`, independent of
`seq_len`; `6 * num_q * cand_cap` bytes) instead of an `O(num_q × seq_len)` logit
matrix. The gate is seeded from `prefix_logits`, the logits of a prefix `kv[:P]` that
the caller computes with any dense kernel. For chunked prefill, placing the previous
chunk's selected positions in the prefix gives a tighter seed so even fewer candidates
survive the scan.

## 🔄 Changes since the previous revision

Restructured against `main` as a **self-contained experimental package**, following the
existing `flashinfer.experimental.*` convention:

- Everything now lives under `flashinfer/experimental/dsa_indexer/`, with `csrc/**`
  registered in `pyproject.toml` so non-editable installs ship the CUDA sources.
- **Dropped the vendored DeepGEMM headers.** The kernels now compile against the SM100
  headers of the installed `deep_gemm` package (the layout of DeepGEMM `891d57b4`, the
  commit the FlashInfer EP image installs). The DeepSeek MIT license is retained
  alongside the sources.
- The public entry point is gated by `@flashinfer_experimental_api`, so **no
  `flashinfer/__init__.py` change** and no automatic backend selection — calling it is
  the opt-in.
- The API now returns a `status` tensor alongside the indices, so a row the candidate
  buffer cannot certify is reported rather than silently wrong.
- Added a benchmark script and a substantially expanded test suite (below).

### API

```python
import flashinfer

# q:             [num_q, 32, 128]   fp8_e4m3
# kv:            [seq_kv, 128]      fp8_e4m3   (seq_kv <= 2**20)
# kv_scales:     [seq_kv]           fp32       (per-position dequant scale, padded to a multiple of 4)
# weights:       [num_q, 32]        fp32       (per-head gate weights)
# prefix_logits: [num_q, P]         fp32       (gate seed; 2048 <= P <= 8192 or P == 12288)
# cu_end:        [num_q]            int32      (exclusive causal end per query)
idx, status = flashinfer.dsa_indexer.dsa_indexer_topk(
    q, kv, kv_scales, weights, prefix_logits, cu_end,
    top_k=2048,
    cand_cap=49152,   # candidates per row, constant and seq_len-independent
)  # idx: [num_q, 2048] int32, unordered; status: [num_q] int32, nonzero marks an invalid row
```

The prefix positions are candidates too, and the scan covers `[P, cu_end[i])`. A caller
that reorders `kv` to build a tighter prefix must keep every query's visible set (hot
positions below `cu_end.min()` first, the rest in order) and map the returned indices
back.

### Limitations

- SM100 (compute capability 10.0) only; requires the `deep_gemm` package installed.
- 32 heads, head dim 128, fp8 e4m3 `q`/`kv`, `top_k == 2048` (GLM-5).
- `P <= cu_end.min()` is required but not checked.
- Indices are unordered; among positions whose scores tie at the selection boundary,
  the kept ones can differ between runs.

## 📊 Results

**Kernel-level validation (B200, real GLM-5.2 indexer tensors, Q=8192, top_k=2048).** We compared LiteTopk against the dense logits + TopK baseline. The main motivation is the substantial memory overhead of the dense path, which grows rapidly with context length: **8 GB at 256K, 12 GB at 512K, 24 GB at 768K, and 32 GB at 1M**. The fused kernel removes this overhead while preserving the top-k result.

| seq_len | dense memory overhead | our memory overhead | dense logits + top-k | fused | speedup | recall vs dense |
|--------:|----------------------:|--------------------:|---------------------:|------:|--------:|----------------:|
|    256K |                  8 GB |              1.5 GB |            13.04 ms  |  11.95 ms |  1.09×  |        100.00 % |
|    512K |                 12 GB |              1.1 GB |            25.99 ms  |  21.95 ms |  1.18×  |        100.00 % |
|    768K |                 24 GB |              0.7 GB |            39.57 ms  |  31.87 ms |  1.24×  |        100.00 % |
|      1M |                 32 GB |              0.0 GB |            52.64 ms  |  42.06 ms |  1.25×  |        100.00 % |

- Fused-vs-dense TopK recall is **100.00%** across tested settings.
- In end-to-end GLM-5.2 prefill, LiteTopK achieves **1.2×** speedup at 1M context and **1.1×** speedup at 768K context without loss.

`benchmarks/bench_dsa_indexer_topk.py` reproduces the latency and memory comparison
against the dense path (`deep_gemm.fp8_mqa_logits` + `flashinfer.top_k`):

```bash
python benchmarks/bench_dsa_indexer_topk.py --num-q 8192 --seq-kv 262144 1048576
```

## 🗂️ Files

Self-contained under `flashinfer/experimental/dsa_indexer/`, matching the existing
`flashinfer.experimental.*` packages.

| File | Lines | Role |
|------|------:|------|
| `flashinfer/experimental/dsa_indexer/csrc/dsa_indexer_scan.cuh` | 787 | Fused fp8 MQA scan + online bucket gate |
| `flashinfer/experimental/dsa_indexer/csrc/dsa_indexer_select.cuh` | 510 | Exact top-k over the candidate buffer |

| `flashinfer/experimental/dsa_indexer/csrc/LICENSE.deepseek-deepgemm` | 21 | DeepSeek MIT license |

| `pyproject.toml` | +2 | Ship `csrc/**` as package data |

## 🧪 Tests

`tests/experimental/test_dsa_indexer.py`, gated to SM100 (skips on non-Blackwell) and
`importorskip`s `deep_gemm`:

- `test_recall` — `recall.mean() > 0.999` and `recall.min() > 0.99` against a dense
  `deep_gemm` fp32 reference, over `seq_kv ∈ {65536, 262144}`, `num_q ∈ {128, 1024}`,
  `prefix_len ∈ {8192, 12288}`. Also asserts every index is in range, no duplicates,
  and `status == 0`.
- `test_shape_edges` — odd `num_q`/`seq_kv`/`prefix_len` combinations and padded row
  strides.
- `test_boundary_ties` — all-tied scores at the selection boundary.
- `test_candidate_overflow_sets_status` — a prefix too poor to certify the rows sets a
  nonzero `status` and returns `-1` indices rather than a wrong answer.
- `test_empty_batch` — zero queries.

title: perf(cake_kda): regenerate the BF16 KDA modules from the current Cake revision
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

Follow-up to #5363 (merged as `c6ec2cc`); this branch is rebased on `main`
and contains only the regeneration commit.

The BF16 KDA prefill modules published by #5278 were generated before the Cake
codegen changed its lane-id derivation and `griddepcontrol` placement. The
346-row source-versus-export replay in #5363 measured those modules 1-22%
slower than the kernels the current Cake revision generates for the same
schedule (largest: `fused_checkpoint_direct_m128_page64_n32x2`, 1.18x on B200
and 1.21x on GB300), while the one module #5363 generated from the current
revision replayed at parity. Output was bitwise identical in both cases.

This PR regenerates every SM100a and SM103a BF16 module from Cake `74220f6`
(the #5363 source revision) with `export_bf16.py --replace-existing`: each
published specialization now points at its regenerated module, the superseded
generated sources are removed, and modules whose generated code did not change
keep their identity. No host dispatch, public API or routing change.

### Export parity and Triton comparison

Same protocol as #5363: for every one of the 346 inventory rows, in one
process per row, the Cake source dispatcher (Cake `74220f6`) and the exported
FlashInfer API are prepared on identical fixtures, must select the same
schedule, are compared bitwise on output, final state and checkpoints, and are
then captured into caller-owned CUDA graphs and replayed under cold-L2 CUPTI
(three alternating groups, median). The pinned SGLang FLA `chunk_kda` Triton
baseline (`24c9251a`, the #5278 baseline) is captured and replayed the same way
in the same process, with sigmoid applied to logit beta on the host as in the
#5278 campaign. "Before" is the #5363 head measured in #5363; "after" is this
branch with a fresh JIT workspace. B200 rows ran on NSC (148 SMs), GB300 rows
on OCI AGA (152 SMs).

Triton/export speedup over 346 rows: min 1.20x, median 3.34x, max 12.88x; rows below 1.0x: 0.

## Description

`test_gdn_decode_bf16_state_fla_scatter_padded_pool` builds a padded, non-contiguous pool but passes `pool_padded.clone()` to the kernel. `clone()` preserves strides only for dense tensors, so the clone is contiguous and the test compares the flat scatter path with itself. It never compiles a `per_token_pool_scatter_flat=False` kernel.

The test now clones the backing allocation and re-slices it, asserts that the pool under test is non-contiguous, and checks that the per-slot padding is unchanged after the call (vLLM keeps conv state there).

Test-only. The slot-slice fallback is correct on SM120: it matches the flat path bit for bit.

title: feat(mla): uniform LSE base semantics via return_lse_base_on_e
body:
## 📌 Description

`return_lse_base_on_e` is a guarantee about the *units* of the returned LSE, not a
transformation request: `True` yields base-e and `False` base-2 whichever backend ran,
while `None` preserves each backend's historical default. Before this PR the parameter
was only honored by some paths, so the same flag could return different units depending
on which kernel the dispatcher picked.

All three MLA backends compute LSE in base 2 internally, so the parameter is realized as
a float multiplier applied **at the store site** rather than as a Python post-scale. That
keeps the semantics uniform instead of having one backend scale in Python and the others
in the kernel.

- **trtllm-gen** — `lseScale` on `TllmGenFmhaRunnerParams`, applied in `lse.cuh` as
  `lse[out_idx] = lse_scale * (log2e * m + log2(d))`.
- **cute-dsl monolithic** — log scale plumbed through `mla_dispatch` into both the fp16
  and fp8 decode kernels, which carry separate LSE stores.
- **sparse (SM120/SM121)** — threaded to the three user-facing stores: the decode merge
  kernel shared by both decode entries, plus the SG and MG prefill epilogues.
  `double` at the three TVM-FFI entries, `float` below, mirroring `sm_scale`.

`None` keeps existing behavior per backend: base-2 for trtllm-gen and sparse, base-e for
monolithic cute-dsl. The non-MLA trtllm-gen decode/prefill entry points pass
`lse_scale = 1.0`; that ABI widening is signature-only, no behavior change.

AI-assisted: analysis, debugging, and the tests were written with Claude Code; the kernel
and plumbing changes are the author's.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Two new suites, both gated on the hardware they need:

- `tests/attention/test_mla_lse_base.py` — 25 cases, green on **B200** (trtllm-gen and
  cute-dsl). Covers both `split_kv` branches of the monolithic kernel, since the epilogue
  and the reduction kernel each own a user-facing LSE store, and both bf16 and fp8, since
  `mla_decode_fp16.py` and `mla_decode_fp8.py` are near-duplicate files.
- `tests/attention/test_sparse_mla_sm120_lse_base.py` — 44 cases, green on **8× RTX PRO
  6000 Blackwell** (sparse). Pins one shape per kernel store, since SG and MG prefill are
  separate templates with their own epilogues, and additionally covers the `attn_sink`
  merge, per-token `topk_length`, caller-supplied `lse` buffers, and the empty-row
  sentinel.

Both suites assert the *other* base is not returned, so a no-op wiring can't pass on
tolerance alone, and assert `None`/`False` are bit-identical where the backend's native
base is 2.

## Reviewer Notes

A few deliberate choices worth a look:

1. **The `-1e30f` empty-row sentinel is written unscaled** at every sparse store
   (`(x != -1e30f) ? lse_scale * x : x`). It marks a row with no candidates rather than a
   log-domain value, and callers compare against the literal, so scaling it would
   silently break that comparison. Happy to flip this if you'd rather it scale — it's
   three call sites and one test assertion.
2. **The scale arithmetic is duplicated inline at the three sparse stores** rather than
   factored into a helper, so the multiply is visible at the point of the store. Same
   reasoning for the three `return_lse_base_on_e` → float derivations in `_core.py`
   (trtllm-gen, cute-dsl, sparse): they differ only in what `None` means, and a shared
   helper would need a `default_base_e` keyword plus a decision about non-`bool` input
   that the three sites currently answer differently. Easy to unify if you prefer it.
3. `lse_scale` sits **immediately after the LSE output** in every signature, C++ and
   Python alike. TVM-FFI is positional, so this was chosen to make a misordering a
   compile or type error rather than a silent swap with `sm_scale`.

title: feat(comm): add fused decode CP A2A + LSE reduce
body:
## 📌 Description

### Why this is needed

In context-parallel decode, the KV cache is sharded by sequence across ranks. Each rank runs attention against
its local KV shard and produces, for every query token and head:

- `o_r`: a partial attention output
- `lse_r`: the log-sum-exp that records that shard's softmax normalization

The `o_r` values cannot be summed directly: each was normalized over a different KV shard. To reconstruct
full-context attention, the partial outputs must be exchanged and merged with weights derived from all ranks'
LSEs:

`out = Σ_r softmax(lse)_r * o_r`

Each rank's input carries a `cp_size` axis containing the slices destined for the CP ranks. The `heads` axis may
contain either local or total heads: this op treats every batch/head entry independently and does not shard or
otherwise reinterpret the head axis.

### What this PR adds

Adds experimental `decode_cp_a2a_lse_reduce`, which fuses that all-to-all exchange and LSE-weighted merge into one
cooperative CUDA kernel.

```python
decode_cp_a2a_lse_reduce(
    partial_o: torch.Tensor,
    partial_lse: torch.Tensor,
    workspace: torch.Tensor,
    cp_rank: int,
    cp_size: int,
    lse_mode: Literal["base2", "basee"] = "base2",
) -> torch.Tensor
```

Input and output shapes:

- `partial_o`: `[batch, heads, cp_size, head_dim]` (`float16` or `bfloat16`)
- `partial_lse`: `[batch, heads, cp_size]` (`float32`)
- output: `[batch, heads, head_dim]`, with the same dtype as `partial_o`

More generally, arbitrary matching leading dimensions are supported:
`[..., cp_size, head_dim]` + `[..., cp_size]` → `[..., head_dim]`.

`lse_mode="base2"` accepts the base-2 LSE produced by FlashInfer MLA; `lse_mode="basee"` accepts natural-log
LSE. The op does not expose `enable_pdl` because its NCCL device kernel does not use programmatic dependent launch.

- Sends each peer's partial output and LSE together, then merges received contributions in the same kernel.
- Uses NCCL device load/store-accessible (LSA) symmetric memory rather than composing separate framework collectives.
- Supports eager execution and CUDA Graph replay with a collectively created, rendezvoused workspace.
- Requires all CP ranks to be in one NCCL LSA/NVLink domain. A workspace is single-stream; concurrent streams or
  graph-capture streams need separate workspaces.

This implements the NCCL-LSA scope of #4575.

## 🔍 Related Issues

- Implements the NCCL-LSA scope of #4575.
- Related design RFC: https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-extensions/issues/10

## 🧪 Tests

Focused validation:

- ✅ Distributed DCP LSE-reduce test: `15 passed` per rank with 4 processes
- ✅ CPU-safe DCP API/reference tests: `12 passed`
- ✅ DCP trace signature, axes, and completeness checks: `3 passed`
- ✅ All configured pre-commit hooks on the modified PR files
- ✅ Python syntax compilation for modified Python sources
- ✅ `git diff --check`
- ✅ Four-process BF16 benchmark on four H100 80 GB GPUs in one NVLink-connected LSA domain versus unfused legacy
  A2A plus LSE merge (max-rank median; 10 warm-ups, 30 samples, 50 launches/sample):

| Shape | Fused eager | Fused + graph* | Legacy A2A + merge | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| batch 1, heads 2, dim 64 | 12.14 µs | 10.15 µs | 178.91 µs | 14.7× |
| batch 1, heads 8, dim 128 | 15.04 µs | 13.24 µs | 179.22 µs | 11.9× |
| batch 4, heads 8, dim 128 | 18.04 µs | 16.40 µs | 178.73 µs | 9.9× |
| batch 16, heads 8, dim 128 | 18.96 µs | 17.02 µs | 180.88 µs | 9.5× |

* Fused + graph: groups 50 ops in one graph, reporting per-op average.

The largely flat legacy baseline shows that these decode-sized cases are dominated by fixed launch/collective
overhead; the speedup primarily reflects eliminating that overhead rather than a bandwidth improvement.

## Reviewer Notes

- This is the first FlashInfer op that directly uses NCCL device APIs. The new public API, AOT registration,
  trace template, documentation, tests, and benchmark are included in this PR.
- The restricted LSA/NVLink scope and the one-workspace-per-ordered-stream contract are intentional.

## Fused-kernel algorithm

For each token and attention head, every rank starts with a partial attention output $O_r$ and log-sum-exp $L_r$
from its local KV shard. The cooperative kernel completes the exchange and merge in one launch:

1. Block 0 advances a device-side epoch and selects one of two workspace slots, allowing safe slot rotation during
   CUDA Graph replay.
2. Each source rank writes its destination-specific output and LSE directly into the destination's NCCL
   symmetric-memory window using LSA/NVLink stores.
3. Sources publish system-scope release flags after their payloads are visible. Each destination acquire-waits for
   every source, then the cooperative grid synchronizes.
4. One block processes each token/head row. It computes stable rank-axis softmax weights:

$$
m = \max_r L_r, \qquad
w_r = \frac{\exp(L_r-m)}{\sum_j \exp(L_j-m)}.
$$

It then accumulates the combined output in FP32:

$$
O_{\mathrm{combined}}[d] = \sum_r w_r O_r[d].
$$

Base-2 LSE mode uses $2^{L_r-m}$. NaN and $+\infty$ LSEs are treated as $-\infty$; if every shard is empty, the
output is zero. The result is converted back to FP16 or BF16.

This removes the separate NCCL all-to-all and reduction launches by fusing peer transfer, readiness synchronization,
and the LSE-weighted merge. The implementation supports up to 64 ranks, requires one NCCL LSA/NVLink domain, and
requires each workspace to stay on one ordered CUDA stream.

title: fix(attention): materialize block_valid_mask for padded CUDA-graph prefill launches
body:
## 📌 Description

With CUDA graphs on and split-KV off, FA2 prefill can crash with `illegal memory access`.

Under CUDA graphs the kernel launches more blocks than the batch needs.
The extra blocks must be masked off.
The mask was only created when split-KV was on.
Without it the extra blocks read plan entries that were never written.
If the workspace still holds an earlier plan, they read out of bounds.

Who hits it:
- SGLang with `--enable-deterministic-inference` (tensor-core decode uses this planner).
- NVFP4 KV cache on Blackwell, where FlashInfer turns split-KV off itself.

Reproduced on an RTX 6000 Ada with the calls SGLang makes (16 requests, SGLang itself not run).
Fresh workspace: output happens to be correct.
Workspace reused from an earlier plan: crash.
With this PR both are correct.

Fix: create the mask whenever CUDA graphs are on.
Pass it to the kernel in every run function that uses the plan: ragged, paged, POD, batch POD.
Cost: `padded_batch_size` bytes of int workspace.
Plans without CUDA graphs no longer allocate the unused mask.

The regular cases are selected independently for each test using deterministic pairwise coverage (a strength-2 covering array). They are not sampled globally from the complete set of test nodes.

A full Cartesian product covers every higher-order interaction across all parameter axes, but grows exponentially. Selecting only one occurrence of every individual value is much cheaper, but can leave parameter values correlated and miss important two-parameter interactions. Pairwise coverage is the compromise:

> For every pair of parameter axes, every combination of their values appears in at least one regular case.

For example, three binary axes have eight full combinations. The following four cases cover every pair of values across `A/B`, `A/C`, and `B/C`:

```text
A0 B0 C0
A0 B1 C1
A1 B0 C1
A1 B1 C0
```

The selector:

1. Builds the set of all required value-pairs across every pair of axes.
2. Generates deterministic candidate rows containing each required pair.
3. Fills the remaining positions deterministically without materializing the complete Cartesian product.
4. Repeatedly selects the candidate covering the most uncovered pairs.
5. Stops when every required pair has appeared.

This greedy algorithm is deterministic and reproducible, although it does not guarantee the mathematically smallest possible covering array. Grouped parameter values remain atomic, preserving the valid combinations from the original tests.

title: feat(moe): opt-in fixed-order finalize for the SM12x b12x fused MoE
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## Description

`b12x_fused_moe` and `B12xMoEWrapper` get a keyword-only `use_fused_finalize` flag (default `True`, behaviour unchanged), with the same name and contract as `cutlass_fused_moe` (#3598) and the SM100 CuTe-DSL MoE (#3976). The unified b12x runners now pass `MoEFinalizeConfig.use_fused_finalize` to the wrapper; they ignored it before.

With `use_fused_finalize=False` every launch goes to the existing static kernel (#4718), which stores one BF16 contribution per route and sums top-k in FP32 in a fixed order. The micro kernels are skipped and the dynamic kernel is never selected. MoE output is per token, so inputs past the static band (1024 routed rows for NVFP4, 640 for MXFP4) run as token chunks of `band // top_k` tokens that write into slices of the output. There are no kernel changes. In this mode the wrapper allocates one chunk-sized static workspace and no dynamic workspace. `quant_mode="w4a16"` has no fixed-order finalize and raises `NotImplementedError` for the flag.

The docstrings of `b12x_fused_moe` and `B12xMoEWrapper` now state which paths repeat bit for bit.

### Measurements

RTX 5070 Ti (SM120), CUDA 13.2, torch 2.14.0+cu130, nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0. Setup from #5221: NVFP4, 8 experts, hidden 2048, intermediate 1024, identical inputs, outputs compared as int16 against a baseline call.

Default path on main @ 6870e3f, 3 repeats per shape (backend inferred from the dispatch thresholds):

| Default backend | Shapes (tokens x top-k) | Elements differing |
|---|---|---|
| MMA micro | 1 and 4 tokens x 1/2/4/8 | 24% to 85% |
| static | 16 and 128 tokens x 1/2/4/8, 512 x 1/2 | 0 |
| dynamic | 512 x 4/8, 4096 x 1/2/4/8 | 55% to 81% |

With `use_fused_finalize=False`: 0 elements differ in 3 repeats at 1 x 1, 4 x 8, 8 x 2, 16 x 8, 130 x 8 (2 chunks), 512 x 8 (4 chunks) and 4096 x 8 (32 chunks), and the SHA-256 of every output is the same in a second fresh process. 4096 x 8 cannot run as one static launch; `allocate_sm120_static_workspace` rejects it at the 2^31-1 memref limit.

Default path unchanged: at 16 x 1, 16 x 8, 128 x 8 and 512 x 2 (static backend) the default output hash on this branch equals upstream main for the same inputs. The micro and dynamic backends are not repeatable, so they cannot be compared this way; the existing b12x suites pass.

Other default paths:

- Direct micro (NVFP4 decode, intermediate <= 512; kernel selection instrumented): 0 differing in 5 repeats at 1 x 1, 1 x 8, 2 x 2, 3 x 8 and 7 x 4.

title: perf(cake_kda): route one-wave BF16 grids to the M64 value split
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

Follow-up to #5278. The BF16 KDA prefill export was slower than the pinned
SGLang FLA Triton baseline on B200 for `short/H12/mixed` (0.935x) and near
parity on three more packed rows, while the same rows ran 2-4x faster in
TF32. The export reproduced its source bit for bit; the source BF16 dispatcher
selected direct M128 tiles for those grids where its existing two-CTA M64
value split is faster.

This PR updates the BF16 host dispatch in `flashinfer/cake_kda_tf32_runtime.py`
(mirroring the source change) and adds the generated M64 modules that the new
routes select:

- One-wave rule: BF16 compute, bounded gate, 32-token aligned checkpoint
  interval and `2 * tasks <= sm_count` (both M64 value CTAs of every
  `(sequence, head)` task resident in one wave) replace a resolved direct M128
  route with the M64 value split. Forced tiles and TF32 are unchanged. Logit
  beta whose token pitch is not TMA-encodable is refreshed into a padded
  carrier every launch; short H12 grids (<= 256 tokens) that would need that
  copy keep their direct tile, because the H12 direct tiles load scalar beta.
- Active FP32 beta (`beta_is_logit=False`) takes the native M64 path on those
  grids instead of the per-launch `logit` + BF16 copy, except where the BF16
  affine split is eligible.
- Enabled on SM100a and SM103a.

### Measurement basis (source dispatcher, cold-L2 CUPTI)

Automatic route versus forced N16 / N32 / M64 / BT16 schedules on every
case (cold-L2 CUPTI, `bench_gpu_time`, 8 warmups / 48 samples):

| Sweep | Hardware | Cases | One-wave cases | M64 versus the automatic tile inside one wave |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| Shape grid: H1/H6/H12/H24, 64-4096 tokens, uniform and mixed packed, CP64/NoCP, logit and active beta | B200 (148 SM) | 369 | 290 | never slower beyond 2% noise; median 1.25x |
| Short grid: 8-65 tokens, same axes | B200 | 120 | 120 | min 1.01x, median 1.25x, max 5.71x |
| Shape grid | GB300 (152 SM) | 340 | 269 | never slower beyond 2% except 3 affine-eligible grids, which stay on the affine split; median 1.31x |

Outside one wave the direct tiles win (B200 H12 96x128: N16 24.7 us versus M64
34.3 us) and are retained. M64 output/state/checkpoint differ from the direct
tiles by at most 2.7e-4 / 4.8e-3 / 5.9e-3 (BF16 tolerance 1e-2).

title: SM120 DSV4 dual-cache prefill: instantiate CM family at TK ∈ {128,192,256,512} (backport of eb5f05be fix class)
body:
## 📌 Description

**Backport target: `release-v0.6.18`.** The SM120 DSV4 dual-cache sparse-MLA prefill dispatch compiles only for main topk=128. DeepSeek-V4's vision variant widens every prefill sliding-window index row from 128 to `128 + vision_max_n_token` (= 512 with `vision_max_n_token=384`) in `get_image_visible()`, so any VL prefill through this backend dies at engine init:

```
Unsupported sparse-MLA prefill configuration: model=DSV4 num_heads=32 topk=512 page_block_size=64 topk_extra=512 extra_page_block_size=64
```

Reproduces on the day-0 `vllm/vllm-openai:deepseekv4-flash-vision` image (vLLM 0.28.1rc1.dev137, flashinfer-python 0.6.18, DGX Spark GB10 / sm_121a). Text passes only because `max_image_tokens == 0` keeps main topk at 128.

The MG dual kernel uses `TOPK` only for the index-row stride and the runtime-length clamp: the KV pipeline is a 2-slot double buffer of BI=64-entry tiles and `SmemLayoutMG` has no TOPK parameter (101,008 B at any TK; SM121 allows 227 KiB opt-in). A wider TK costs nothing but loop trips. This PR instantiates the CM (runtime-length) family at TK ∈ {128, 192, 256, 512} with BF16 QK — the same numeric route main forces for every dual-cache shape (`QkBF16PvFP8` since eb5f05be).

**Relationship to main:** fixed on main by eb5f05be (#5197, planner rewrite, runtime topk) — main needs no change. This is the bounded backport for the 0.6.x line pinned by the day-0 DSV4-Vision image; no release contains the main-side fix (`git tag --contains eb5f05be` is empty).

**No behavior change at TK=128**: same template instantiation as before; FULLTILE (null-length callers) stays TK=128; decode untouched.

## 🔍 Related Issues
- Main-side fix: eb5f05be / #5197
- Prior 0.6.x topk work: #4380 (single-cache 192/256)

## 🚀 Pull Request Checklist
### ✅ Pre-commit Checks
- [x] `pre-commit run` on the changed files (clang-format, ruff, whitespace hooks all pass)

## 🧪 Tests
- [x] Tests added: `test_sparse_mla_sm120_prefill_dsv4_dual_wide_main_topk` (20 cases: topk 192/256/512 × extra 512 × extra-page 64/2 × heads {8,16,32,64,128}) and `test_sparse_mla_sm120_prefill_dsv4_dual_wide_main_topk_length_truncation` (per-row main+extra lengths, zero/non-tile-aligned rows, sink on/off)
- [x] `pytest tests/attention/test_sparse_mla_sm120.py -k "prefill_dsv4 or dsv4_public_api"`: **165 passed, 0 failed** on DGX Spark GB10 (sm_121a). Tests auto-skip off SM12x.

## Reviewer Notes

Numerics evidence (packed fp8 DSV4 caches, VL shape heads=32, topk=512, extra=512, runtime main+extra lengths, sink on/off):

| comparison | max_abs | max_rel | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| extended kernel vs slice-merge oracle (out) | 1.2e-4 | **0.0086** | exact LSE merge of 4×128-wide slices through the TK=128 kernel; the oracle's own bound is 1% |
| extended kernel vs fp32 dense reference (out) | 1.1e-3 | 0.105* | *BF16 output rounding at \|ref\|≈0.019; **identical max_abs on the stock TK=128 path** with the same inputs — baseline error class, not added error. Zero elements fail both rel>1% and abs>2e-3 |
| LSE vs reference | 2e-6 | — | sink on and off |
| TK=128 regression (text shape) | 1.1e-3 | 0.104 | unchanged baseline |

End-to-end: the day-0 VL image + this patch boots DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp (warmup prefill at topk=512 passes) and the vision smoke passes (image-token math 315∈[314,317] and 111∈[110,113] on controlled grids, image+text mix, text-only regression, 2-way concurrency).

The slice-merge oracle design is from vcruz305's `patch_dsv4_vl_sm120_wide_swa.py` (Apache-2.0) — used as the correctness reference; no code borrowed.

One convention note: fully empty rows (main_len=0 ∧ extra_len=0, no sink) report LSE=−1e30 per the kernel family's existing sentinel (`softmax_lse`, also asserted by the pre-existing dsv3_2 zero-length test); the new test expects that convention.

Perf: a VL prefill row costs 16 tile trips vs 10 for text (512+512 vs 128+512 entries) — inherent to the widened attention; no TK=128 regression (same instantiation).

title: [release-v0.6.18] fix(gemm): probe for CuTe DSL without importing cute_dsl.utils
body:
## 📌 Description

Cherry-pick of #4668 to `release-v0.6.18`.

`release-v0.6.18` carries #4526 as cherry-pick `d5e45b38` and therefore has the same unguarded import that has been breaking the nightly wheel builds on `main` since Aug 20:

```
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'cutlass'
```

`flashinfer/gemm/kernels/__init__.py` imports the CuTe DSL availability probe at module scope from `flashinfer/cute_dsl/utils.py`, which does an unconditional top-level `import cutlass`. The guard cannot be imported without the thing it guards, so the optional CuTe DSL becomes a hard requirement of plain `import flashinfer`.

Both wheel build backends import the package while building and neither declares `nvidia-cutlass-dsl` in `build-system.requires`:

- `flashinfer-cubin/build_backend.py:21` — `from flashinfer.artifacts import download_artifacts`
- `flashinfer-jit-cache/build_backend.py:121` — `from flashinfer import aot`

### Why this matters for the release

`release.yml` builds `flashinfer-cubin` and `flashinfer-jit-cache` with the same isolated `python -m build --wheel` the nightly uses, so **the v0.6.18 release build fails the same way without this.**

Affected tags, verified with `git merge-base --is-ancestor d5e45b38 <tag>`:

| tag | affected |
| --- | --- |
| `v0.6.18rc1` – `v0.6.18rc3` | no |
| `v0.6.18rc4` – `v0.6.18rc7` | **yes** |

The file is byte-identical to `main`'s pre-fix version, so both commits cherry-picked cleanly with no conflicts and no adaptation.

## 🔍 Related Issues

Cherry-pick of #4668. Refs #4651 — leaving the issue to be closed by the `main` PR.

## 🚀 Pull Request Checklist

### ✅ Pre-commit Checks

- [x] I have installed `pre-commit` by running `pip install pre-commit` (or used your preferred method).
- [x] I have installed the hooks with `pre-commit install`.
- [x] I have run the hooks manually with `pre-commit run --all-files` and fixed any reported issues.

## 🧪 Tests

- [ ] Tests have been added or updated as needed. — none added; see #4668 Reviewer Notes
- [x] All tests are passing (`unittest`, etc.).

### Test plan

Verified on this branch, not just inherited from #4668:

- **Without `cutlass`** (simulating the isolated build env by dropping the `nvidia_cutlass_dsl` entry from `sys.path`): both build-backend entry points import cleanly on this branch, and both fail on unpatched `v0.6.18rc7` (`3b3e688a`) with the reported traceback.
- **With `cutlass` installed:** `flashinfer.gemm.kernels.__all__` is identical between this branch and `rc7` — the same five names (`bmm_fp8_cute_dsl`, `cute_bmm_fp8_can_implement`, `SM107_AUTOTUNE_CONFIGS`, `get_valid_sm107_configs`, `PersistentDenseGemmKernel`).
- `pre-commit run --files flashinfer/gemm/kernels/__init__.py` — all hooks pass (mypy, ruff check, ruff format).

Repro:

```python
import importlib.util, sys
sys.path[:] = [p for p in sys.path if "nvidia_cutlass_dsl" not in p]
assert importlib.util.find_spec("cutlass") is None

from flashinfer.artifacts import download_artifacts   # flashinfer-cubin
from flashinfer import aot                            # flashinfer-jit-cache
```

## Reviewer Notes

Ordering is up to maintainers — this can land before #4668 if you want to unblock an rc8 sooner, since the two are independent and touch the same single file identically.

Note also that #4469 (open, targets `main`) works around the same failure by injecting `nvidia-cutlass-dsl` into both build backends' `get_requires_for_build_wheel`. If that approach is preferred over fixing the import, this cherry-pick becomes unnecessary — worth deciding before merging both.

title: feat(quantization): expose NVFP4 4over6 recipe through the public API
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

Partially addresses #5141 (fused-MoE kernels: see Related Issues).

NVFP4 "4over6" (#3264) was reachable only through four process-wide environment variables (`FLASHINFER_NVFP4_4OVER6*`). That makes the recipe implicit and process-global:

- a framework cannot express "this model uses 4over6 / MSE" in its own config.
- two models in one process cannot use different recipes.
- tests must mutate `os.environ`.

This PR makes the recipe an explicit argument on every NVFP4 quantization entry point and on the unified MoE `QuantConfig`, with the environment kept as a byte-for-byte compatible, **deprecated** fallback.

```python
from flashinfer import NVFP44Over6Config, make_nvfp4_global_scale, nvfp4_quantize

recipe = NVFP44Over6Config(e4m3_max=256, err_mode="MSE")
gs = make_nvfp4_global_scale(x, per_token_activation=True, nvfp4_4over6_config=recipe)
xq, sf, per_tok = nvfp4_quantize(x, gs, per_token_activation=True, nvfp4_4over6=recipe)

nvfp4_quantize(y, gs2, nvfp4_4over6=None)   # 4over6 off, env ignored
nvfp4_quantize(y, gs2)                      # omitted: legacy env read (+ FutureWarning when it enables 4over6)
```

`NVFP44Over6Config` fields, one per legacy variable:

- `e4m3_max` (448 or 256, `..._E4M3_USE_256`): top of the E4M3 block-scale range the global scale is built for. 256 leaves headroom so the 1.5x tighter `amax / 4` candidate stays representable.
- `err_mode` (`NVFP44Over6ErrMode.MAE` / `.MSE` or the strings `"MAE"` / `"MSE"`, `..._ERR_MODE`): metric that picks between the `amax / 6` and `amax / 4` candidates after quantize-dequantize. MSE penalizes the few clipped outliers harder, so it picks the tighter candidate less often.
- `err_use_fast_math` (`..._ERR_USE_FAST_MATH`): evaluate that error in fp16 instead of fp32. Cheaper, and a distinct recipe because near-ties can flip.

### One public type, three cases

`nvfp4_4over6` is `Optional[NVFP44Over6Config]`, the same two-state type the kernel drivers have always used internally (`None` = off). "Defer to the environment" is spelled by the *default value* (a private `_UNSET` sentinel), not by a third public type:

| `nvfp4_4over6=` | Meaning | Environment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| omitted (default) | legacy behaviour | read per call. `FutureWarning` when it turns 4over6 on |
| `None` | 4over6 off | ignored |
| `NVFP44Over6Config(...)` | on with exactly this recipe, no per-field merge | ignored |

When the environment shim is retired, the default flips to `None` and no signature changes. `make_nvfp4_global_scale` / `nvfp4_e4m3_max` take the resolved recipe as `nvfp4_4over6_config=` and never read the environment (their pre-existing contract).

### Data flow

- Python to kernel, in order:
  1. `resolve_nvfp4_4over6(setting)` → `Optional[NVFP44Over6Config]` (`None` = off). The only place that reads the environment.
  2. `nvfp4_4over6_code(config)` → one `int64` across the custom-op / TVM-FFI boundary: `-1` argument omitted (C++ reads the env), `0` off, bit 0 set = explicit recipe with bits 1..4 = `e4m3_max` / `err_mode` / `err_use_fast_math`.
  3. `resolveNVFP4Recipe(code)` → `NVFP4RecipeSpec`, the only thing the kernels read. Same recipe as `NVFP44Over6Config`. It carries a `use4Over6` flag so "off" is an ordinary struct instead of an optional. Encoder, decoder and bit layout: `csrc/nv_internal/tensorrt_llm/kernels/nvfp4Recipe.h`.
- Unified MoE: `QuantConfig.nvfp4_4over6` takes the same value. Runners opt in via `MoERunner.supports_nvfp4_4over6` and reject an explicit setting otherwise. `CuteDslRunner` honors it on the per-token path. `CuteDslConfig.prepare_weights(..., nvfp4_4over6=...)` pins the matching `fc2_input_scale`.

### Bugs fixed along the way

1. Autotuner replayed tactics across recipes: `MoERunner._cache_key_extras` now keys the **resolved** recipe.
2. `globalScaleInv` / `e4m3Max` desync in `trtllm_fused_moe_runner.cu`: one `NVFP4RecipeSpec` per launch.
3. Caller/callee recipe mismatch on the per-token global scale is now validated for explicit recipes.
4. The recipe-blind TMA CuTe-DSL kernel is no longer selected when a recipe is active.
5. `enable_pdl` landed in the wrong positional slot of `fp4_quantize` from `_fp4_quantize_custom_op`.
6. The four env vars are now documented in `CLAUDE.md` and enforced by `scripts/pr_checks/check_cross_sources.py`.

### Out of scope (still read the environment)

- CUTLASS fused MoE and TRT-LLM gen MoE (`trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe`): see Related Issues.
- `flashinfer/prims_ts/moe/runner.py` and the `moe_ep` bridge.
- `FLASHINFER_DISABLE_FP4_QUANT_FAST_MATH`: a separate debug knob, not part of the recipe.
- Trace templates.

Backends that have not opted in raise `NotImplementedError` on an explicit setting rather than ignoring it.

## 🔍 Related Issues

- Partially addresses #5141.
  - Done: `fp4_quantize`, `nvfp4_quantize`, `silu_and_mul_nvfp4_quantize` (CUDA and CuTe-DSL) and the CuTe-DSL MoE accept `nvfp4_4over6=`.
  - Not done: the CUTLASS fused MoE and the TRT-LLM gen fused MoE still read `FLASHINFER_NVFP4_4OVER6*` in their kernels (`TODO(aleozlx, #5141)`).
  - Follow-up PR: carry an `int64` recipe code in `MoERunnerArgs` (TRT-LLM gen) and `QuantParams::fp4` (CUTLASS), pass it as a trailing FFI argument, decode it with `resolveNVFP4Recipe()` at the two env-reading sites, then set `supports_nvfp4_4over6` on both runners with CuTe-DSL's per-token guard.
- Original 4over6 implementation: #3264. CuTe-DSL 4over6 and `NVFP44Over6Config`: #3448.

## 📌 Description

Add an explicit `vsa_sm90_blk64` backend for FP16/BF16 block-sparse attention on Hopper.

The SM90 host path follows the existing SM120 FP blk64 contract and reuses its Hopper-compatible warp-MMA/TMA kernel class. It adds SM90-specific runtime checks while keeping the existing SM120 host, kernel, and tests unchanged. The shared BSR planner now sizes each q2k row by its actual maximum nonzero count instead of the full KV-block count.

- SM90 `BlockSparseAttentionWrapper.plan()` and `run()` dispatch;

  --backends vsa_sm90_blk64,fa2

|---|---|---:|---:|
| FP16 | `vsa_sm90_blk64` | 5.106 ms | 315.2 TFLOPS |

title: feat(moe_ep): Support MiniMax-M3 MegaMoE

## 📌 Description

Integrate the MiniMax-M3 MegaMoE changes from NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM#18605 into FlashInfer's CuTe DSL NVFP4 MegaMoE backend. The backend now supports uniform `swiglu_alpha` / `swiglu_beta` constants and computes `(up + beta) * gate * sigmoid(alpha * gate)` after gate/up clamping. title: [blk64] Let the output TMA write BSHD directly instead of transposing…
body:
… afterwards

The kv_splits=1 path allocated a contiguous BHSD buffer for the kernel and then did `out_bhsd.transpose(1, 2).contiguous()`, with a second `copy_` on top whenever the caller passed `out`. At S=37759, h_local=14, d=128 that is a 135 MB full-tensor copy on every sparse-attention call.

The existing comment gave the reason as "a transposed view of `out` would hand the kernel a non-contiguous destination, which the upstream kernel does not expect". That turns out not to hold: the output TMA atom is built from mO's own layout (make_tiled_tma_atom in bsa_fwd_sm100.py), so a transposed view of a BSHD buffer is a legal destination under exactly the condition maybe_contiguous() already relies on for the Q/K/V loads -- head_dim innermost with stride 1, other strides 16B aligned. _bshd_out_is_tma_writable() checks that and falls back to a staging buffer otherwise.

The split-KV path is unchanged: its combine step produces a fresh contiguous BHSD tensor, so it still needs the transpose.

Verified bit-identical to the previous behaviour on production-shaped inputs (q/k/v as last-dim slices of one packed post-all-to-all buffer, S=37759 so the last 64-block is ragged): torch.equal True, checksum unchanged. Measured on B200, same shape: 2826.9 -> 2696.8 us per forward.

title: feat(prims-ts): Add balanced MLA decode scheduling
body:
## Summary

This PR adds a capture-stable, load-balanced scheduler for PrimsTS paged MLA decode. It supports both the 1CTA and 2CTA kernel families, BF16 and FP8 query/KV inputs, on-device schedule rebuilding inside CUDA graph replay, inactive graph-padding slots, and a production admission gate that selects ordinary PrimsTS when balanced scheduling is not expected to help or the current device has no registered calibration.

The new scheduler targets decode batches whose sequence lengths are highly uneven. In these batches, assigning each request as one indivisible unit leaves a long tail: most SM partitions finish their short requests while a few partitions remain occupied by the longest requests. The balanced scheduler splits only the requests that need it, distributes those pieces across the available partitions, and combines partial results for split requests.

The existing ordinary PrimsTS path remains available and is selected by `plan_auto()` whenever the balanced admission gate rejects the configuration.

The balanced kernel and scheduler was originally written by @leavelet (Yuanhang Sun) for trtllm-gen. This is a port to PrimsTS, specifically for MLA, with optimizations targeting this case. This PR does not handle GQA, but the implementation can be extended for it later (not in scope for this PR).

## Motivation

MLA decode work is approximately proportional to each request's KV length. Production batches can contain a mix of very short and very long sequences, so equal request counts do not imply equal work:

```text
request lengths: [512, 512, 512, ..., 131072]

request-level placement:
  partition 0: short request       ┐
  partition 1: short request       ├─ finish early
  ...                              │
  partition N: long request        ┘  determines launch latency

balanced placement:
  split the long request into costed pieces
  place all pieces and unsplit requests across physical partitions
  combine only the requests that were actually split
```

This is most valuable for ragged and production-distribution batches. Dense, nearly uniform batches do not provide work to redistribute and can be slower if forced through the balanced path. For that reason this PR exposes both force-balanced and production-auto planning APIs.

## Design

### Plan, schedule, run

`BatchMLADecodePagedTSWrapper` now supports a three-stage lifecycle:

1. `plan_balanced(...)` compiles the fixed kernel geometry, allocates or binds workspace, creates stable-address scheduler and descriptor tensors, and seeds the first schedule with the optimized CUDA scheduler.
2. `schedule(device_seq_lens)` reads live contiguous CUDA `int32` lengths and rewrites the descriptors in place. It is captured once before all compatible attention layers and executes on every graph replay without a host round trip.
3. `run(...)` launches attention using the published descriptors. With `validate=False`, both scheduling and execution are suitable for CUDA graph capture and replay.

`plan_auto(...)` applies the production gate and installs either a balanced or ordinary PrimsTS plan. If the gate admits balanced execution but the exact CUDA device has no registered cost-model calibration, it emits a `RuntimeWarning` and installs the ordinary plan. It returns `True` only when a balanced plan was installed and `False` when it installed the ordinary plan.

The schedule and workspace are mutable and must not be used concurrently. Compatible sequential layers can share one wrapper and one schedule, allowing frameworks to pay scheduling cost once per replay rather than once per layer. Independent execution streams need separate wrappers/workspaces or explicit ordering.

### Balanced schedule

The production CUDA scheduler:

- reads live sequence lengths and selects the calibrated workload bucket on device;
- expresses K work in CTA units of `num_instances_kv * tile_size_kv`, so pieces respect the amount of KV work one CTA instruction group actually consumes;
- evaluates aligned candidate target piece sizes using the calibrated latency model;
- keeps small requests whole when possible;
- splits expensive requests across the physical partitions;
- ranks the resulting pieces by modeled cost and folds them across partitions to reduce the predicted makespan;
- emits packed work descriptors ordered per partition; and
- emits a compact combine-descriptor list containing only split requests.

One-piece requests write directly to the public output and do not enter the reducer. Split requests write compact partial O/LSE state and are reduced once through the combine list.

Both balanced kernel families consume the same CUDA-emitted descriptor ABI. `scheduler="optimized"` is the two-kernel production rank-and-fold policy; `scheduler="exact"` is a deterministic four-kernel reference policy. These are the only placement implementations. Python owns the replay-stable tensors and checked-in calibration configuration, but descriptor placement and replay-time workload-bucket selection remain on device.

Native scheduler sources live under `csrc/prims_ts/`; the Python lifecycle, gate, cost model, documentation, and tuning tools live under `flashinfer/attention/prims_ts/balanced_scheduler/`.

### Kernel integration

Balanced scheduling is a compile-time specialization of the existing PrimsTS MLA kernels:

- 1CTA and 2CTA producers consume the packed descriptor queue;
- descriptor K ranges replace request-level static ranges only in balanced builds;
- split partials use compact addressing;
- reducers launch over the compact combine list;
- inactive requests with KV length zero are omitted from work and receive zero output; and
- ordinary scheduler paths compile the balanced branches out.

The implementation also includes correctness hardening for persistent work-tile replay, causal split boundaries, flat and packed query layouts, logical output strides, producer/reducer dependency ordering, bounded descriptor coordinates, checked scheduler workspace layout, and transactional plan replacement. Balanced and ordinary trace schemas remain distinct so balanced inactive slots are represented by the correct non-negative sequence-length constraint.

### CUDA graph behavior

Initial planning remains an eager operation because it compiles and allocates. Replay scheduling is a pair of CUDA nodes inside the captured graph. A balanced graph retains the wrapper, scheduler workspace, descriptors, metadata, live sequence-length storage, page table, and output storage for its lifetime. Before a replay whose KV lengths changed, the caller must:

1. update the existing CUDA `seq_lens` and page-table storage in place;
2. order those updates before replay; and
3. replay the graph, whose captured `schedule(validate=False)` rebuilds and publishes the schedule before the first compatible attention layer.

The default `optimized` scheduler performs no host copy or synchronization during replay. Its nonvalidating capture path publishes device error metadata instead of reusing a stale schedule if live lengths are invalid. Eager `schedule(validate=True)` remains available for synchronized validation and diagnostics. A balanced `run(validate=True)` requires the latest schedule call to have used `validate=True`; otherwise it raises rather than silently running without a sequence-length snapshot to compare against the live metadata.

Positive-to-zero, zero-to-positive, mostly inactive, all-inactive, and single-active transitions are covered for both BF16 and FP8.

## Production admission policy

The production gate is capture-stable: it uses deployment or graph-bucket declarations, never live replay lengths, to choose the captured kernel family. The caller provides:

```text
FLASHINFER_MLA_EXPECTED_MEAN_SEQ_LEN
FLASHINFER_MLA_EXPECTED_MAX_SEQ_LEN
```

or passes the equivalent arguments directly. Explicit arguments take precedence. Supported auto configurations require both declarations; missing, invalid, or inconsistent declarations raise `ValueError`. Unsupported shapes and dtype combinations route directly to ordinary PrimsTS without requiring declarations.

Balanced is selected only when:

```text
max_seq_len_q == 1
min(expected_max_seq_len, max_kv_len) >= 2 * expected_mean_seq_len
batch_size >= minimum_batch[heads, dtype]
expected_mean_seq_len * batch_size >= minimum_work[heads, dtype]
```

The B200 admission table is:

| Query heads | Dtype | Minimum batch | Minimum expected KV tokens |
|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 128 | BF16 | 2 | 8,192 |
| 64 | BF16 | 4 | 32,768 |
| 32 | BF16 | 2 | 131,072 |
| 16 | BF16 | 4 | 262,144 |
| 128 | FP8 | 4 | 131,072 |
| 64 | FP8 | 4 | 262,144 |
| 32 | FP8 | 4 | 262,144 |
| 16 | FP8 | 4 | 524,288 |

Unsupported query widths, dimensions, head counts, or dtype pairs select ordinary PrimsTS without requiring declarations. If the gate selects balanced but the exact device has no checked-in calibration, `plan_auto()` emits a `RuntimeWarning` and installs ordinary PrimsTS before balanced compilation or CUDA allocation.

`plan()` remains force-ordinary and `plan_balanced()` remains force-balanced for testing, tuning, and explicitly managed integrations. Unlike automatic planning, `plan_balanced()` is fail-closed and raises `NotImplementedError` when the exact device is not calibrated.

## Calibration tooling

The calibration and scheduler benchmarks are colocated with the implementation rather than in the repository-wide benchmark directory:

- `flashinfer/attention/prims_ts/balanced_scheduler/tune_cost_model.py` runs the production calibration workflow through `python -m flashinfer.attention.prims_ts.balanced_scheduler.tune_cost_model`; and
- `flashinfer/attention/prims_ts/balanced_scheduler/benchmark_scheduler.py` measures scheduler-only, attention-only, and scheduler-plus-attention graphs, or compares `exact` and `optimized` scheduling on identical draws.

The cost-model tuner is resumable and production-oriented. It:

- forces candidate targets through the production optimized CUDA scheduler and measures them with CUDA graph replay;
- records the complete emitted schedule and a schedule identity hash;
- separates immutable measurement identity from append-only fit generations;
- reinstalls the measured candidate schedule for paired validation; and
- emits source-ready calibrated coefficient tables.

The checked-in B200 v2 calibration contains:

- 752 successful forced-schedule measurements;
- 24 family/dtype/workload-bucket fits; and
- 54 paired finalist validations.

The worst finalist/measured-best ratio was `1.000464x`; none exceeded `1.01x`. There were no capacity, correctness, or execution failures during calibration.

## Performance

### Methodology

- GPU: NVIDIA B200, 148 SMs
- MLA dimensions: KV rank 512, RoPE dimension 64
- Kernel policies: H16 1CTA, tuned H64 automatic selection, and H128 2CTA
- Dtypes: BF16 and FP8 E4M3 for both query and KV
- Page size: 32
- Query length: 1
- Static matrix: 112 uniform and 140 ragged configurations
- Static batches: 8, 16, 64, and 128 for H16/H128; additionally 4 and 32 for H64
- Uniform KV lengths: 2K, 8K, 16K, and 128K
- Ragged batches: one long request and otherwise 512-token requests; long request 2K, 8K, 16K, 128K, or 512K
- Distribution matrix: RL and production distributions at batches 32, 64, and 128 for H16/H128, and batches 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128 for H64
- Distribution sampling: 100 deterministic samples per configuration, master seed `20260831`, identical sequence hashes for every compared mode
- Timing: H16/H128 use 10 graph warmups and the minimum of five trials of 200 captured replays; the H64 family-selection sweep uses five warmups and the minimum of three trials of 100 replays, with suspected outliers repeated using the stricter five-by-200 protocol

Attention latency excludes schedule construction. The device scheduler is captured before the first compatible attention layer and is measured separately from these kernel-family comparisons.

### Actual `plan_auto()` route versus ordinary PrimsTS

The following projects the implemented production gate onto the completed measurements. Admitted configurations use balanced PrimsTS; rejected configurations use the existing ordinary PrimsTS path. Speedups are configuration-level geometric means of ordinary PrimsTS latency divided by routed latency, so higher is faster.

| Workload | Configurations | Balanced route | Speedup over ordinary PrimsTS | Routed configurations >5% slower than ordinary |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| All | 300 | 103 | 1.66x | 0 |
| Static | 252 | 59 | 1.58x | 0 |
| Uniform | 112 | 0 | 1.00x | 0 |
| Ragged | 140 | 59 | 2.29x | 0 |
| RL | 24 | 22 | 1.79x | 0 |
| Production | 24 | 22 | 2.46x | 0 |

Forced balanced execution is not universally faster: the worst forced uniform regression in the original H16/H128 matrix was 40.24%. The concentration term rejects all 112 uniform configurations, and the complete routed policy has no configuration more than 5% slower than its actual ordinary-PrimsTS route.

### RL and production distributions

The benchmark labels refer to two synthetic discrete KV-length distributions. Each request in a sampled batch draws its length independently according to the relative weights below:

| Distribution | Sequence lengths in tokens | Relative weights |
|---|---|---|
| RL | 100, 1K, 2K, 3K, 10K, 30K, 50K, 100K, 110K | 7, 18, 200, 200, 400, 780, 600, 80, 65 |
| Production | 4K, 8K, 16K, 32K, 64K, 128K | 35, 20, 15, 12, 10, 8 |

Sampled lengths are rounded up to a multiple of 128 tokens before execution. Each distribution, batch size, kernel family, and dtype combination uses 100 batches generated with master seed `20260831`; both kernel modes receive identical batches.

The table covers 4,800 deterministic sampled batches. Every configuration-level routed result improves on or ties ordinary PrimsTS, and no routed configuration regresses by more than 5%. H64 BF16 B4 has a draw-level tail: 22/200 RL/production draws are more than 5% slower even though the two cell aggregates improve by 1.17x and 1.19x. Both the old and new H64 policies use 2CTA at B4, so this is an admission-gate limitation rather than a family-selection regression. Speedup is ordinary PrimsTS latency divided by the actual `plan_auto()` route, so higher is faster; the gate rejects balanced execution for H64 FP8 B4/B8, and those rows therefore use ordinary PrimsTS and report 1.00x by construction.

| Heads / selected family | Dtype | Distribution | Batch | Speedup over ordinary PrimsTS |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| H16 / 1CTA | BF16 | RL | 32 | 2.05x |
| H16 / 1CTA | BF16 | RL | 64 | 2.61x |
| H16 / 1CTA | BF16 | RL | 128 | 2.29x |
| H16 / 1CTA | BF16 | Production | 32 | 3.06x |
| H16 / 1CTA | BF16 | Production | 64 | 3.83x |
| H16 / 1CTA | BF16 | Production | 128 | 3.15x |
| H16 / 1CTA | FP8 | RL | 32 | 1.99x |
| H16 / 1CTA | FP8 | RL | 64 | 2.93x |
| H16 / 1CTA | FP8 | RL | 128 | 2.31x |
| H16 / 1CTA | FP8 | Production | 32 | 2.91x |
| H16 / 1CTA | FP8 | Production | 64 | 4.23x |
| H16 / 1CTA | FP8 | Production | 128 | 3.15x |
| H64 / 2CTA | BF16 | RL | 4 | 1.17x |
| H64 / 2CTA | BF16 | RL | 8 | 1.37x |
| H64 / 1CTA | BF16 | RL | 16 | 1.61x |
| H64 / 1CTA | BF16 | RL | 32 | 1.85x |
| H64 / 1CTA | BF16 | RL | 64 | 2.10x |
| H64 / 1CTA | BF16 | RL | 128 | 1.84x |
| H64 / 2CTA | BF16 | Production | 4 | 1.19x |
| H64 / 2CTA | BF16 | Production | 8 | 1.79x |
| H64 / 1CTA | BF16 | Production | 16 | 2.28x |
| H64 / 1CTA | BF16 | Production | 32 | 2.89x |
| H64 / 1CTA | BF16 | Production | 64 | 3.03x |
| H64 / 1CTA | BF16 | Production | 128 | 2.59x |
| H64 / gate rejected balanced | FP8 | RL | 4 | 1.00x |
| H64 / gate rejected balanced | FP8 | RL | 8 | 1.00x |
| H64 / 1CTA | FP8 | RL | 16 | 1.59x |
| H64 / 1CTA | FP8 | RL | 32 | 1.82x |
| H64 / 1CTA | FP8 | RL | 64 | 2.10x |
| H64 / 1CTA | FP8 | RL | 128 | 1.82x |
| H64 / gate rejected balanced | FP8 | Production | 4 | 1.00x |
| H64 / gate rejected balanced | FP8 | Production | 8 | 1.00x |
| H64 / 1CTA | FP8 | Production | 16 | 2.19x |
| H64 / 1CTA | FP8 | Production | 32 | 2.65x |
| H64 / 1CTA | FP8 | Production | 64 | 3.09x |
| H64 / 1CTA | FP8 | Production | 128 | 2.58x |
| H128 / 2CTA | BF16 | RL | 32 | 1.96x |
| H128 / 2CTA | BF16 | RL | 64 | 2.07x |
| H128 / 2CTA | BF16 | RL | 128 | 1.64x |
| H128 / 2CTA | BF16 | Production | 32 | 2.98x |
| H128 / 2CTA | BF16 | Production | 64 | 3.04x |
| H128 / 2CTA | BF16 | Production | 128 | 2.27x |
| H128 / 2CTA | FP8 | RL | 32 | 1.82x |
| H128 / 2CTA | FP8 | RL | 64 | 1.89x |
| H128 / 2CTA | FP8 | RL | 128 | 1.53x |
| H128 / 2CTA | FP8 | Production | 32 | 2.71x |
| H128 / 2CTA | FP8 | Production | 64 | 2.78x |
| H128 / 2CTA | FP8 | Production | 128 | 2.08x |

### Replay scheduler latency

The synchronous host `replan()` path has been removed. Production uses the two-kernel `optimized` CUDA scheduler captured before the first compatible attention layer. The following B200 measurements use H128/2CTA, page size 64, and 100 deterministic RL and production draws for both BF16 and FP8. Each range is the minimum and maximum across the four dtype/distribution cells at that batch size.

| Batch | Scheduler p50 range | Scheduler p95 range |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 32 | 20.629-24.760 us | 24.714-28.782 us |
| 64 | 22.694-30.784 us | 24.752-30.893 us |
| 128 | 24.747-33.057 us | 26.797-34.982 us |

These timings include both CUDA scheduler kernels and their dependency gap. They exclude a separate graph-launch charge because production captures the scheduler as nodes in the graph that already contains the first attention call. Scheduler-only time and measured scheduler-plus-attention minus attention-only time agree within a few microseconds. The cost is therefore on the replay critical path, but it is paid once per compatible layer group rather than once per layer; there are no sequence-length D2H copies, descriptor H2D copies, Python normalization, or host synchronization on replay.

### Ordinary-path neutrality

Ordinary PrimsTS was compared with the pre-feature baseline on six deterministic CUDA-graph anchors. Outputs and private LSE were bitwise identical in every case. Five anchors ranged from 3.74% faster to 0.91% slower. A repeated alternating-order q64 FP8 stress test measured approximately 0.3% overhead from the required per-work-tile scratch reset.

## Correctness and validation

- All 132 H64 family-selection acceptance cells completed without an execution or correctness error
- Representative H64 maximum absolute difference: `0.001937866` for BF16 and `0.006439209` for FP8
- Balanced CUDA scheduler suite: 63 passed
- Complete balanced MLA attention subset: 54 passed
- Focused family/dtype/crossover execution matrix: 10 passed
- CUDA graph replay coverage for BF16/FP8, 1CTA/2CTA, fixed and packed queries, inactive slots, compact reduction, and persistent multi-descriptor queues
- Ruff, mypy, clang-format, `git diff --check`, and pre-commit hooks passed

## Public API example

```python
import torch

from flashinfer.attention.prims_ts import BatchMLADecodePagedTSWrapper

wrapper = BatchMLADecodePagedTSWrapper()

selected_balanced = wrapper.plan_auto(
    device=query.device,
    batch_size=batch_size,
    num_heads=num_heads,
    kv_lora_rank=512,
    qk_rope_head_dim=64,
    page_size=page_size,
    max_kv_len=max_kv_len,
    max_seq_len_q=1,
    packed_query=False,
    q_data_type=query.dtype,
    kv_data_type=kv_cache.dtype,
    o_data_type=torch.bfloat16,
    seq_lens=host_seq_lens,
    expected_mean_seq_len=expected_mean_seq_len,
    expected_max_seq_len=expected_max_seq_len,
    workspace_buffer=workspace,
)

# Validate and warm the selected route before capture.
if selected_balanced:
    wrapper.schedule(device_seq_lens)

wrapper.run(
    query,
    kv_cache,
    block_tables,
    device_seq_lens,
    out=output_buffer,
)

# Capture scheduling once before all compatible attention layers. The
# scheduler nodes rebuild the descriptors from live device lengths on replay.
graph = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
with torch.cuda.graph(graph):
    if selected_balanced:
        wrapper.schedule(device_seq_lens, validate=False)

    output = wrapper.run(
        query,
        kv_cache,
        block_tables,
        device_seq_lens,
        out=output_buffer,
        validate=False,
    )

# Between completed replays, update stable runtime metadata in place.
device_seq_lens.copy_(next_device_seq_lens)
block_tables.copy_(next_block_tables)
graph.replay()
```

## Current limitations

- The production auto gate is limited to single-token decode. Q2/speculative-decode tuning is deferred.
- Balanced auto execution currently requires the checked-in exact-device calibration; this PR provides B200/SM100/148-SM calibration and intentionally fails on an uncalibrated device.
- Public PrimsTS MLA execution returns O but does not expose graph-stable LSE, so DCP/LSE integrations need an API extension.
- A possible ordinary `plan_auto()` route requires positive dummy KV lengths and valid pages. Zero-length graph-padding slots are supported by balanced plans; framework integrations should resolve the capture-stable route before choosing their padding convention.
- CSR/page-size-1 integrations are outside the dense paged-table contract used here.
- The protected-P producer optimization could not be expressed through the current task-scheduler abstraction and is not included. It is a performance follow-up, not a correctness or integration requirement.

## Follow-up integration

The intended serving integration owns one wrapper per static CUDA-graph bucket and execution lane, captures `schedule(validate=False)` immediately before the first compatible attention layer, and shares the published schedule across subsequent sequential layers. Updating the stable device metadata followed by graph replay then rebuilds the schedule without CPU intervention. vLLM integration is intentionally separate from this PR.


## 🚀 Pull Request Checklist

Thank you for contributing to FlashInfer! Before we review your pull request, please make sure the following items are complete.

- [x] All tests are passing (`unittest`, etc.).

  * Added automatic eligibility detection and public planning, scheduling, and plan-inspection APIs.

title: perf(mega_moe): SM90 fp8 megamoe optimization
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

### What this PR changes

Syncs the `sm90_fp8_fp8_bf16_pull_cutedsl` kernel tree with the kernel team's latest Hopper FP8 drop and wires the new knobs through the shim / backend (three commits on top of `main`):

1. **Tail-split pair tasks, per-bucket `group_hint`, FC2 16-byte stores** (kernel tree + shim):
  - `tail_split_pairs`: an expert whose token count is an odd number of CTA tiles used to leave the second CTA of its tail cluster block idle; the scheduler now turns that block into pair tasks (both CTAs compute the single valid token tile against adjacent weight tiles, weights loaded through a second non-multicast TMA atom).  Legal only with a 2-CTA token cluster (swap-AB cga (1,2,1) / non-swap cga (2,1,1)); the dispatch-driven token-back expects `ceil(W/2)` fc2_done publishes per split tail.
  - `group_hint` (scheduler group size) becomes a per-bucket entry of the heuristic table (264 on per_tensor 512-8192, blockwise 512-2048 / 8192); FC2 epilogue writes 16-byte stores on the non-swap and swap-AB local paths.
  - heuristic table retuned: per_tensor 1024-32768 -> swap-AB ping-pong M128N128 cga(1,2,1) with tail split (2048-8192 with group_hint), blockwise 1024-8192 -> epi_warps with group_hint 264, blockwise 32 / 8192 with tail split.
  - shim/backend: new `tail_split_pairs` config field (None = table value), `group_hint` / `tail_split_pairs` resolved from the heuristic row through `tuner.default_knobs` (dropped when a knob-cache / `knobs=` entry moves the geometry), autotune candidates carry them (19 geometries x 2 token-back modes = 38), bench CSV records them; multirank `tail_split_pairs` cases (both layouts x both token-back placements at an odd CTA-tile count) and the drop's scheduler-contract test.
  - same-node 2-round A/B vs `main`: e2e geomean **+6.0%** (per_tensor +8.3%: pt1024 +21%, pt2048 +29%, pt4096 +27%, pt8192 +18%, pt32768 +11%; blockwise +3.7%: bw1024 +20%, bw2048 +18%, bw8192 +7%), no bucket below −1%.
2. **Fused swap-AB `generate_c` store**: the raw gate/up values are stored per token group inside the SwiGLU pass from the already scaled registers (`cvt.rn.bf16x2`, lane transpose, one 16-byte store) instead of a separate pass that kept all 128 accumulators live and made the M128N128 ping-pong kernel spill.  generate_c overhead on the new per_tensor 2048-32768 rows 5.9-16.3% -> 1.0-3.1% (per_tensor geomean 5.1% -> 1.1%); the generate_c=off kernels are unchanged (same-node off-vs-off within ±1.6%), so the per_tensor 16384 training override is removed again.

3. **`group_hint` 264 on the small buckets (8-256)**: at these token counts a launch is one pass over the active experts' weights; with the one-wave scheduler group the FC2 tiles of an expert are handed out right behind its 48 FC1 tiles and the activation TMA producer spends ~25% of its time in the fc2 fc1_done spin (kernel team's IKET trace).  Six experts per group removes it.  Same-node 2-round A/B vs the 2026-09-18 table: e2e geomean +3.7% (pt16 +13%, pt64 +10%, pt128 +14%, bw32 +18%, bw256 +19%, the other small buckets +2..+5%; 512 and up unchanged).

Docs: `TUNING.md` refreshed (tables, same-node before/after, knob entries).



### Pull backend sweep performance

**Environment.**  1 node, 4x NVIDIA H200 141GB (sm_90, SM clock locked at 1830 MHz) over NVLink, EP=4; Python 3.12, torch 2.12.0+cu130, nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.7.0, nvshmem4py-cu13.  All numbers in this document (the sweep below and the pull/push comparison in the next section) were taken in one session (2026-09-19) on that node, back to back, with the current heuristic table and knob defaults (`tail_split_pairs` / `group_hint` from the table, `compact_pull_buffer` on).  Same clock lock as the 2026-09-12 revision of this page, so the tables are comparable bucket by bucket up to the usual ~2% node-to-node offset; the code-attributable changes are the same-node A/Bs quoted in section 1 (e2e geomean +6.0% and +3.7%).

**Method.**  `torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 benchmarks/bench_moe_ep_sm90_mega.py` (defaults): DeepSeek-V4-Pro geometry (384 experts, top-6, hidden 7168, intermediate 3072), heuristic launch config per point, block-permutation balanced routing, drop perf data recipe, 5 s cooldown before each timed series, warmup 3 + 20 barrier-aligned CUDA-event iterations.

- **Setup.**  Same environment and geometry as section 2; a standalone comparison harness times the full `MoEEpLayer.forward` for both backends with identical inputs (same seeds, same balanced routing) at their own DEFAULT knobs, one torchrun invocation per backend (the two communication runtimes are kept in separate processes). title: perf(moe-a2a): reuse dispatch receive views instead of rebuilding them per call
body:
<!-- .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

`moe_a2a_dispatch` rebuilds its receive views on every call:

```python
for input_payload, offset, size in zip(input_payloads, recv_offsets, recv_sizes, strict=True):
    output_payloads.append(
        moe_a2a_wrap_payload_tensor_in_workspace(
            workspace, [ep_size, runtime_max_tokens_per_rank], offset, offset + size,
            input_payload.dtype))
```

and each `moe_a2a_wrap_payload_tensor_in_workspace` performs four tensor-creating operations
per payload — `view(uint8)` → slice → `view(dtype)` → `view(shape)`. A BF16 MoE dispatch ships
three payloads (activation, expert ids, weights), so that is **twelve tensor constructions per
dispatch**, on every iteration, each costing Python plus a PyTorch dispatcher round trip.

The view is a pure function of `(ep_size, runtime_max_tokens_per_rank, offset, size, dtype)`,
all constant across calls at a given `runtime_max_tokens_per_rank`. The returned tensor is a
**view onto the persistent workspace**, so a reused view still observes the bytes written by the
current call — only the Python-side reconstruction is skipped.

This PR adds an optional `recv_view_cache` argument to `moe_a2a_dispatch` and has
`MoeAlltoAll` own the cache.

Two deliberate choices:

- **Opt-in.** `recv_view_cache` defaults to `None`, which preserves today's behaviour exactly,
  so direct callers of the free function are unaffected.
- **Instance-owned, not module-level.** The cache lives on `MoeAlltoAll`, which keeps
  `self.workspace` alive. A module-level cache keyed on a data pointer could alias a
  freed-and-reallocated workspace.

## 🔍 Results

Measured on 8 × B200, EP8 single node, NVLink scale-up, bf16 dispatch, `hidden=7168`,
`top_k=6`, 384 routed experts, 2048 samples per point. Chained dispatch→combine period, p50:

| tokens/rank | before | after | delta |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 62.8 µs | **47.8 µs** | −15.0 µs |
| 2 | 62.1 µs | **51.4 µs** | −10.7 µs |
| 8 | 62.7 µs | **51.8 µs** | −10.9 µs |
| 32 | 62.0 µs | **53.8 µs** | −8.2 µs |
| 64 | 62.1 µs | **55.9 µs** | −6.2 µs |
| 128 | 64.1 µs | 64.0 µs | −0.1 µs |
| 512 | 123.6 µs | 123.5 µs | −0.1 µs |

The saving appears **only while the host is the bottleneck**. Below ~64 tokens/rank the GPU work
per iteration is short enough that dispatch-side Python sits on the critical path; above it the
same work overlaps GPU execution and is already hidden. That is the expected shape for removing
host work, and it targets exactly the MoE **decode** regime.

For scale: CUDA graph replay of the same case is 38.4 µs at T=1, so this recovers **61% of the
eager-to-graph gap** without requiring graph capture.

## 🧪 Validation

- Correctness checked at every point above against an implementation-independent
  dispatch/combine oracle (two-level reduction, FP32 intra-domain); all points passed.
- The same change was measured twice by independent means — once as a runtime monkeypatch of
  `moe_a2a_wrap_payload_tensor_in_workspace`, once as this patch applied to the installed
  package — agreeing to 0.1 µs at T=1 (47.9 vs 47.8 µs).
- Numbers above were taken on 0.6.8.post1 plus this patch, since that is the version in the
  container used for the measurement. The changed code path is identical on `main`.

I was not able to run `tests/comm/test_mnnvl_moe_alltoall.py` in this environment (it needs an
`mpi4py` multi-rank harness I did not have set up); happy to add a unit test for the cache-hit
path if you would like one, or to adjust the design — e.g. keying the cache differently, or
placing it on `_A2AState` instead.

## 🔗 Related

Follow-ups I did not include here, in case they are of interest:

- `moe_a2a_combine` allocates a fresh output tensor per call when `output=None`;
  `moe_a2a_combine_into` with a caller-owned persistent buffer already avoids this.
- `get_moe_alltoall_module(backend)` is resolved per call in both dispatch and combine, though
  the result is constant for the lifetime of a `MoeAlltoAll` instance.

## 🚀 Pull Request Checklist

- [x] I have read and followed the [Contributor Guidelines](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [x] The change is backwards compatible (new argument defaults to `None`)
- [x] Performance impact measured and reported above
- [ ] Unit test for the cache-hit path — happy to add on request


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Performance**
  * Improved Mixture-of-Experts dispatch efficiency by reusing receive-tensor views across calls when workspace data remains valid.
  * Automatically refreshes cached views when the underlying workspace changes, preventing stale references.
  * Preserved existing behavior when view caching is not enabled.

* **API**
  * Added an optional receive-view cache parameter to the dispatch interface, allowing applications to control reuse across calls.
  * Documented the cache’s workspace lifetime requirements.

title: feat(cake_kda): add TF32 and BF16 prefill kernels for SM100a and SM103a
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

Adds prepared KDA inference APIs backed by generated native CUDA kernels, with
separate TF32 and BF16 computation modes:

| Public API | Computation mode | Generated targets in this candidate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `flashinfer.prepare_tf32_kda_prefill(...)` | TF32 | SM100a and SM103a |
| `flashinfer.prepare_bf16_kda_prefill(...)` | Native BF16 | SM100a and SM103a |

Both APIs use BF16 Q/K/V and output, FP32 external initial/final recurrent state,
and BF16 checkpoints. The computation mode selects the corresponding native
kernel family. The supported head dimension is 128. The TF32 path uses Tensor Core
TF32 multiplication with FP32 accumulation; FP32 recurrent state does not imply
full-precision FP32 multiplication. Export preserves the source computation mode.

Preparation compiles the selected kernels on first use and allocates reusable
workspace and launch metadata. The returned object's `launch()` submits the
complete operation on the current stream and supports caller-owned CUDA Graph
capture. Tensor storage must remain alive at the same addresses for the lifetime
of the prepared call. These APIs are inference-only.

- Packed variable-length sequences use host-provided `sequence_lengths` matching
  `cu_seqlens`, with optional indexed state pools and BF16 checkpoints.
- Beta inputs may be BF16 logits or active FP32 probabilities selected with
  `beta_is_logit=False`.
- BF16 routes requiring logits refresh reusable buffers with
  `logit(eps=1e-6)` followed by a BF16 copy on every launch, including graph
  replay. Padded or strided beta storage preserves the logical token extent.
- JIT dispatch selects generated modules for the actual GPU architecture.

Native BF16 export is complete on both architectures. The combined candidate
`80bb132ed62a` contains the regenerated TF32 exports, BF16 inverse-fragment repair,
packed state/checkpoint scaling, the SM103 packed-product/FTZ-predicate update,
and packed triangular scaling for one SM100 TF32 module. All seven shapes
using that changed module select their new formal outcome, including failures.
The other 1,377 cells retain their actual measured revisions, hardware and timing protocols;
exact module, binding and common-dependency identities support their inheritance.
This is one combined implementation with mixed measurement provenance, not
1,384 fresh measurements of the combined commit. No fixed-clock policy was adopted.

All original and preceding C/D/R evidence remains visible. The earlier quiet,
paired and null controls select no formal cells; rejected inverse-FMA and clock
experiments do not alter acceptance. A passing new observation does not establish
the cause of the historical regression or drift. There is no repeat-until-pass
or fastest-run selection. Raw gate failures remain visible; the four current D
exceptions accepted for submission are recorded below.
The tables compare each recorded export measurement with its corresponding
source implementation and pinned Triton baseline.

CI follow-up `cd0088a73a55` fixes only a stale selector-test route. Kernel implementation and measured performance remain those of `80bb132ed62a`.

with no missing cells. The denominator remains 346 shapes × SM100/SM103 × TF32/BF16.

The pinned Triton implementation uses FP32 live and external recurrent state.
Current numerical acceptance rejects NaN/Inf and retains source/export equality,

### Per-shape speedup vs. SGLang FLA Triton baseline

Pinned baseline: SGLang FLA Triton `chunk_kda` at `24c9251ac52ada1660f372922c72c1d3af722247`. TF32/BF16 are computation modes; both use FP32 recurrent state and BF16 Q/K/V, outputs and CP64 checkpoints.

Each hardware/mode has a **`T/E;Δ%`** column and a separate **speedup** column, e.g. **1.84x**. T and E are the pinned Triton baseline and export medians from the same paired comparison in **μs**. **Speedup = T/E** (higher is faster; below 1x is slower than Triton). Δ is 100×(export/source−1), in **percent**, from the separate source/export paired run, not the Triton comparison; per-cell % signs are omitted.
